articles.title: Live: Russia hits Kyiv’s Southern Bridge again as Moscow continues to pound capital
articles.body:
Live: Kyiv in ‘very dramatic situation’ as Russia steps up bombing, mayor says
Kyiv is in a “very dramatic situation”, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Friday, as Russia pummelled key infrastructure across the capital. Russian drones hit Kyiv’s Southern Bridge for a fourth time in 24 hours, forcing authorities to close traffic on it. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
Kyiv's mayor says Russian strikes are tearing the capital apart
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Ukrainian capital was in a "very dramatic situation" as Russia stepped up its deadly barrages.
"The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it's no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime," Klitschko said on Telegram.
"The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart," he added.
Polish city reopens Cold War shelter as Russian attacks in Ukraine intensify
The Polish city of Lublin has revived a Cold War-era air raid shelter as Russia steps up attacks in Ukraine, with one symbolic change reflecting a shift in perceived threats: its emergency exit now faces west, not east.
Poland is currently on heightened alert after several Russian missile and drone incursions into its airspace. Residents of eastern regions have been issued warnings to seek shelter during Russian airstrikes on neighbouring western Ukraine.
One of the shelters available during recent alerts is a modernised facility beneath the premises of municipal bus operator MPK in Lublin. Built in the mid-1980s at the height of Cold War tensions, it was upgraded to meet current standards.
“It provides shelter for 200 people for up to 72 hours, ensuring access to air, water and electricity independent of external power grids,” Kamil Rzad, a civil defence inspector at MPK Lublin, told Reuters.
The number of shelters is estimated by the government at around 2,000, enough for about 300,000 people. Poland also has over 86,000 places of refuge offering a lower level of protection such as basements, underground garages or subway stations, and catering for around 23 million people.
Seoul's anger with Kyiv over POWs may be driven by worries about ties with NKorea
While Ukraine may have revealed its transfer of North Korean POW’s to Ukraine to garner public support in the northeastasian country, Seoul’s anger may be explained by fears that it will further deteriorate its ties with Pyongyang.
The North Korean soldiers’ transfer could complicate Seoul’s push for talks with Pyongyang, because North Korea has previously reacted with fury to defections of its citizens and accused the South of kidnapping them.
“Our government’s policy is restoring severed dialogue with North Korea and easing tensions ... So it wanted to handle the POW issue in a low-key manner,” said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has said his government has been making coordination efforts to resume talks between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump, hoping that would help restart its own talks with the North and boost peace on the Korean Peninsula.
Traffic chaos in Kyiv after Russian drone strikes on bridge
Traffic has come to a standstill in Kyiv after one of the city’s main bridges was closed and restrictions were placed on others after another wave of deadly Russian drone strikes.
Long queues of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads in the Ukrainian capital as commuters sought alternative routes – or even made their way on foot.
“I’ve been travelling for three hours... to get to work,” said Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam. “It’s impossible to cross the bridges today,” she said.
Ukraine has long feared an attack on its major transportation bridges since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukraine denies F-16 crisis over maintenance and parts
Ukraine denies that it is facing maintenance and supply problems with its F-16 fighter jets, insisting it can keep them in the air throughout winter.
The Wall Street Journal reported this week that delays in maintenance and a shortage of parts had grounded more than half of Ukraine’s fleet, and all of its US-made aircraft could be affected by the year-end.
Foreign ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhy acknowledged that Ukraine’s F-16s operate “intensively and under demanding conditions” and maintenance was “challenging”.
“Certain components for this early F-16 variant are no longer in production and are becoming increasingly difficult to source,” he wrote on X. “However, recent reports alleging catastrophically low aircraft availability rates and excessively long maintenance turnaround times are simply false,” he added.
Ukraine hits oil facilities in Russia’s Samara and Volgograd regions, Zelensky says
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had hit oil facilities in Russia’s Samara and Volgograd regions.
He also announced “successful operations” against the enemy in the Black Sea and in the Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, and Krasnodar regions, “targeting airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a missile and space center, and an ammunition depot belonging to the occupiers”.
Zelensky calls for more sanctions as Russia ‘critically dependent’ on foreign components for drones
In his post on X, Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelensky also noted that regardless of how hard Moscow tries to localise its production of drones and missiles “its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components”.
“These are supply chains running from Europe, the United States, China, Japan, and many other countries,” he wrote.
“Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia. Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line,” he said, calling for tougher santions.
Russia also destroyed Kherson kindergarten in latest attacks, Zelensky says
“Last night, the Russians launched more than 100 attack drones at Ukraine, nearly 50 of them jet-powered, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X, saying that although Ukraine managed to destroy “most of them” there were also hits, including the deadly one on a Kyiv apartment building.
“In Kherson, the Russians ‘defeated’ a kindergarten”, he said, “in Kharkiv, they attacked a grocery store, and an institute and critical infrastructure were damaged. Enemy strikes also hit apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy. The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava, and Rivne regions also came under attack.”
Russia says company in Tuapse slightly damaged in drone attack
Company facilities in the Russian town of Tuapse in the southern Krasnodar region has been slightly damaged by drone debris, local authorities said, without providing details.
The Black Sea port town of Tuapse hosts an oil refinery and port facilities, including a sea grain terminal.
Second bridge shut in Russian strikes on Kyiv
Following full closure of Kyiv's Southern Bridge, another – Paton Bridge, located further north, has had traffic restricted, according to reports by authorities.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Southern Bridge, which connects the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro river, was "completely closed" to traffic in both directions.
The Paton Bridge, was only open one way, he added, but there were no reports that it had been hit.
Russian drones target Southern Bridge 'four times in 24 hours'
In the past 24 hours, Russian drones have struck Kyiv’s Southern Bridge a total of four times, FRANCE 24’s Ukraine correspondent Gulliver Cragg said, noting “they keep hitting it in the same place”.
Cragg said it is one of Kyiv’s eight bridges and is very important for the city.
Watch his full report in the video below.
Hungary welcomes Ukraine’s bill strengthening Hungarian minority right
Hungary welcomes Ukraine’s move to submit to parliament draft legislation that strengthens the education rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.
“The bill strengthens the legal guarantees of education in the Hungarian language, and the network of educational institutions,” Magyar said in a Facebook post.
Kremlin says cutting weapons and fuel supplies to Ukraine via Black Sea is key priority
Russia aims to completely halt supplies of weapons and fuel to the Ukrainian military via the Black Sea, the Kremlin said.
“It is very important for us to completely halt maritime deliveries to Ukraine of military equipment, ammunition, fuel for the armed forces of Ukraine, and the like – actions that are currently under way and will continue,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Russia has repeatedly rejected the idea of a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea, where both sides have escalated attacks since July on shipping, ports and energy terminals.
Read more: Russia’s ahead-of-winter attacks on Ukraine’s power grid have begun
Russia says it also struck electrical substation in Kyiv region, port facility in Odesa region
Russia’s defence ministry said the country’s forces had also struck an electrical substation in the Kyiv region with the help of drones as well as an industrial complex at Izmail port in the Odesa region.
The ministry said the Izmail facility handled military cargo and fuel supplies for the Ukrainian military.
It also said a dry cargo vessel carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to the port of Odesa was hit in the Black Sea.
South Korea warns of ‘further measures’ unless Ukraine apologises over POW disclosure
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said that Seoul would take “further measures” if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean POWs being sent to South Korea.
Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia’s war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.
Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, South Korea’s Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs’ relatives.
“If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures,” the South Korean president said, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a “liar”. “This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked,” he said in a post on social media.
At least one person killed in Russian attack on Kyiv apartment building
At least one person has been killed and two people have been injured after a Russian attack on a Kyiv apartment building, authorities said on Telegram.
Russian drones hit Southern Bridge in Kyiv again, mayor says
Russian drones have again hit the Southern Bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge and another one, the Paton Bridge, was closed in both directions, authorities said, as they were redirecting transports via alternative routes.
Klitschko also said Russian drones had smashed into a school, and that the attacks had triggering fires in the city.
Good morning and welcome to our liveblog on the war in Ukraine.
(FRANCE 24 with AP, AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says new ballistic missile used in combat
articles.body:
- 
  Ukraine used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Writing on Telegram on Thursday, the Ukrainian president said: “First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next – production.” He did not say where or how the FP-7 had been used. The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme, called Freyja, launched this year. Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km (125 miles), likening it to the US army Tactical Missile System but much cheaper. Ukraine – whose missile production is well behind Russia’s – has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element of its response to Russia’s frequent use of them in its attacks.
- 
  Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and an important bridge over the Dnipro River on Thursday, triggering fires in the capital, officials said. The school was struck early in the morning, but all the students were in a shelter and no injuries were reported, city authorities said. As Russian forces engaged in almost non-stop attacks on the city, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two drones hit the Southern Bridge around noon. A new strike late in the evening damaged a support, part of the road surface and protective structures around the metro crossing the bridge. On Wednesday, Russian forces unleashed what Ukrainian officials described as the start of a cold-weather strike campaign against Ukraine’s power grid.
- 
  Meanwhile, Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. He added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Ukraine also attacked the Russian city of Volgograd, home to a large oil refinery, with drones targeting industrial facilities, Governor Andrei Bocharov said on Telegram on Friday. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
- 
  Europe has become increasingly dependent on US fuel after banning Russian imports because of the war and after the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted supplies from the Middle East. The Trump administration has told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease soaring global fuel prices or face a potential US diesel export ban, according to three people close to the discussions.
- 
  At a Group of 20 meeting this week, trade ministers agreed it was “not acceptable” for countries to target food supplies in conflicts, France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier said on Thursday, adding that European leaders took aim at Russia on the issue. Forissier’s comments come as trade ministers from the G20 met for a second day in the midwestern US city of Milwaukee, where European officials criticised Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s grain sector. Forissier said European leaders’ comments against “the aggression of Russia in Ukraine” on food exports merely constituted “the truth”.
- 
  Moscow warned Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave and seaport located on the Baltic Sea, should any members of the military alliance try to cut it off. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”. Asked on Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with Nato or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.”
- 
  Putin said also on Thursday Russian assets of western companies that Moscow had seized could be returned in a “favourable scenario”. Last month, the Russian president ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro. He also said Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted Ukraine to be a neutral country after the end of hostilities.

articles.title: Russia tries to freeze Ukraine as it suffers record casualties and retreats
articles.body:
Russia tries to freeze Ukraine as it suffers record casualties and retreats
Moscow has suffered further losses of occupied territory, but is using new drones to beat Ukraine’s defences ahead of winter.
Russia suffered its highest losses of 2026 in September, when 46,230 of its soldiers were killed or wounded, according to the Ukrainian military.
The new record comes after Russian casualties of about 40,000 a month since June, and is close to the goal Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set in January of 50,000 Russian casualties a month. Russia reportedly lost 2,090 troops on September 28 – its highest 24-hour casualty rate of the war.
Al Jazeera cannot verify casualty claims from either side. Ukraine says it has video of each casualty, as more than 90 percent of them are caused by first-person view (FPV) drones.
But despite setbacks, Russia has been trying to seize the remaining areas of Ukraine’s eastern regions of Luhansk and Donetsk that it doesn’t control — which is where casualties have been heaviest.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has inflicted particularly heavy losses in the area around Lyman, where the third phase of a counteroffensive called Operation Vivaldi has reclaimed 176sq km (68sq miles) of territory in recent weeks.
Corps commander Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky said it succeeded by feigning an attack from the west, and “forced it [the Russian army] to senselessly burn through its reserves in counterattacks precisely in that direction”. Then it attacked from the north.
Among its tactics was the use of remotely operated Russian armoured personnel carriers filled with explosives that smashed into Russian defences.
A Ukrainian commander on the Lyman front described how Vivaldi’s first phase eliminated a vanguard of Russian soldiers. Ukrainian drone operators have also been busy disrupting Russian ammunition and fuel supplies, starving the front.
Russia denied the Ukrainian counteroffensive’s gains, posting videos as purported evidence.
Russia has frequently claimed to hold positions and gain territory. But assessments by the Institute for the Study of War and DeepState, organisations that track territorial gains using open source, geolocated footage, rarely reflect Russian claims on their maps.
The ISW has estimated Russia’s net gains this year at 148sq km (57sq miles), nowhere near the 5,300sq km that Russia claims.
Russia pounds Kyiv
Still, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities during the past week, striking energy infrastructure but also residential buildings, kindergartens, schools, office buildings and other nonmilitary targets.
Several people were killed on September 28, when a drone destroyed part of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv.
Kyiv experienced power outages on September 30, when Russian drones struck a thermal power plant in the Kyiv region. At least five people were killed across the country.
“Since the summer, there has not been a single day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. However, such a massive and combined attack has not occurred since the end of the last heating season,” wrote Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi on social media.
Zelenskyy has warned for weeks that Russia intends to strike Ukraine’s energy sector hard to cause suffering this winter.
On September 30, Russia also tested a drone with a cumulative cutting warhead “specifically designed to destroy high-voltage pylons,” said Ukraine’s defence ministry electronics adviser Serhii Beskrestnov. “I believe the enemy’s plan is to attack important high-voltage power lines.”
Russia has also targeted data centres during September, in an apparent effort to disrupt connectivity and digital commerce.
Ukraine has been suffering from a shortage of interceptors with which to stop ballistic missiles, and several got through on September 30, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine believes it can manufacture interceptors faster and more cheaply than its allies if the technology is shared.
Zelenskyy had persuaded US President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to manufacture interceptors for the Patriot system under licence at the NATO summit last July, but Trump later retracted the offer.
Jet-powered drones are a recent challenge, too. Ukraine had mastered the art of shooting down propeller-powered ones, eliminating well over 90 percent. During the week ending October 1, however, they downed only 81 percent of the 1,933 long-range aerial drones Russia launched because many of them were jet-powered.
“Ukraine’s interception rate for jet-powered “shaheds” is now 55 percent,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Worse may be to come. Beskrestnov said Russia was working on a system of radio beacons to better guide drones.
“This system will allow them to navigate deep within our territory, at a distance of up to 100 km. This essentially means the ability to accurately attack a vast portion of Ukraine,” he wrote.
Zelenskyy said Russia planned to spend $12bn on jet-powered drones and loitering munitions next year.
Ukraine strikes back
Ukraine, too, has continued deep strikes against Russian refineries to starve its war machine of fuel and disrupt its economy.
Ukrainian drones struck the Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries on September 25, and the Ilsky refinery the following day. Two days later, they struck four oil deposits in the Krasnodar Krai region.
Ukraine also struck defence industries. On September 25, it struck the NPP Zavod Iskra factory, which makes electronic components for the Kh-59 cruise missiles Russia flies into Ukraine, and the Pantsir-S air defence system. It also struck the Efremovsky Synthetic Rubber Plant, which makes solid rocket fuel for the Iskander-M ballistic missile.
The next day, Ukraine hit the foundry and five buildings of the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, which makes optics for artillery, missile and antitank weapons.
Cost overruns
Both Russia and Ukraine have outspent their defence budgets for the year.
Ukraine said it was looking for an additional $27bn, in meetings with the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund.
“Part of these resources is needed immediately for advance payments for supplies that are expected to arrive in the first quarter of 2027,” said Prime Minister Koretskyi.
Some of the money would come “by reallocating funds”, he said, but “we are also counting on support from the EU”.
It was a similar story in Russia, which has spent 30 percent more on its war in the first half of the year than the same period last year, according to the Ukraine Foreign Intelligence Service.
Reuters cited leaked Russian government documents indicating that Russia plans to raise its defence spending by another 27 percent next year. It put the estimated budget at $204bn for 2027.
Moscow planned to pay for the increase through extra borrowing and budget cuts to nonmilitary expenditures.

articles.title: Russia’s Rostec Claims Cheaper Jet Drones Can Deliver Cruise Missile-Level Performance
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia’s Rostec Claims Cheaper Jet Drones Can Deliver Cruise Missile-Level Performance
On September 30, Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec presented the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T as lower-cost jet-powered substitutes for cruise missiles, claiming all three are already being used against Ukraine, Defence Blog reported on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, according to the outlet, describing the weapons as a new category between attack drones and missiles.
Defence Blog noted that the company provided no prices, production numbers or performance figures. It added that the figures and Rostec's claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
Rostec argued that a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle, though not every such drone qualifies as one. Its statement, as quoted by Defence Blog, claimed that “in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased.”
The report described Rostec's assertion that the drones combine the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles at a significantly lower price. Rostec also expects the gap between the two kinds of weapons to keep narrowing as drone production matures.
The company anticipates that the drones will become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023, the outlet wrote.
Rostec told the state news agency TASS that the S-71M and S-71K are designed for launch from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Defence Blog stated. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57's internal weapons bay, allowing the jet to carry them without compromising its radar-evading shape.
Russia's arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September, the report noted.
Ukrainian military intelligence has examined debris from both, Militarnyi reported, as cited by Defence Blog. According to those findings, the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance.
The S-71M, called Monokhrom, reportedly contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small US-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board. The outlet cautioned that some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec also told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets, a claim that Defence Blog did not independently verify. The company stated that the weapon can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones. Based on the outlet's reading, this suggests Rostec is targeting the Dan-T at export buyers.
Defence Blog described conflicting accounts of the weapon's origin. Some analysts present it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt. Ukrainian experts, by contrast, have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T's range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, per the Defence Blog account. The outlet cited Ukrainian intelligence officials, who noted that Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025, the report explained. It is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region.
Ukraine's military intelligence found a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly US-made electronics inside the weapon, Euronews reported, as relayed by Defence Blog.
The outlet emphasized that cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build. That logic mirrors Russia's mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Defence Blog added that Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons. That family includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group's KUB loitering munitions.
The pitch comes as jet-powered munitions already make up a growing share of Russian salvos.
During the large-scale attack on August 21–22, Russia launched 217 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and decoys, of which more than 50 were jet-powered.
Ukrainian defenses destroyed or suppressed 191 aerial targets that night, among them six Banderol munitions. Several Banderol weapons strayed into Belarus, with at least one reportedly flying around 75 miles into Belarusian territory before running out of fuel and crashing in a field.

articles.title: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.body:
US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
Massive US military deployment in the Middle East includes 50,000 troops, F-35s and Marines to pressure Tehran.
The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.
The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow
- list 2 of 3US-Iran talks in New York: What’s the latest?
- list 3 of 3Trump administration ‘must be changed’: Iran’s IRGC appeals to US voters
By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.
The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.
Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.
The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.
Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.
Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure, sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.
Diplomatic track
Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap, conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
The plan was then rejected by Trump.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.
Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”
Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.
Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.
Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting, according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Putin speaks on Russia’s economic sustainability, Europe’s aggression
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Despite the existing problems, Russia continues to develop, and its economy remains healthy and sustainable, Russian President Vladimir Putin told the plenary session of the 23rd Valdai International Discussion Club.
He also said that Russia’s offensive in the special military operation zone is gaining momentum, and that Europe’s aggressive attitude towards Russia is aimed at diverting attention from domestic economic failures.
Below are the Russian leader’s key remarks.
Russia’s sustainability and way to future
Russia is ready to forge its path to the future with realistic assessment of risks, opportunities and necessary goals, "and, of course, it is ready to engage in such efforts jointly with other countries and peoples."
"We do have some difficulties, but we are resolving them. Macroeconomic indices show that our economy is healthy, and that our financial system and economic institutions are working in a sustainable manner."
Russia’s economy has certain problems and issues that need to be solved, but "who does not?" "Look at any other region of the world. Everyone has its own problems."
Russia had inflation problems: "We jump-started the economy, we overheated it. And we made a deliberate choice to cool it down. We did it deliberately, being perfectly aware that if the Central Bank raises the key rate, investment will decline. It was obvious to everyone, and it did lead to such consequences. What matters now is to make sure that we don’t overcool the economy."
This year, inflation nearly halved compared to 2025. "This year’s budget deficit is around three percent. I’m sure that next year it will be two."
Situation in special operation zone
The situation in the special operation zone is gaining momentum, with over 1,300 square kilometers of territory taken under Russia’s control in September alone. "This is 2.5 times higher than in the previous months."
The government of Ukraine and the European Union claim they will be able to hold the remaining 11% of Donbass’s territory over the next year and a half or two. "We believe that it will happen way sooner, given the pace of our advance, which, as I have just mentioned, is accelerating."
For Russia, the situation around Ukraine is not a question of land, it’s a question of people. "It’s not about a piece of territory, it’s about people. The point is that we need to create conditions not for a temporary truce, but for a lasting peace. And we need security guarantees for that."
It is necessary to strive for peace agreements on Ukraine: "If they [Western countries and Ukraine] agree to terms that Russia also finds acceptable, it will be better to put an end to these sad events and avoid additional casualties on both sides."
Russia is ready to launch and complete negotiations on Ukraine as promptly as possible, but, "naturally, on conditions that the Russian Federation and its people find acceptable."
"However, it appears that the other side simply does not want to end the hostilities."
Russia’s response
Kiev troops started to strike Russian cargo ships in the Black Sea, and Russia had to respond: "Well, we gave our answer. And now they are asking us to stop via all channels. But they [the Kiev government] were the ones to start this."
"They started attacking our refineries, openly declaring that their objective is to harm our economy. They attained their goal to a certain extent because, according to our estimates, we lost about 1% of our GDP. They deliberately started striking civilian targets. Well, they got a tit-for-tat response."
The Russian armed forces started delivering strikes on sites that are crucial for the Ukrainian economy: "Now, by their own admission, they effectively have no metallurgical industry left."
Europe’s aggression
At this point Europe’s leading countries "are much more hostile towards Russia than the United States."
While the United States "is seeking to end the conflict," many European countries, "have now perhaps become the ‘instigators’ of aggressive attitude toward Russia, creating additional crises between Russia and Europe." They are "driven by the unfavorable situation in their own economies, and, consequently, by the unfavorable situation for the ruling elites, combined with shifting political moods."
European politicians want "to justify the need of preparations for war, and to mobilize as many supporters around themselves as possible in order to remain in power." "The logic is very simple, and I’m sure that this constitutes a significant portion of the reasoning behind Europe’s behavior towards the Russian Federation."
"We are not threatening anyone, and we have no intention of attacking anyone, neither in 2029, nor in 2030, nor in 2050. However, if we face aggression, we will be forced to respond. European citizens should clearly understand this and distinguish between our position and the stance taken by certain political leaders in their countries."
The continuous stoking of rhetoric by many European countries is driven by the serious worsening of their domestic economic and political situation. "Look at what is happening in the economy, look what is happening in the social sphere and the quality of life in major European countries. In this situation, they have to shift the focus of their citizens’ attention from domestic issues to outside problems."
"We have no preconditions for resuming and restoring relations with Europe in general or with particular countries."
EU countries "will collapse on their own" because they continue to make mistakes that negatively impact their own economies. "But this is none of our business. We are not interfering."
Weapons as competitive advantage
Russia understands that in case of a direct attack by NATO, it will have to face "an adversary more than twice our size in terms of numbers." "They have huge economic potential, huge military potential. Indeed, our forces and assets would not be that extensive to counter such a threat. And we will have to use our competitive advantages in this struggle."
One of Russia’s main competitive advantages are its strike capabilities. "Yes, of course, France and the United Kingdom are nuclear powers. We understand that, and we are fully aware of that. However, no one else possesses the strike capabilities that Russia has today. And this is our competitive advantage."
"We are not threatening anyone. We simply make it clear that our tools to defend ourselves are not that numerous."
Russia has advanced new weapons systems: "We have new, modern capabilities, including entirely new missile defense penetration systems, advanced medium-range weapons, and state-of-the-art systems that other nations do not possess yet."
"All nuclear powers are highly technologically advanced countries. They will have it at some point in the future. But now they don’t, only we do."
While building new facilities, Russia is taking modern methods of warfare into account: "I assure you, we are currently considering this, and, when we build new enterprises in this sector, we are taking modern methods of warfare into account and do everything possible to ensure they are located in the safest areas possible." "Construction is under way."
Relations with US
Factors marring and damaging Russia-US relations have developed over decades: "We would very much like to see these divisive factors to become a thing of the past, allowing new prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation to emerge."
Russia has proposed and continues to propose to the United States to resume dialogue on strategic arms limitations: "We don not mind resuming this dialogue; we have never been against it. We have offered it, and we are offering it now. There is no answer. Well, if there is no answer, then so be it."
It was Washington that withdrew from agreements curbing the arms race and the proliferation of nuclear weapons: "We were not the ones to walk out of these treaties. The United States did it, under this or that pretext."
"I have quite good, long-standing relations with President (of the US Donald - TASS) Trump. I’m thankful for his efforts to resolve the Ukrainian crisis, and, as I’ve said many times, he is doing it in good faith. And I’m thankful for that, too."
Partnership with China
Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping understand each other without words or interpreters: "You know, what is interesting. It only took one word from him or me, and without interpreters - and without knowing each other's languages - we understood each other instantly."
China never seeks to resolve emerging problems and issues through pressure or military force. This is alien to its philosophy, which is fundamentally rooted in pursuing solutions through peaceful means. For its part, Russia recognizes Beijing's approach, shares this perspective, and notes the strong outcomes generated by the joint efforts of Moscow and Beijing.
"Can China play any role [in promoting peace] at this point? Of course it can. And, first of all, this stems from its growing economic and military potential, from its readiness to expand the zone of free cooperation, and this is what Chinese President Xi Jinping’s initiative ‘One belt, One Road’ is aimed at."
"Together with China, we are developing this initiative, aligning it with Russia's respective projects, including the Greater Eurasian Partnership. We are working jointly, and this is yielding strong, positive results."
Moscow and Beijing will undoubtedly establish a joint framework to actively utilize the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to serve the interests of Russia and China.
Indian premier and peace initiatives
The diversity and unity of Indian culture are highly admirable: "There is something about Indian culture that possesses such uniqueness - a distinctiveness and unity at the same time - that it undoubtedly serves as an exemplary model. This, of course, deserves to be an example."
At every meeting, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi raises the question of resolving the conflict in Ukraine: "He comes up with very good ideas, aimed at searching for mutually acceptable - specifically mutually acceptable - solutions."
The head of the Indian government has a neutral stance, which is nevertheless aimed at bringing the conflict to an end: "By the way, we are grateful to the Indian premier for his desire to resolve this conflict peacefully, and as quickly as possible."
Multipolarity and BRICS
The world should be multipolar; it cannot be bipolar: "It should take into account the interests of all participants of international relations. And, as we have said many times, there is the cornerstone, basic principle: the security of one nation cannot be achieved at the expense of the security of others. This is one of the cornerstones that we believe should form the foundation of the future world order."
"We cannot say exactly how this world will look like. <...> But we need to strive to jointly determine <…> the pillars of the future world order. And this needs to be done without any preconditions."
"An organization such as BRICS may certainly become the prototype for building the future world order."
At this point, BRICS represents nearly half of the planet’s entire population, and its share in the global economy is constantly growing. "This is happening every year, and we can see it in the statistics. And, most importantly, the principles of BRICS' formation and functioning stipulate that everyone is equal. There is no domination of any kind there, and this is what makes it so attractive."
So far, it is hard to say what role BRICS will play in the new architecture of international relations, but it can already be said with certainty that it is "a useful mechanism."

articles.title: Russian Strike on European Arms Factory Would Trigger Article 5, EU Defense Chief Says
articles.body:
A Russian strike on a weapons factory in a European NATO country would trigger the alliance’s mutual defense clause, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said.
He made the remarks to TVP World on the sidelines of a meeting of the European Parliament’s Security and Defense Committee in Brussels on Thursday, Oct. 1. Only a day earlier, Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine could become military targets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I would say if Russia will hit our factories in European territory, that would be Article 5,” Kubilius said.
NATO’s Article 5 treats an armed attack against one NATO member as an attack against all, requiring allies to come to the targeted country’s assistance. Twenty-three of the EU’s 27 members are also NATO members.
Moscow’s threats
On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that weapons factories in European countries that produce arms for Ukraine are possible military targets for Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated the threat at the Valdai Discussion Club forum held on Thursday, saying Russia was monitoring European factories supplying Kyiv.
“I am not saying that we are going to strike enterprises in the countries supplying weapons to Ukraine, but this is a threat,” Putin said.
In August, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO itself because alliance members are supplying Kyiv with intelligence and weapons.
Putin Raises Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad, Says Russia Monitors Arms Factories in Europe
Comments likely to stir unease within NATO
An aide to Kubilius confirmed that the commissioner was referring specifically to an aerial bombardment or missile attack on a factory, Politico reported on Thursday.
Nevertheless, Kubilius’ statement is likely to cause unease within NATO, given the sensitivity of discussions around Article 5 and the EU’s on-military role compared with the alliance.
“When Kubilius will become secretary general of NATO he might be able to claim what triggers or doesn’t trigger Article 5,” a NATO diplomat told the outlet.
Suspicious incidents at arms factories
Kubilius’ warnings come amid a growing number of incidents at arms factories across Europe, some of which have been attributed to Russia.
On Sept. 29, Estonia said Russian intelligence services ordered an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a Tallinn-based defense company whose unmanned ground vehicles are used by Ukrainian Defense Forces.
However, the Kremlin rejected the accusation – as it did after an explosive-laden drone was found at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport in August and following other suspected Russian drone and sabotage incidents in Europe.
According to Politico, Poland, Slovakia and other countries are also investigating similar incidents.
Rising tensions with NATO
The exchange follows months of escalation between the Kremlin and Europe.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium said it had delivered a position to NATO’s International Secretariat and Belgium’s Foreign Ministry warning that Moscow was ready to deploy its entire arsenal if alliance members tried to isolate the Kaliningrad exclave.
The embassy also accused NATO of an aggressive policy, without specifying which actions had prompted the warning.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said the alliance had replied to the informal document, condemning Moscow’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” and reiterating that NATO is exclusively a defensive alliance.
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would disappear from the map if it lifted its ban on nuclear weapons on Sept. 11, claiming that NATO would not invoke Article 5 as that would lead to a “global catastrophe.”
Separately on Sept. 25, Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states, the same argument the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Meanwhile, NATO officials increasingly warn that Moscow’s nuclear signaling is a part of a broader campaign of hybrid pressure, including sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference and drone incursions, aimed at weakening Western support for Ukraine.
Several member states have already stopped referring to the attacks as “hybrid,” instead calling them direct attacks.
During his final press conference at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that European calls to prepare for a possible war with Russia could become a “self-fulfilling prophecy,” while simultaneously dismissing warnings of a Russian attack on Europe as “nonsense.”
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday that NATO’s combined strength exceeds Russia’s and that he does not take the nuclear threats seriously.
During the same summit in Brussels, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev warned that Putin retains a “nuclear trump card” and called for increased diplomatic efforts to reduce the risk of escalation.
Kubilius rejected that approach, saying past diplomacy with Moscow had failed and called for a tougher European response to Russia’s hybrid attacks.

articles.title: Russian Strike on European Arms Factory Would Trigger Article 5, EU Defense Chief Tells TVP World
articles.body:
A Russian strike on a weapons factory in a European NATO country would trigger the alliance’s mutual defense clause, EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius told TVP World on Thursday.
His comments came a day after Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine were “potential military targets for Russia.” Her words raised concerns about the prospect of a direct confrontation between Moscow and NATO.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking to TVP World on the sidelines of a meeting of the European Parliament’s Security and Defence Committee in Brussels, Kubilius said: “I would say if Russia will hit our factories in European territory, that would be Article 5.”
Article 5 treats an armed attack against one NATO member as an attack against all, requiring allies to come to the assistance of the country targeted.
“If Russia were to hit our factories, I would say that would be Article 5,” said EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius [@KubiliusA], speaking exclusively to TVP World. 
His comment was in response to Russian claims that European factories could be considered legitimate… pic.twitter.com/rqxBp6L48Y
Putin issues nuclear warning over Kaliningrad
Tensions along NATO’s eastern flank have risen amid suspected Russian-linked sabotage and cyberattacks across Europe, as well as a series of Russian missile and drone strikes close to the alliance’s borders.
The incidents have fueled fears that the war in Ukraine could spill over into NATO territory.
Russian President Vladimir Putin added to those concerns on Thursday by warning that Moscow could resort to its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave bordering NATO members Poland and Lithuania, came under direct attack.
Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
“This is inevitable,” Putin said.
No Western official has indicated there are any plans to attack Kaliningrad.
                                                                                                                                                                         
‘Familiar intimidation tactic’
Philippe Dickinson, deputy director of the Transatlantic Security Initiative at the US-based Atlantic Council think tank, told TVP World that Putin’s remarks were consistent with Moscow’s previous use of nuclear threats.
“It’s a very familiar intimidation tactic. It is not at all outside of the usual Vladimir Putin playbook,” Dickinson said.
He said NATO should remain “calm,” “united” and “focused” rather than allow Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric to alter the alliance’s course.
Dickinson also backed drawing clear red lines over any attacks on NATO territory.
He said, however, that any decision to invoke Article 5 rested with NATO members, rather than the European Union.
“I’m glad that Commissioner Kubilius has done so, but... we need to note that he’s an EU commissioner. This is a NATO decision,” Dickinson said. “These are different bodies, and it’s for NATO member states to make that determination.”
He added that despite Russia’s escalating rhetoric and actions, he did not believe Moscow wanted a direct Article 5 confrontation with NATO.
Russia ‘not capable’ of NATO invasion
Lieutenant General Piotr Błazeusz, Poland’s military representative to the NATO and EU military committees, said on Thursday that Russia currently lacked the military capacity to invade a NATO country.
“Russia, for the moment thanks to the Ukrainian side, is not able to start any invasion on [a] NATO country. They are just not capable,” Błazeusz said.
He warned, however, that Moscow could continue to challenge NATO through hybrid operations designed to remain “below the threshold of war.”

articles.title: ‘No Rules Now’: Putin Orders Civilian Attacks, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites, President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Friday, Oct. 2.
Zelensky cited intelligence obtained by Ukrainian agencies, including what the FT described as intercepted communications between Kremlin officials. Kyiv has not publicly released the intercepts, and their contents could not be independently verified.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said, referring to the alleged order from Putin.
According to Zelensky, the instruction was issued in September, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and increasingly struck schools, hospitals, telecommunications facilities and data centers.
Zelensky speaks from school bomb shelter
Zelensky spoke to the FT inside the bomb shelter of a Kyiv school struck by a Russian jet-powered drone on Thursday.
The school’s director said 104 students and 60 teachers survived because they reached the underground shelter before the drone hit shortly after 9 a.m.
The drone’s 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead pierced the floor but failed to detonate, Ukrainian authorities said. The impact nevertheless damaged the building and started a fire.
Zelensky later called attacks on educational institutions “a deliberate tactic”, saying Russia was attempting to terrorize civilians and disrupt ordinary life.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
The FT said debris recovered at the school bore markings from Russian manufacturers and handwritten Russian text. Some components were reportedly manufactured in Russia on July 28, while others appeared to be Western-made.
Russia has denied deliberately attacking civilian sites. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the FT that Russian forces do not strike schools or hospitals.
However, Ukraine’s Education Ministry has recorded more than 4,700 attacks on educational institutions since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The World Health Organization has verified more than 3,000 attacks affecting healthcare facilities.
Deliberately attacking civilians or civilian objects constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Russia seeks to pressure civilians
Zelensky said Russia had previously concentrated much of its long-range campaign on military and energy infrastructure, although civilian sites have been repeatedly struck throughout the full-scale invasion.
He alleged that Moscow had now deliberately expanded its target list because Russian forces had failed to achieve their objectives on the battlefield, particularly in the Donbas.
The new campaign seeks “to pressure people,” Zelensky said, describing the strikes as an attempt to frighten civilians, force residents to leave Ukrainian cities and weaken the country’s ability to continue resisting Russia.
On Monday, a Russian drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. Russia also repeatedly attacked the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv on Thursday, damaging a support column, the road surface and a barrier and disrupting transport across the Dnipro.
Recent Russian strikes have also damaged Ukrainian schools, healthcare facilities, warehouses, businesses and communications infrastructure. A Sept. 23 attack damaged Kyiv data centers, disrupting internet service for some residents.
Jet-powered drones strain Ukrainian defenses
Zelensky said Russia had launched around 500 drones over the previous day, approximately half of them jet-powered models that fly considerably faster than conventional Shahed-type drones.
Ukraine intercepted around 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with between 85% and 90% of conventional models, he said.
Russia’s use of jet-powered drones increased eightfold between June and August, according to figures previously released by Ukraine’s Air Force. Their higher speed gives defenders less time to detect and intercept them and can force Ukraine to use comparatively expensive aircraft and missiles.
Zelensky said F-16 fighter jets had proven effective against the new drones. However, around half of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet was spending extended periods outside the country for maintenance and repairs, he said.
Kyiv is seeking Western assistance to move more maintenance work into Ukraine so that aircraft can return to service faster.
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor drone models. Zelensky said one model could enter production at a rate of approximately 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remained in testing.
He identified shortages of suitable engines and insufficient financing as the main obstacles to mass production.
Western pressure ‘not enough’
Zelensky also criticized the US and European governments for failing to apply sufficient economic and diplomatic pressure on Putin to end the war.
Asked whether Ukraine’s partners were doing everything possible to help, he replied: “Not enough, of course not enough.”
Zelensky argued that Russia’s partners had the leverage required to increase the cost of continuing the invasion but lacked the political will to use it fully.

articles.title: Ukraine calls for tighter sanctions as Russian attacks spark Kyiv gridlock
articles.body:
Ukraine calls for tighter sanctions as Russian attacks spark Kyiv gridlock
Closure of bridges struck by drones in Ukrainian capital causes traffic chaos.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on allies to tighten sanctions against Russia after a wave of strikes triggered gridlock across Kyiv.
Traffic chaos gripped the Ukrainian capital on Friday after Russian drone attacks overnight closed key bridges. Zelenskyy called for allies to act to prevent Moscow from sourcing components for its arsenal as Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine face attacks around the clock.
Recommended Stories
