- list 2 of 4Row between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs
- list 3 of 4Russia tries to freeze Ukraine as it suffers record casualties and retreats
- list 4 of 4UK arrests British-Iranian suspect over RAF ‘plot’: What we know
Kyiv’s Southern Bridge and Paton Bridge, key routes for cars and public transport across the Dnipro River, were closed in both directions after the attacks. The Metro Bridge was closed in the direction of Kyiv’s right bank, the city administration said.
Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that Iranian-type Shahed kamikaze drones struck the Southern Bridge “several times”. One person was killed as Russia launched more than 100 drones across the country.
The president, who has persistently called for additional help to boost Ukraine’s air defences during Moscow’s concentrated air campaign, noted that supply chains for such weapons trail through Europe, the United States, China and Japan.
“No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localise the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia.”
“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries,” he continued. “If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened.”
Last month, European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was “working on new proposals to tighten sanctions enforcement” and implement new measures.
US President Donald Trump separately signed a sweeping Russian sanctions package into law, taking aim at Russian President Vladimir Putin, banks, other financial institutions, and the energy and defence sectors.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russian strikes targeted a kindergarten in Kherson, a grocery store in Kharkiv and apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy, Zelenskyy said.
The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava and Rivne regions also came under attack with at least four people reported wounded.
The Russian Ministry of Defence earlier said on Telegram that its drones hit a bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, a power station in the surrounding region, the Izmail port near Odesa and a cargo vessel. It claimed all the sites were used for Ukrainian military purposes.
Ukraine’s military carried out its own overnight attacks on Russia and said they hit a Lukoil facility in the city of Volgograd as well as an oil dispatch station in the Samara region with fires breaking out at both sites.
Ukrainian forces also carried out missions in several other Russian regions that targeted airfields, industrial sites and other facilities, including in the Black Sea, Zelenskyy said.
Russian authorities in the Black Sea port town of Tuapse said an enterprise was damaged by drone debris, but they did not provide details.

articles.title: Russian troops liberate 17 communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 17 communities in the Kharkov, Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of September 26 - October 2, including three settlements during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Petropavlovka, Lozovaya, Khripuny, Kreidyanka, Shabelnoye, Nesternoye and Rublenoye in the Kharkov Region and yesterday they established control of the settlements of Grachevka and Serdobino in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. <…> In addition, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Maryino, Ulanovo and Tolstodubovo in the Sumy Region and yesterday they gained control of the settlement of Malaya Rybitsa in the Sumy Region. In the Kharkov Region, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlement of Vysokaya Yaruga," the ministry said in a statement.
"During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Novovodyanoye and Vesyoloye Pole in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active offensive operations. <…> Over the past week, Battlegroup East units kept advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Yegorovka in the Zaporozhye Region," it said.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian logistics and telecommunications centers, electric power generation facilities and Flamingo missile depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On September 26 - October 2, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting logistics and telecommunications centers, electric power generation facilities, transport and port infrastructure used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, military airfields, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, depots with ammunition, ground-based Flamingo cruise missiles, fuel and materiel, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, and also fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian army were degraded, it said.
"During the week, 17 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry reported.
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarts Ukrainian attempts to break out of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units continue tightening the ring of encirclement of enemy formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. <…> All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement were thwarted," the ministry said.
Over the week in that area, the enemy lost more than 265 troops, nine armored combat vehicles, six motor vehicles, five all-terrain vehicles and three ground robotic platforms, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup North liberates 352 sq. km since encircling Ukrainian troops in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North has liberated 352 sq. km of territory and 20 communities since surrounding Ukrainian armed formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Overall, 352 sq. km of territory and 20 communities have been liberated since the Ukrainian combat group was surrounded in the northeast of the Kharkov Region. Battlegroup North units have destroyed over 1,085 [Ukrainian] troops, 32 armored combat vehicles, 19 motor vehicles, 18 all-terrain vehicles and 31 ground robotic platforms," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 2,000 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 2,000 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 21 enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of six mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, an airmobile brigade, an unmanned systems brigade, an assault regiment, an unmanned systems regiment of the Ukrainian army, four territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 2,000 personnel, 21 armored combat vehicles, 144 motor vehicles, four field artillery guns, two Grad multiple rocket launchers and 11 electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,510 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,510 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 13 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade, a National Guard brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,510 personnel, 13 armored combat vehicles, 86 motor vehicles, nine field artillery guns and five electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,360 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,360 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two airmobile brigades, an unmanned systems brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and two marine infantry brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,360 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 164 motor vehicles and 10 field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center advancing in Dobropolye in Donetsk region
Russia’s Battlegroup Center units are advancing in the western and eastern parts of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic and keep tightening the ring of encirclement of Ukrainian armed formations in that area, the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, units of the 51st Army are developing an offensive in converging directions in the town’s western and eastern parts and continue tightening the ring of encirclement of formations from the 425th assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, the 4th and 15th National Guard brigades. All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement or rotate troops have been thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces have eliminated over 375 enemy personnel and two pickup trucks since surrounding Ukrainian troops in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 3,125 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 3,125 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 17 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and four National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 3,125 personnel, 17 armored combat vehicles, 74 motor vehicles, seven field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,740 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,740 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 13 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an airmobile brigade, three air assault brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,740 personnel, 13 armored combat vehicles, 55 motor vehicles and five field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 220 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 220 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 220 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 74 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and seven electronic warfare stations were destroyed," it said.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,031 Ukrainian UAVs, four cruise missiles over week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,031 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 37 guided aerial bombs, four rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles and 5,031 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 250,151 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,096 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,784 multiple rocket launchers, 36,607 field artillery guns and mortars and 73,407 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

articles.title: Russia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow
articles.body:
Russia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow
Putin warned the West he would deploy nuclear weapons if necessary to defend the Russian Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv.
“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘I wanted to live’: A Ukrainian orphan’s journey through Russian occupation
- list 2 of 3Russian attacks on Kyiv region kill four people, target power grid
- list 3 of 3Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with these strikes, with attacks on Russian oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia was now responding in kind.
Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.
Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to be a neutral country after the end of hostilities.
The nuclear option
He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” he said.
On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

articles.title: Zelensky lashes out at Ukraine’s Western backers
articles.body:
Zelensky lashes out at Ukraine’s Western backers
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, who is dealing with a major hole in his country’s budget and high-profile corruption scandals in his government, has criticized Kiev’s Western backers for their reluctance to provide him with more money.
Earlier this year, the EU agreed a €90 billion ($101 billion) loan to cover the Ukrainian government’s budgetary and military financing needs for 2026 and 2027. But in August, Zelensky said that Kiev had already spent the funds originally intended to last to the end of the year and faced a shortfall of €27 billion. The announcement came after the Ukrainian leader’s 40-day PR pressure campaign on Russia, which involved long-range strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure, failed to deliver the desired results and triggered a harsh response by Moscow.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Friday, Zelensky complained that the acute budget deficit is stopping Ukraine from developing and manufacturing some key weapons.
When asked if he believed that his foreign supporters were doing all they could to assist, the Ukrainian leader replied: “Not enough, of course not enough.”
The FT noted that the introduction of faster jet-powered drones by Russia in recent weeks had become an additional challenge for Ukraine, which is already experiencing a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors and other air defenses.
Zelensky acknowledged that a lack of money to purchase engines for interceptor UAVs was one of the hurdles. “We really import a lot of engines. There are some engines of our production, but not enough,” he said.
A Russian drone and missile campaign against military-related targets in Ukraine intensified this year in response to terrorist attacks by Kiev, crippling its energy infrastructure and leading to blackouts and fuel shortages. It has also destroyed most of the country’s storage spaces, affecting the supply of food and other goods. Wheat and other exports have also been reduced significantly by attacks on the port of Odessa and Ukraine-bound vessels in the Black Sea, leaving Zelensky’s government almost entirely dependent on foreign aid.
Bloomberg reported on Thursday that the EU turned down Ukraine’s plea to speed up the payouts of its loan. Officials in Brussels expressed belief that doing so would not solve the problem, but only delay it until 2027, the agency said. The bloc suggested that Kiev’s other partners, including Canada and Japan, could provide the funds to cover its pressing needs, it added.
EU bureaucrats were surprised to learn that Ukraine ran out of money so fast, according to Bloomberg. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned earlier this year that the bloc’s loan to Kiev would be swiftly plundered by Zelensky and other corrupt officials from his team.
On Thursday, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) reported about a scheme involving the supply of EU-funded handguns to Ukrainian security services at prices inflated threefold. Kiev and it Western backers are “traditionally” plugging the $27-billion hole in Ukraine’s budget “using funds taken from ordinary citizens of European states,” the SVR said.

articles.title: F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer
articles.body:
Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East.
Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities
Another pilot currently stationed in Europe received a DFC for a mission in the Middle East, but the Air Force did not say when or where the actions that earned that pilot the award occurred.
The six Airmen from Langley were decorated for their actions escorting B-2 Spirit stealth bombers that struck the Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites in Iran. The strike package also included F-16 Fighting Falcons and F-35 Lightning II fighters, and pilots from those units received DFCs earlier this year; tanker crews from multiple units have also received the award for supporting the mission. No individual awards have yet been announced for the B-2 aviators who participated in Midnight Hammer.
The DFC recognizes acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement in the air and is the military’s fourth-highest award for heroism.
Four of the pilots came from the Active-Duty 94th Fighter Squadron, part of the 1st Fighter Wing at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va., and two pilots came from the associated Virginia Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Squadron, part of the 192nd Wing.
The medals were presented Aug. 31 by the head of Air Combat Command, Gen. Adrian L. Spain, in a ceremony at the Virginia base.
The F-22s were among an armada of fighters that escorted the seven B-2s that dropped 14 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weapons on Iran’s nuclear facilities. Around 125 U.S. aircraft of all types were involved in the mission, which came after a nearly two-week Israeli air campaign against Iran. The stealthy F-22s serve as the Air Force’s premier air-to-air fighters and can use their capabilities to penetrate defended airspace.
“Their job was to provide air superiority,” Spain said, according to an account of his remarks provided by the 1st Fighter Wing. “The bombers and the rest of the support package relied on these Raptor pilots to clear the skies, shield them from surface threats, and ensure a safe route through heavily contested airspace.”
Officials from Air Combat Command and the 1st Fighter Wing declined to provide further details on the mission that earned the pilots their decorations or medal citations, or to publicly disclose pilots’ identities, citing operational security concerns.
“We haven’t awarded many of these in the last few decades, as it’s intended to recognize true heroism and highly exceptional accomplishment in flight, which means that it should be rare, and it is,” said Spain.
Iran’s air force was largely destroyed during the 2026 air campaign against the country, Operation Epic Fury. But even during Midnight Hammer, Iran posed a limited air-to-air threat, with most of its capability consisting of aircraft purchased before the Iranian revolution in 1979. Before the Shah was overthrown and a theocratic government took over, Iran was the largest purchaser of American arms. Iran also has Soviet-designed fighters.
Still, Iran showed the ability to generate some airpower, launching aircraft to attack Gulf countries after Israel and Iran began their air campaign on Feb. 28 of this year, and was able to strike a base in Kuwait used by the U.S. with one of its aging fighter jets.
F-22s from Langley deployed to support Operation Epic Fury and follow-on actions against Iran earlier this year but have since returned.
“It was your support that enabled their excellence—from the maintainers, the operations team, the intel professionals, and the logistics involved,” Spain said. “Let there be no doubt heroism like this is earned by the entire formation. These pilots were the leading edge that day, but the foundation of their success was laid by the hard work of the entire organization in the days prior and every day since. And that’s what Air Force readiness looks like.”
The seventh F-22 pilot received their decoration Sept. 22 from U.S. Air Forces in Europe commander Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds for leading a strike package during a mission in the Middle East that operated in contested airspace, according to a release from the command. U.S. officials did not immediately say whether the mission was part of Operation Epic Fury, Operation Midnight Hammer, or Operation Rough Rider, the 2025 campaign against the Houthis in Yemen.
The pilot faced “challenging conditions including enemy threats” and “directed the aircraft formation, making critical decisions with limited time and little margin for error,” according to USAFE.
The command, like ACC, withheld the Airman’s identity.
“For more than an hour, [the pilot] remained focused on protecting teammates” and “acted decisively to protect the larger force, and ensured the formation could safely return,” Hinds said. “Their actions helped give the strike package the time and freedom needed to accomplish its mission.”

articles.title: I went curtain shopping during a Kyiv air raid. And not because I’m ‘resilient’ | Diana Berg
articles.body:
I was standing in front of a locked basement door in a building in our neighbourhood, laughing, as Ukrainian air defence shot down drones directly above me. I had run into the first residential building I could reach, and I even took a photo of the locked door – a shelter, and the shelter locked – because I wanted to remember it. I was on my way to buy curtains.
I hadn’t checked whether there was an alert before I left home. I had simply set out for the shop, 20 minutes away through our residential district, on foot. But somewhere along the way, things started exploding in the sky above me – and I was suddenly walking through a city under attack because I had decided that my windows needed new curtains. What the fuck was I laughing at? I should have been terrified, and I was. It was just that I still wanted the curtains, and the absurdity was hilarious.
The curtain shop was closed because of the raid – this international chain, it turns out, shuts when the sirens go off, unlike many Ukrainian-owned stores. So I came back the next day and bought them. They are better than the old ones and cover the windows properly. Only after I had hung them did I realise that they also let me see less of the war from my sofa: the flashes of air defence, the smoke, whatever was happening outside. I had not made the war any safer. I had only made it slightly harder to see.
I had been away from Kyiv for a month and while I was gone, the rhythm of the war, which I have lived with for years, had changed: attacks now came by day, alerts could swallow half of it, and explosions, drones and smoke had become part of the daytime soundscape in a way that felt new even to me. My response, apparently, was to buy curtains.
In January 2022, back in Mariupol, when everyone around us was waiting for Russia to invade, my husband bought an expensive coffee machine. I thought it was ridiculous. He told me he was tired of living in fear and anticipation, that he wanted to live here and now, and that if the machine survived only a couple of weeks he didn’t care. Since the full-scale invasion, he has bought a television, an electronic piano, a huge monitor for my laptop, a washing machine and a dryer – every year something large that could be smashed in a second.
We don’t do the big things. Our flooring still needs repairing, and the flat we have lived in since we fled Mariupol in 2022 needs renovation. We don’t invest in it because spending serious money, time and energy on a place a missile could destroy tomorrow feels slightly insane. There is a strange logic in this, a logic that isn’t really there when I look at it closely. But the small things keep sneaking in.
I left all my books in Mariupol. When we fled, they were not exactly high on the evacuation priority list, and later they were lost when our rented flat was destroyed in the airstrike on the Drama Theatre. I started buying books again in Kyiv, one at a time, and somehow I now have a bookcase full of them. We got plants. We got cats – four now, two from Mariupol and two adopted during the full-scale war. One of them can barely see, barely hear and limps after an accident; we chose him in 2023, apparently deciding that what our lives really needed was another vulnerable creature to worry about.
The rational wartime strategy would be to own less, need less, attach yourself to less. We have left home twice, both times with only what we could carry, so nobody needs to explain to us what attachment costs.
It isn’t that we don’t know what can happen. Last week a building belonging to my husband’s workplace was hit. He was in a different one, but he could have been there, and I don’t know how to convey that fear. I keep my Instagram mostly to cats, standup, sport, beauty and interiors, because I don’t want to spend every waking hour looking at war – but the news gets through even those filters.
In my feed I saw a post from a soldier at the front, showing footage from the site of that building: the car park, the burnt-out cars, and the news that his wife, who had worked with my husband, had been killed there. There were photographs of the two of them walking into the new house they had bought and planned to renovate, the walls still bare, the new car they had bought 10 days earlier – and then that same car, gutted in the car park along with everything around it. She had been inside. It was one and the same strike. What is there to say?
During an attack, we have our own little scale of urgency. Ballistic missile: bathroom. Now. Cruise missile: you can finish your coffee. Drones take the longest, so you can usually carry on. For now.
In fact, I am writing this column from the bathroom, the safest place in the flat. There is an air-raid alert and I can hear air defence outside; the four cats are with me. On Telegram, people post live videos from all over Kyiv, often before anything appears in the official news, and as I write this, Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv is on fire. One person has been killed. People are climbing out of upper-floor windows on to fire ladders. I am sitting in the bathtub, watching it live on my phone and writing about curtains.
During another alert that lasted through the afternoon and into the night, we visited friends for a Sunday barbecue. We sat outside while something was burning or being intercepted somewhere above us; meanwhile, someone turned meat on the grill and my friend’s mum told me about the new flowers in her garden. At some point I had the very clear thought that, theoretically, something could fall straight on to my plate. Then I looked back at the flowers.
This is what I find difficult about the word “resilience”, so often used about people living in war zones. It sounds like a virtue, something noble you develop when tested – but it feels much less noble than that. The curtains hide a little of the war from me. I feel guilty for shutting my eyes to the horror outside, but in reality it’s more like refusing to allow the war to make every decision.
So the curtains are hanging now. They make the room warmer and they cover the windows better. The photo of the locked door is still on my phone. Next: I need to paint the walls in the bathroom. I’ve already chosen the colour.
- 
  Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion

articles.title: 646 Drones, Oil Fires and Explosions: Massive Attack Rocks Russia Overnight
articles.body:
A massive overnight drone attack sparked fires near a major oil refinery and chemical plant in Russia’s Volgograd region, while another strike was reported at a huge oil storage facility in Samara.
The attacks came as Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses had intercepted or destroyed 646 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Volgograd Regional Governor Andrey Bocharov said early Friday, Oct. 2, that drones had targeted “industrial infrastructure” in the region.
He also reported a fire in an apartment building in Volgograd’s Krasnoarmeysky District. One person was hospitalized, and the fire was contained, Bocharov said.
Local residents reported numerous explosions across the city.
Rosaviatsia, Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, imposed flight restrictions at Volgograd Airport at around 1 a.m. The last evening flight to Moscow and the first morning flight from the capital were delayed, while another aircraft was diverted to Samara.
Footage analyzed by Russian outlet Astra reportedly showed a large fire near two adjacent industrial facilities – the Volgograd Oil Refinery and the Kaustik chemical plant.
The Volgograd refinery, operated by Lukoil subsidiary Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka, is among Russia’s 10 largest oil refineries, with an annual processing capacity of about 14.8 million metric tons.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
The facility produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen. It was previously targeted by drones on July 31, when key production units were damaged and primary oil-processing units AVT-1 and AVT-6 were reportedly shut down.
Located near the refinery, JSC Kaustik is a major chemical-industry enterprise that supplies products to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
Major oil storage facility reportedly hit in Samara
Astra also reported an overnight strike on the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) – a major Transneft oil storage facility.
“The Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) – Europe’s largest tank farm and part of the Transneft system – was likely targeted in Samara,” the message read.
The facility covers more than 216 hectares and contains 71 storage tanks with a combined capacity of over 1.6 million cubic meters of oil, as well as two pumping stations and an oil-blending station.
Four trunk pipelines converge at the Samara LPDS, bringing oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, Orenburg and Kazakhstan.
Samara authorities have not officially commented on reports of a fire at the facility, although explosions were reported in the city. A particularly loud blast was heard at around 6:30 a.m., according to local reports.
Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov later announced the suspension of ground public transport. The city’s metro remained operational as a shelter, while the missile threat alert was lifted.
Russia claims 646 drones intercepted
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Oct. 1 and 8 a.m. on Oct. 2, its air defenses intercepted or destroyed 646 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones.
According to the ministry, the drones were detected over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Tula, Oryol, Rostov, Saratov, Volgograd, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Astrakhan Oblasts, as well as Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
The figures and reported damage could not be independently verified.
“Inherent right to self-defense” – Ukraine confirms strikes
Later, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed that Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka oil refinery in Volgograd early on Oct. 2.
“Explosions and a fire were recorded at the facility,” the General Staff said.
The General Staff also reported a strike on the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station near the settlement of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region, where a fire was also recorded.
According to the report, the station receives oil through trunk pipelines from Tatarstan, Western Siberia and other Russian oil-producing regions.
The facility blends high- and low-sulfur crude from various oil fields to produce Urals export-grade crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia’s total oil exports, according to the General Staff.
“The enterprise is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian armed forces,” the General Staff added.
The results of the strikes are still being assessed.
“Striking such facilities represents Ukraine exercising its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and aims to reduce the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also reacted to the overnight strikes, saying Ukraine was responding to Russia’s escalating attacks with its long-range capabilities.
“We are responding appropriately to Russian escalation with our long-range capabilities. There are significant results practically every day. Over the past 24 hours, oil facilities in the Samara and Volgograd regions were struck,” Zelensky wrote.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces also carried out successful operations in the Black Sea and in Russia’s Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd, Samara and Krasnodar regions.
He said the operations targeted airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a rocket and space center and an ammunition depot belonging to Russian forces.
Zelensky thanked the Ukrainian military for what he called their precision and professionalism.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Five High-Speed Drone Interceptor Models to Counter Russia’s Jet-Powered Attacks
articles.body:
Ukraine is testing five high-speed interceptor drone models designed to shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published Friday.
One of the five models could reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain under testing, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Zelensky said Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine in a recent 24-hour period, about half of them jet-powered. Ukraine is currently destroying about 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with 85% to 90% of conventional drones, he told the FT.
The faster drones have created a new challenge for Ukraine’s layered air defenses. Reuters reported in September that some Ukrainian interceptor prototypes struggled to remain controllable at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour during testing, showing the technical difficulty of developing drones capable of chasing and destroying the new Russian weapons.
Ukrainian manufacturers have nevertheless begun developing interceptors specifically for the threat. One model unveiled in September, the Zorelit v5, has a reported top speed of 416 kilometers per hour and a range of up to 47 kilometers.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
Its manufacturer says it can be used against both conventional Shahed-type drones and faster jet-powered variants.
The biggest obstacle to rapidly scaling production is not only technology but supply.
“Engines are key,” Zelensky told the FT. “We really import a lot of engines.” He said Ukraine produces some engines domestically but does not have enough to meet demand. He also cited a shortage of budget funding for the development and mass production of air-defense weapons.
Ukraine has been working to expand domestic production of the technology. Zelensky said last week that new decisions had been made to establish production of several types of jet engines inside Ukraine, following tests of interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shaheds.
The interceptor program has become increasingly urgent as Russia intensifies its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.
The new interceptor drones are intended to provide Ukraine with a cheaper and more scalable layer of air defense against the faster weapons, reducing pressure on scarce surface-to-air missiles and fighter jets.
Zelensky said US-made F-16s have proved effective against the new Russian drones, but argued that too many Ukrainian aircraft are undergoing lengthy maintenance in Europe. Kyiv wants more repair work moved inside Ukraine so the fighters can return to service faster.
What changed in Russia’s drone war in Ukraine?
Since Aug. 27, Kyiv has been living under a near-continuous drone campaign.
Russia shifted its long-range drone tactics that day, replacing the large swarms once or twice a week that Kyiv residents had become accustomed to with repeated waves across Ukrainian airspace.
The change was particularly noticeable in the capital, where attacks have increasingly continued into daytime hours.
As of Friday, Oct. 2, there has been no clear let-up. Repeated drone attacks have disrupted life in Kyiv, while strikes on warehouses, businesses and other civilian infrastructure have increasingly affected economic activity.
Russia has also sharply increased its use of jet-powered drones.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered UAVs in September as of Sept. 29, compared with 2,850 drones of all types in August.
“We have already had more drones this month than in the previous month overall,” Ihnat said, adding that Russian forces were continuing to attack in waves.
Kyiv and the Kyiv region remained the main focus, he said, while Kharkiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kherson and Dnipro were also repeatedly targeted.
The increase marks a dramatic escalation from earlier in the summer. Ihnat previously said Russia used about 350 jet-powered drones in June, 1,500 in July and 2,850 in August.
The new drones are significantly faster than the older piston-engine Shahed variants, making them harder for Ukraine’s existing low-cost interceptors to catch.
