articles.title: As tankers hit in Hormuz, Trump deploys thousands of US troops
articles.body:
The US military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the region, a US official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon
Yemen's Houthis launched attacks across front lines in Taiz governorate, seeking to build on their recent offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast. Yemeni government forces claimed to have inflicted heavy losses
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any alleged ceasefire agreements
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
US oil prices dropped sharply Friday as G7 leaders held urgent talks to coordinate action on lowering fuel prices, after the EU said earlier it would work with the International Energy Agency on releasing further stocks to global markets.
West Texas Intermediate was down 4.0 percent at $89.15 a barrel, having fallen as far as five percent, while the international benchmark Brent crude was down 2.6 percent at $99.63 after several days of trading above the psychological threshold of $100 a barrel.
Italy says EU naval mission in Red Sea still insufficient
Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said on Friday that contributions to an EU naval mission protecting Red Sea shipping remain insufficient, as Rome presses allies to do more to safeguard traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
In a statement issued after meeting in Rome with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Crosetto welcomed a decision by some member states to contribute additional assets to Aspides, without identifying the countries involved
However, those contributions are still not enough to guarantee the safe passage of merchant vessels, Crosetto said
Italy last month urged allies to increase their involvement, saying it was ready to deploy its own ships to avoid delays caused by the EU's decision-making process
Kallas said last month that Aspides would need more than 10 warships to effectively carry out its mission
The European Union's Aspides mission was launched in 2024 to protect commercial shipping from attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, with diplomats saying six warships are currently deployed
The Houthis have made rapid gains in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast, further complicating navigation in a region that also includes the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic had already fallen sharply amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.
IRGC member killed in Sistan-Baluchestan explosion
The Iranian Revolutionary Guard announced today, Friday, that one of its members was killed as a result of a roadside bomb in Sistan and Baluchestan province.
IRGC did not provide additional details regarding the circumstances of the explosion.
An IRGC member was killed by a roadside bomb in the Sistan-Baluchestan province. [Getty]
Saudi Arabia to host emergency meeting of Mecca pact
Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar told reporters that an emergency meeting of the strategic political defence committee under the pact between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia will be held next week, focuing on Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
Three in four families go hungry in parts of Yemen
Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the "absolutely devastating" impact of a surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said on Friday.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi group since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacksin 2022. The renewed conflict could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes.
Within just a few weeks, the fighting has driven the share of households without sufficient food to 74% in government-controlled areas accessible to WFP, the UN hunger body's Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations told reporters in Geneva. The total population of government-held areas is estimated at around 10 million people.
"The effect of this latest flare-up of insecurity on the food security situation threatens to be absolutely devastating," Hollingworth told reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome.
Israel Supreme Court overturns Joint List, Ra'am, Cassif ban
Israel's Supreme Court has overturned the ban on several Palestinian parties and a Jewish-Israeli candidate from running in the upcoming elections by Israel's Central Elections Committee (CEC).
In a decision announced on Friday, the court allowed the Joint-List—consisting of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad - alongside Ra'am, as well as Hadash MK Ofer Cassif, to run in the upcoming election set for 27 October.
An OPEC+ review to help to determine members’ 2027 oil output quotas has been delayed after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted projects to expand capacity across the Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, two sources close to the matter told Reuters.
OPEC+, which comprises the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries plus Russia and other allies, had ordered its production capacity review for all members in late 2025 before setting 2027 quotas, with completion due by the end of September 2026.
The deadline has slipped, the sources said, with one saying the review is now expected to be completed by mid-November.
Russia's A7 payment platform, sanctioned by the US for helping Iran evade sanctions as part of President Donald Trump's operation Economic Outcast, denied any links to Iran in a statement on Friday.
The US Treasury Department said on Thursday it was prohibiting any transactions with A7 and its sub-agents, calling the company "a significant transnational criminal organisation" and expanding previously imposed sanctions to the whole network.
A7, set up in 2024 by the defence sector-focused bank PSB, has become the leader in Russia's cross-border payments market as the country seeks to develop alternative payment systems with its main trading partners, such as China and India, spanning cryptocurrency, gold, and non-Western currencies.
"A7 categorically rejects any allegations that it has worked with Iran or terrorist organisations," the company said in a statement.
It added that it was providing "uninterrupted payment settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures".
EU warns diesel export ban would 'undermine trust' in US
The European Union on Friday slammed a threatened US ban on diesel exports, an idea floated by President Donald Trump, warning it would undermine trust in Washington as a reliable partner.
"We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," said European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, adding the bloc was ready to work with the International Energy Agency on the possible release of fuel reserves to bring down energy prices.
"The European Union is ready for collective action in the context of the International Energy Agency. It is their role to organise possible stock release," she told a press conference.
Diesel prices have sky rocketed due to the US-Israeli war on Iran. [Getty]
The average pump price of a litre of diesel fuel hit £2 ($2.64) in Britain for the first time on Friday, according to data compiled by the RAC motoring organisation, the latest landmark in a global surge in fuel prices.
The UK-wide average pump price of a litre of diesel reached 200.01 pence
Prices have been inching steadily higher after on Monday passing the previous high of 199.09 pence, which was set in June 2022 shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine
RAC head of policy Simon Williams said the rise in prices was "showing no signs of slowing"
Anti-Zionism is not antisemitism, US rights commission finds
A bipartisan US civil rights report found anti-Zionism is not inherently antisemitic, challenging Trump's crackdown on pro-Palestinian campus activism.
Yemen's Houthis and Saudi-backed forces fought over an area located not far from a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows, killing 80 combatants over the past day, sources on both sides told AFP on Friday.
Fighting in Taiz has raged since the Iran-backed Houthis began a lightning offensive against the internationally-recognised, Saudi-backed government.
In their offensive, the Houthis also took control of the whole of the Red Sea coast, notably the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which is crucial not just for Saudi energy exports but for global shipping as a whole.
According to Houthi military sources, at least 55 anti-government fighters have been killed over the past 24 hours in fighting against government troops in the Taiz area.
Government sources meanwhile told AFP that 26 troops on their side had been killed.
Fighting around Taiz is raging on several fronts, including in highlands overlooking the coastal areas seized in recent weeks by the Houthis.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, the chairman of the left-wing Balad party, said he would withdraw from Israel’s upcoming election after the country’s Supreme Court president said a majority of justices were prepared to uphold his disqualification.
Abu Shehadeh’s candidacy was challenged over an editorial he wrote in the newspaper The New Arab the day after Hamas-led 7 Oct. attack on Israel. The article did not condemn Hamas and argued that, given conditions in Gaza, it was surprising violence hadn’t erupted earlier.
In a subsequent article, Abu Shehadeh, a former member of Israel’s Knesset, called Hamas’ attack both unacceptable and a crime. He said he hadn’t known the scale of the violence when he wrote the first.
The court weighed whether his remarks violated an Israeli law barring candidates who reject Israel’s existence, incite racism or support armed struggle against Israel. His lawyers said that barring him would reinterpret the law and create a new threshold.
For Abu Shehadeh, who was running on the Arab parties’ Joint List, withdrawing avoids a court precedent that could be used to disqualify Palestinian candidates in future Israeli elections, his party said.
Macron urges major powers to act on diesel shortage
French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday urged G7 countries to avoid export restrictions to help ease fuel prices, as President Donald Trump suggested tapping Europe's strategic diesel reserves and backed curbs on US gas exports.
"The president stressed that G7 countries had a common interest in acting in a coordinated way, without export restrictions," the Elysee said after a call between the French and US leaders.
The US military has sent two Patriot missile batteries to the Gulf region in recent weeks, aimed at protecting oil and gas infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, according to Axios, citing two US officials and an additional regional source.
Yemeni military commander killed during clashes with Houthis
The Yemeni Ministry of Interior announced the killing of the Chief of Staff of the Emergency Forces of the Ministry of Interior, Major General Muhammad Salem Abdullah Al-Khawlani, during confrontations with the Houthi group on the Al-Kadha front in Taiz Governorate, southwest of the country.
The ministry indicated that Al-Khawlani was killed while "performing his national duty" against the Houthis, considering that his killing represents a "loss for the security establishment," stressing that government forces will continue their confrontations against the Houthis.
Al-Khawlani is considered the highest-ranking security and military official whose death the Yemeni government has announced since the return of the military escalation last July.
EU discusses with IEA when to release diesel due to Iran war
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam made a visit to the Nabatieh area in southern Lebanon which has been at the forefront of Israel's near-daily attacks despite an alleged ceasefire agreement.
El Al airline cancels flights for Israelis from Dubai
Israel's flag carrier El Al said Friday it had cancelled repatriation flights from Dubai, which it had planned due to flydubai suspending service to Tel Aviv following an in-flight attack.
An El Al spokeswoman told AFP that flights Friday were cancelled with no new date set. The transportation ministry said Israel had not yet secured the approval it needed in the United Arab Emirates to run the flights.
A man with dual UK-Iranian citizenship was arrested Thursday over a mysterious "major incident" at an airbase in southwest England as Israel said it had warned London about an attack.
The sixth arrest came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford", a base used by the US military in its war against Iran.
Iran denounced the British government's "baseless accusations" and condemned London for making military bases and facilities under its jurisdiction "available for the planning and execution of the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran".
Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement Thursday that a "25-year-old man, a dual UK/Iranian national, was arrested" in Westminster in central London "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts".
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Majid Al-Nuzaili said that the air force’s warplanes carried out 20 precise air strikes during the past three hours, targeting “movements, reinforcements, gatherings, elements, vehicles and military vehicles” belonging to the Houthis in Taiz Governorate.
Trump vows to hit Iran 'very hard' if linked to flydubai
US President Donald Trump warned on Thursday that Iran will be "hit very hard" if it is found to be linked to a pilot's attack on a flydubai flight to Israel.
Trump's warning came as the United Arab Emirates opened an investigation into whether the incident was linked to terrorism and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the suspect had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
"I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes but we're working on it right now," Trump told reporters Thursday when asked at the White House whether Iran was involved in what happened on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
On whether the United States would retaliate against Iran if it was found responsible, Trump replied: "Oh, they'll be hit very hard, don't worry."

articles.title: AI weapons systems are already here. Algorithms must not decide who lives and dies | Kenneth Roth
articles.body:
As tech leaders warn about the threats of artificial intelligence, most conjure up images of AI agents running amok, such as hacking systems used to run our critical infrastructure, banks or even militaries. Yet one serious danger is mentioned less frequently – the threat posed by AI–empowered lethal weapons. Fully autonomous versions of these weapons are colloquially known as killer robots.
Israel’s conduct in Gaza shows that, in an important respect, such AI weapon systems are already here. An algorithm has been deciding who lives and who dies.
For more than a decade, governments have been meeting in Geneva to stop the development of autonomous AI weapons. In early September, 128 governments met to approve a report that could serve as the foundation for a binding treaty.
But a collection of lawyers sent by Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin teamed up to water it down. Notably, they weakened a provision that requires humans to review military targets developed by AI before a strike.
Fully autonomous weapons remain the focus; the use of AI to determine targets for conventional weapons is not. At risk is the longstanding quest to maintain a “human in the loop” – that is, meaningful or effective “human control” of AI-empowered weaponry.
For many people, talk of killer robots conjures up images of Arnold Schwarzenegger’s The Terminator. I have often thought about the problem in the context of the Tahrir Square uprising at the height of the Arab spring that led to the ouster of the Egyptian president Hosni Mubarak.
Mubarak’s fate was sealed when the Egyptian army made clear it would refuse to fire on Egyptian protesters. But killer robots would have had no such qualms. If Mubarak had been able to deploy them, he might have stayed in power.
The negotiators in Geneva are not even addressing this problem. The Trump-Putin lawyers made sure that the agreed report referred only to war, not repression.
Today, amid the drone warfare in eastern Ukraine, Russian and Ukrainian troops are experimenting with fully autonomous weapons to overcome jamming of the signals used to control drones. We can expect these nascent deployments to expand.
Yet the “killer robot” metaphor is deceptive. If we look at targeting decisions more expansively, AI has already taken over. In Gaza, the Israeli military is using AI to target Palestinians.
Israel has long monitored phone communications in that territory. After the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israel used an AI system called “Lavender” to uncover patterns that it equated with the phone of a Hamas operative. People whose phones AI determined met these criteria could be killed.
Because it was easier to target suspects at home, a separate automated system called “Where’s Daddy?” tracked them there, meaning that their families were often killed too. There was no pretense that Hamas was using its operatives’ homes for military purposes. It was simply easier for the AI system to find suspected Hamas fighters where they slept. The families were the collateral damage.
Theoretically, a human remained in the loop because an AI-picked target was routed through intelligence officers who approved it and sent it to others who launched the attack. In fact, this human role was nominal.
In the past, Israeli targeting decisions were subject to significant review. But in Israel’s killing spree that followed the Hamas attack, the intense demand for targets took precedence over such review.
Israeli intelligence officers who received the AI selections routinely passed them to the attackers without second guessing. As one officer described: “I would invest 20 seconds for each target at this stage, and do dozens of them every day. I had zero added-value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. It saved a lot of time.”
From computer to killing, the human judgment exercised was perfunctory – a “rubber stamp”. In essence, an algorithm played God.
One Israeli officer suggested the practice might be justified because AI makes better decisions than humans do. It is dispassionate, while people’s judgment can be clouded, such as by the animosity toward all Palestinians that some Israelis felt after the Hamas attack.
As one Israeli soldier explained: “I have much more trust in a statistical mechanism than a soldier who lost a friend two days ago. Everyone there, including me, lost people on October 7. The machine did it coldly. And that made it easier.”
Yet AI algorithms are inevitably affected by human input. How much evidence is required to identify someone as a Hamas fighter? What margin of error is tolerated?
The answer to such questions depends on the judgment of the AI programmers and their commanders – ordinary Israelis who might have devalued Palestinian civilian life in the fury that followed the Hamas attack. Even the Israeli military conceded that about 10% of the human targets slated for assassination were not members of the Hamas military wing at all.
The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, epitomized the heedless attitude toward Palestinian civilians when he said: “It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It’s not true, this rhetoric about civilians were not aware, not involved – it’s absolutely not true. They could’ve risen up, fought against that evil regime.”
That same contempt contributed to the Israeli military’s shocking willingness to tolerate civilian deaths. The Israeli military permitted an anticipated 20 dead for the killing of a mere suspected low-level Hamas fighter.
Under the rule of proportionality, international humanitarian law prohibits a wartime attack if it “may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life … which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated”. Although international law doesn’t specify the number of civilian casualties that are acceptable in a given situation, virtually no legal expert considers Israel’s shocking 20-to-one ratio to be lawful.
These are war crimes. They reflect an appalling devaluing of Palestinian civilian life.
Evoking for me Hannah Arendt’s “banality of evil”, ordinary soldiers became complicit in extraordinary cruelty by trusting what they call the “system”. The essence of that system remained people – the generals who ordered its creation, the military lawyers who excused the unjustifiable, the programmers who tweaked the algorithm, the intelligence officers who passed on the computer-generated targets, and the soldiers who launched the attack.
But part of what made it easier to trust the system was the pseudo-scientific precision of AI. We are all familiar with the breezy, authoritative tone of today’s chatbots. When AI is used for targeting, it brings a similar feigned omniscience to killing.
When inevitably flawed human beings make decisions, they can expect others to challenge them. But AI makes it easier for us to defer to its judgments. That deference risks magnifying the human biases that inevitably infect any AI system.
As we seek to curb killer robots, we should also remain attentive to AI that can lull us into complacency about other targeting. The International Committee of the Red Cross calls it “automation bias”.
To have meaningful human control of AI, we need not just nominal endorsement of its decisions. We need intense questioning of its product, and accountability for commanders when junior officers fall short.
Only that skepticism has any hope of ensuring that soldiers who deploy AI remember that real human beings are at the end of the kill chain they enable. Even in war, people should never be snuffed out by the mechanical application of an algorithm.
- 
  Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

articles.title: "It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the story of a Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
articles.body:
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the story of a Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
Mariupol-born Dmytro Hetmanov was used to medicine, with all its difficulties and losses: his entire family works in healthcare, and he himself had barely taken off his white coat since 2013.
But on 24 February 2022, his life was divided into "before" and "after". Suddenly, the civilian urological surgeon found himself having to try and save dozens of people who had been wounded in Russian attacks – many of them fatally.
One of the most challenging cases of Dmytro's life was a teenager who died on the operating table. It was March 2022. A father carried in his wounded son, a boy of 14 or 15.
At first the teenager's wound appeared minor – just a small hole in his chest. But before long, his blood pressure began to drop and his heartbeat slowed. The doctors tried to resuscitate him, but nothing worked.
Dmytro performed a thoracotomy, opening up the boy's chest to carry out direct cardiac massage. It was then that he saw that the heart and blood vessels had been torn apart. There was no way to save him.
The boy's father was waiting outside the theatre.
"I couldn't talk to him. I just couldn't bring myself to do it. I turned around and moved on to the next patient," Dmytro recalls.
At the time, Dmytro was working at Mariupol City Hospital No. 1. People had been bringing wounded civilians in from the early days of the full-scale war. For three weeks, he saved lives in a city where fighting was raging.
When it became almost impossible to continue working, Dmytro left the besieged city with his parents and neighbours. He then spent two years working as a urological surgeon at a university hospital in Poland, but eventually he returned to Ukraine to join the military.
Today, Dmytro is operating on wounded people once again, this time as a military surgeon with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia tells his story.
"I don't remember even a single one of my patients' faces." Surviving Mariupol
Dmytro Hetmanov, who now goes by the alias Hetmani, was born into a family of doctors in Mariupol. Medicine has been his passion since childhood, he says.
In 2013, he graduated from Kharkiv National Medical University and began a urology internship in Donetsk. When the city was occupied by the Russians in 2014, he collected his documents and transferred to a hospital in Kharkiv. After completing his internship in 2015, he returned to his native Mariupol.
Shortly before the start of the full-scale invasion, Dmytro suspected that the war might reach his city. On 23 February 2022, he called his ex-wife and asked her to pack her things.
Dmytro went to his parents' home that night. At around 05:00 on 24 February, he heard the first explosions. His ex-wife left the city with their six-year-old daughter, and Dmytro went to work.
"Everyone was in utter despair, except for some of our junior medical staff. There were some pro-Russian people among them who were delighted that it was happening. They were like, 'The Russians will come now, Putin will hand out money,'" Dmytro recalls.
Some of the doctors left the city during the first few days of the full-scale war. Of the 11 or so urologists working at the hospital, only three initially remained. Later one of them stopped coming in: he lived in another part of Mariupol and could no longer get to work.
The remaining medical staff worked alternate shifts: 24 hours at the hospital, 24 hours off.
"We had a team there: about three or four surgeons stayed. There were two trauma surgeons and two anaesthetists, although in fact there was only one, because the other one took over the running of the hospital," Dmytro says.
The number of wounded patients increased dramatically when Russian forces entered the settlements near Mariupol, including Sartana and Talakivka. More and more casualties began arriving from those areas.
In the early days the emergency services were still able to take the wounded to hospital. Once they stopped operating, people had to find their own way to safety – driving in their own vehicles or walking, sometimes carrying wounded people in their arms.
"It was mostly shrapnel wounds. There weren't any drones back then, but there was a lot of tubed artillery, so it was shrapnel from the shells. And there were penetrating wounds – to the abdomen, chest and so on. We stabilised the patients, then operated on them and continued to care for them afterwards," Dmytro recalls.
Around 30-50 people would arrive at the hospital every day, and around a third of them would need surgery.
"A lot of desperate people whose homes had already been destroyed came to us," Hetmani recollects. "They were looking for shelter and protection in the hospital. The hospital reception was on the ground floor of our surgery building. People used to gather in the corridors.
At first the Russians tried not to hit the hospital. But by mid-March we'd started getting hit too. The hospital was near the Illich Steelworks, where marines from the 36th Brigade were holding the defence. They were under fire from everything, and so were we – tubed artillery, multiple-launch rocket systems, ballistic missiles, mortar fire. Eventually, small-arms fire started up nearby as well. There was close-quarters fighting not far from the hospital."
The doctors were working with no electricity or running water and insufficient medical supplies. By early March, petrol stations, pharmacies and shops had been almost completely emptied.
At home, Dmytro's family shared food with their neighbours. They ate whatever anyone had left – preserves, tinned food and supplies from their freezers. At the hospital, meanwhile, the medical staff prioritised feeding the wounded.
"We didn't eat much. The portions were very small. The wounded were given food first. We'd just grab a little something ourselves and carry on working," Dmytro recalls.
Water was also hard to come by. After his shifts, Dmytro and his family would go to a well near Petrovskyi Park, not far from the cemetery. They boiled the water from the cemetery area and drank it. They collected snow for washing dishes and other household needs. Fortunately, State Emergency Service workers were at least able to deliver non-potable water to the hospital.
Eventually the medical staff ran out of anaesthetics, sutures and dressing materials. Worst of all, however, the hospital had no blood for transfusions. As a result, the post-operative mortality rate was very high, Hetmani recalls.
"Of course the situation in Mariupol was terrible. I've forgotten a lot of it. The mind pushes the bad things away. For example, I can't remember a single face of any of the patients we helped in Mariupol. I don't remember them at all," he says.
There were some lighter moments, however. Dmytro recalls one risky expedition to find diesel.
"I'd come home from a shift and my parents were cooking outside. We'd had a bit to drink – I was stressed. Then some guys we knew came over and said, 'Everyone's looting the petrol stations. You can get some diesel there.'
And I thought, 'We've got a generator at the hospital. Let's grab some containers, go and get some diesel and take it to the hospital,'" Dmytro recalls.
Dmytro drove to a petrol station near the Illich Steelworks. To the sound of artillery fire booming all around him, he drew off the diesel and poured it into plastic containers. He took it to the hospital, then collected some empty containers that had been used for dialysis water and made several more trips.
"When the fuel there ran out, we went to another petrol station where the marines were handing out diesel. I said, 'Guys, let me through, it's for the hospital.' I hadn't even changed yet – I was still wearing my scrubs. And one of the marines says over the radio, 'There's some half-drunk doctor here demanding diesel,'" Dmytro smiles.
Dmytro managed to obtain around 300 litres of diesel – enough to keep the hospital running for four or five days. When he finally returned home, his mother was crying. She had thought he had been killed somewhere in the city.
"The Drama Theatre was burning before my eyes." The escape
On 15 March, Dmytro and his colleagues had an especially hard shift. Many wounded people were brought to the hospital, and the surgeons operated until late into the night. When the work was finally over, Dmytro went to sleep, only to be woken the next morning by an explosion nearby.
"A FAB [a high-explosive aerial bomb – ed.] had landed somewhere nearby. I woke up and went to the stairwell to have a smoke. You could see the village of Volonterivka from a nearby window, and there was already small-arms fire there. I thought, another day or two and the Russians will be here [in the hospital]. We have to do something," the doctor recalls.
That day, the medical staff gathered to discuss how they would continue working. Several older colleagues who could not leave because they were taking care of sick family members decided to stay at the hospital, while the rest of the team decided to try to escape the city.
Dmytro decided to leave as well. He says he realised that once Russian forces were established there, someone might snitch on him because of his pro-Ukraine views.
Back home, Dmytro told his parents they needed to pack immediately. The family also took some neighbours with them whose cars had been destroyed.
"There were seven people and a cat in my car. And my parents had another two or three people in theirs," he says.
To leave in the direction of Berdiansk and then on to Zaporizhzhia, they had to cross Mariupol. Dmytro lived in the Kalmiuskyi district, so their route took them through the city centre, where intense fighting was underway. There was no humanitarian corridor at the time – the family set off at their own risk.
On the way, Dmytro drove past the Drama Theatre. That day, 16 March, Russian forces had bombed the building, where hundreds of civilians had been sheltering.
"It was still burning before my eyes," he recalls.
Dmytro and his family headed west through the port towards the road to Manhush. They managed to avoid the fighting. A convoy of cars had already formed on the road, full of other people trying to escape Mariupol.
Then came the Russian checkpoints. At a checkpoint in Manhush, Russian soldiers nearly confiscated Dmytro's car. He was eventually allowed through after giving money to one of them.
At around 01:00, they reached Tokmak, where they met some of Dmytro's colleagues. Another Russian checkpoint lay ahead, but no one was being allowed through at night.
"There was this huge line of refugees. It was bitterly cold, around -10°C. And I had hardly any petrol left, so I couldn't turn on the heater. Nobody slept that night," Dmytro says.
At around 06:00, the barrier was raised. After being checked, the convoy continued on its way. Dmytro says they passed through around 10 checkpoints in Tokmak alone. Beyond Vasylivka, he saw signs of fighting and burnt-out military vehicles, both Ukrainian and Russian.
Near the line of contact, Russian troops stopped the convoy of civilian vehicles and used it as cover.
"There was a Russian armoured personnel carrier in front, people moving in formation on either side, and all this whistling and roaring overhead – mortar rounds, artillery fire. And they stopped us and used us as cover. They kept us there for about 40 minutes.
I'm sitting behind the wheel thinking, 'Well, that's it. We survived Mariupol, the Russian shells didn't get us, and now our own guys are going to finish us off,'" Dmytro admits.
But the Ukrainian troops did not fire when they saw the civilian vehicles. Eventually, the Russian soldiers allowed the convoy to continue. A bridge on the road to Zaporizhzhia had been destroyed, so the drivers had to take other roads around it. Finally, Dmytro and his family reached Ukrainian-controlled territory.
"I saw the Ukrainian flag and our police officers. I'd never been so happy to see the police in my life. We were home," he recalls.
The police met the evacuees and helped them reach a hub for displaced people in Zaporizhzhia which had been set up in a hypermarket. Dmytro and his family had left Mariupol with almost no food or water, so the first thing they did was look for something to eat.
"I got a can of Coca-Cola and a fresh, warm French baguette. It was the best thing I'd eaten in two weeks," the doctor recalls.
Shortly after Dmytro escaped, Russian forces razed the Mariupol hospital where he had worked to the ground.
"Friends were joining the Armed Forces while I was sitting here. It really ate away at me." Poland
Dmytro's ex-wife and daughter found refuge in Kraków, staying at the home of a Polish woman who was also a medical professional. She invited Dmytro to join them – as the father of a child with a disability, he was entitled to leave Ukraine.
"To be honest, I thought I'd go back straight away. I thought I'd have a month off, then return and join the Armed Forces. Because the guys I'd worked with joined up almost immediately. Most of them went into the Medical Forces. But my ex-wife said to me, 'Why would you go off to fight? You have a child, and you can work as a doctor in Poland. Give it a try.'
So I thought, all right, I'll give it a try. I started going around hospitals and looking [for jobs] online. I was told to get lost a few times. Then I found Professor Andrzej Paradysz in Katowice. He's an amazing person, a very empathetic doctor. I told him my story and he took me on straight away. He has a soft spot for Ukrainians because his family has roots in Lviv. He treated me extremely well," Dmytro recalls.
Later his ex-wife and daughter moved to the US, while Dmytro stayed in Katowice with his parents. At first he assisted doctors during operations. He later obtained his licence and began operating independently. Within six months, he had learnt Polish fairly well and become close with his colleagues. But he says he was plagued by guilt.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life. It just gnawed away at me. I was constantly watching the same Dvizh footage [a YouTube project by the 3rd Assault Brigade – ed.] on social media or military videos.
Then my parents went to Kyiv. They'd been really homesick and had neither the energy nor the inclination to settle in Poland. I told them, 'If that's how you feel, then go.' Once everyone had left, I was on my own. I became terribly depressed. And eventually I couldn't take it any more," Dmytro recalls.
After two years in Poland, Dmytro handed in his resignation to the professor and left a few days later. He obtained a letter of recommendation for a military unit, took it to a military enlistment office, completed basic military training and signed a three-year contract as a soldier.
Dmytro decided to take a break from medicine and joined one of the regiments in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
"I wanted a bit of a break from medicine. I was also interested in working with maps and spatial orientation. I've been interested in military equipment and geography since I was a child," he says.
He spent around six months working in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblasts, and occasionally in Luhansk Oblast. But eventually he began to miss military medicine. His original crew was also starting to be disbanded, as the regiment was being expanded into a brigade.
"I'd done enough 'flying', put it that way. I realised I missed medicine. I was already starting to forget a lot of things, and my hands weren't getting any practice. It's like being a guitarist or a pianist – you've got to keep your hand in," he says.
In 2025 Dmytro saw an ad on social media for the medical battalion of the 3rd Assault Brigade. He applied for a position.
"I didn't want to work in some hospital in a town or city. I like working closer to the battlefield. I wanted to be nearer the action," he says.
"What I probably like most is the camaraderie." Serving with the 3rd Army Corps
Dmytro is once again working as a surgeon with the 4th Separate Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps, but his range of duties is now considerably broader than when he worked as a urologist. For one thing, he has taken part in brain surgery for the first time.
"I'd never operated on someone's head in my life. But Vahus, our neurosurgeon, said to me, 'Come along with me and get some practice.' I assisted him and sutured the dura mater. I have general surgical skills, but I'd never worked in that area before. With his help, though, it was interesting to try something new," Dmytro says.
Dmytro had also never performed an amputation in civilian practice, but he can now take part in such operations as well.
The medical team most often treats soldiers with limb injuries. Many have minor shrapnel wounds or gunshot fractures. Trauma surgeons primarily handle these cases, with Dmytro assisting them.
Dmytro himself most enjoys operating on penetrating abdominal wounds.
"I like operating on the abdomen. I used to work in endourology, so I'm not afraid to go in there now," he says.
Not all of his work in the battalion involves combat injuries. Soldiers also come to Dmytro with ordinary urological conditions. He performs ultrasound scans, gives medical advice and sometimes operates on them. On days when there are few wounded soldiers, he devotes his time to routine procedures.
"I've been with the battalion for almost a year now, and we've all learned to work really well together. We have a great team. We're all very close, we work well together and communicate well with each other. What I probably like most is the camaraderie, the sense that we're all brothers," he says.
Hetmani says he hasn't regretted his decision to serve for a single day, although he does miss his daughter.
"I can see she's upset that I'm not there with her," he says. "Maybe she sees other children's dads picking them up from school, and she doesn't have that. She doesn't talk about it, but I can tell it bothers her.
But this is my duty. I volunteered, so ultimately it was my decision. I need to finish what needs to be done here, and then I can think about what comes next."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Five Interceptors for Russian Jet Drones, One Could Reach 400 Units by Month’s End
articles.body:

Ukraine Tests Five Interceptors for Russian Jet Drones, One Could Reach 400 Units by Month’s End
Ukraine is testing five high-speed interceptor drone designs intended to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones, with one model expected to enter production at a rate of around 400 units by the end of October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times, as reported by RBC-Ukraine on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine is accelerating efforts to develop interceptors capable of engaging the faster jet-powered drones increasingly used by Russia in aerial attacks.
Of the five interceptor designs currently under development, one has advanced far enough for Ukraine to potentially manufacture approximately 400 units by the end of October. The remaining four models are still undergoing testing.
However, Zelenskyy said engine shortages remain a major obstacle to scaling up interceptor production, as Ukraine continues to depend heavily on imports. While some engines are produced domestically, he said current output is insufficient to meet production needs.
The development of new interceptor drones comes as Ukraine works to expand its domestically produced weapons capabilities. On October 1, Zelenskyy announced the first combat deployment of Ukraine’s FP-7 tactical ballistic missile during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Footage published on his official social media channels showed the missile being launched from an undisclosed location.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next is production. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy wrote alongside the footage.
Ukraine’s push to develop faster interceptors also comes as Russia expands production of jet-powered attack drones. Russia is manufacturing approximately 2,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month and has accumulated an estimated stockpile of 10,000 conventional piston-engine strike UAVs.

articles.title: Trump vows Iran war to end "very quickly" as more troops head to Mideast
articles.body:
Live Updates: Trump vows Iran war will end "right after the election" or sooner, as 9,000 troops head to Mideast
What to know about the Iran war today:
- The USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Group are heading for the Middle East, a U.S. official tells CBS News. When they arrive, the U.S. could have three aircraft carrier groups, with around 20,000 forces, in the region.
- "I'm ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended," President Trump said Thursday, insisting that Iran's ruling theocracy "is ready to fold up," and that he believes the U.S. will win the seven-month war "right after the election," if not before the U.S. midterms in early November.
- The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis accused the rebels on Thursday of attacking an electricity distribution station in the Saudi city of Medina, home to the second holiest site in Islam. The alleged attack drew strong condemnation from across the Muslim world.
80 combatants reportedly killed as Houthis battle for ground near Yemen's Red Sea coast
Intense fighting between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed forces over territory near a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows saw 80 combatants killed over the past day alone, sources on both sides told the French news agency AFP on Friday.
Fighting near the Red Sea coast in Taiz province has raged since the Houthis launched a lightning offensive weeks ago against Yemen's internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government.
The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including territory along the the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the sea and thus a crucial chokepoint not only for Saudi energy exports, but for global shipping as a whole.
According to Houthi military sources, at least 55 anti-government fighters have been killed over the past 24 hours in fighting against government troops in the Taiz area. Government sources meanwhile told AFP that 26 troops on that side had been killed.
Fighting around Taiz is raging on several fronts, including in highlands overlooking the coastal areas seized in recent weeks by the Houthis. The rebels have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, however, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The U.N.'s special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grunberg, said Thursday he was alarmed by developments in Taiz, adding that the Houthis' operations pose "grave risks to the civilian population."
CBS/AFP
Netanyahu says if anyone "dispatched" FlyDubai copilot, they "will pay a very heavy price"
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Friday that authorities were investigating whether the FlyDubai co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flight to Israel with 174 people on board could have been "dispatched" by some third party.
The Israeli leader vowed that if that is found to be the case, whoever sent him would "pay a very heavy price."
The co-pilot of the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv allegedly stabbed the aircraft's captain and tried to crash the plane before being restrained by a group of passengers.
"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Netanyahu said Friday. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Iran could be linked to the incident, without offering any evidence or basis for the conclusion.
Asked by reporters if he had been briefed about any possible links between Iran and the co-pilot, Mr. Trump said: "I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes," adding: "But we're working on it right now."
When asked if the co-pilot could have been working for or with Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, Mr. Trump said he "could've been, yeah."
In response to a question about potential U.S. retaliation if Tehran was connected to the attack, Mr. Trump said "they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry."
Lebanese prime minister says country cannot rebuild from war alone
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Friday that rebuilding regions destroyed in the latest Israel-Hezbollah war is beyond the state's capacity, calling for funding as he visited the heavily damaged south.
"I am aware of the magnitude of the crisis," Salam said in Nabatieh, a major southern city hit hard by Israeli airstrikes. "But the scale of the needs exceeds the capacities of the Lebanese state and its ability to bear these burdens alone."
"We still need significant funding" for reconstruction, the prime minister said.
Lebanese militant group Hezbollah drew the country into the broader Iran war in March by attacking Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion. The fighting followed a previous Israel-Hezbollah conflict that erupted in 2023, which led to an all-out war the following year. Lebanese authorities have put the overall death toll from both rounds of fighting at more than 8,900.
Hundreds of thousands of people remain displaced, mainly from the south, where Israeli forces have occupied a self-declared "security zone" stretching about six miles into Lebanon from the shared border with Israel.
Last month, Salam said the estimated total cost of the two wars could exceed $27 billion.
CBS/AFP
Iranian lawmakers advance legislation to declare full control over Strait of Hormuz
Iran's parliament has completed a committee-level consideration of a proposed bill that would establish what lawmakers frame as the future Iranian management of the Strait of Hormuz, including the imposition of fees on commercial vessels using the vital waterway.
Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament's National Security Commission, told the semi-official Tasnim news agency the proposed "Strategic Action Plan for Ensuring Security and Sustainable Development of the Strait of Hormuz" would preserve Iranian control over all traffic through the strait in line with Iran's national interests and security.
Under the bill, Iran would charge vessels for services including navigation, environmental protection, bunkering and fuel. Ships linked to Israel, countries deemed hostile by Iran, countries that have carried out military action against Iran, or vessels carrying military cargo would be prohibited from passing through the strait under the legislation, Ghashghavi said.
Ships from countries not considered hostile would have to obtain authorization from Iran's General Staff of the Armed Forces before transiting the waterway, he added.
The bil will now be debated and voted on by Iran's full parliament and, if approved, would then require review by Iran's powerful Guardian Council and other authorities before becoming law in the country.
The Trump administration rejects Iran's rhetoric suggesting it will control the strait going forward, as well as Tehran's current demands for all commercial vessels to seek permission for transits.
Iran has repeatedly targeted tankers and other ships it accuses of using the strait without its permission, however, seriously limiting the flow of oil and gas out of the Persian gulf since the war began.
U.S. sent more Patriot missiles to protect oil and gas sites in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, Axios reports
The U.S. has sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to help protect oil and gas facilities, Axios reported Thursday, citing two U.S. officials and another unnamed regional source.
President Trump has in recent days threatened to resume U.S. strikes on Iran, telling TIME magazine it was possible that he could give the orders after the November U.S. midterm elections, saying: "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace."
In August, Mr. Trump threatened possible U.S. strikes on Iranian energy and civilian infrastructure, but Saudi Arabia and Qatar urged him not to give the order, according to Axios, out of concern Iran would retaliate by hitting their oil and gas facilities.
Speaking Thursday, Mr. Trump said he was "ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended," insisting the Islamic Republic was "ready to fold up" and that he believed the U.S. would win the war "right after the election," if not before the U.S. midterms.
Iran-Iraq flights to resume soon, says Iraqi ambassador
Flights between Iran and Iraq will resume soon, Iraqi Ambassador to Tehran Yasser Abdul Zahra Al-Hajjaj has said, as the two countries work to resolve disruptions to air travel in the wake of the U.S. imposing sanctions that bar virtually all nations and entities from collaborating with Iranian carriers.
Following a meeting with Iranian Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh, Al-Hajjaj said the neighboring nations were examining mechanisms and initiatives to address the issue amid what he described as U.S. pressure on air transportation.
He highlighted the large number of Muslim pilgrims, students and businesspeople who typically travel between Iran and Iraq, as well as the countries' extensive economic and social ties.
"Flights between the two countries will resume soon," Al-Hajjaj said, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim News agency.
In August the U.S. announced a raft of new sanctions against Iran, including on the country's aviation industry, which has led to multiple countries canceling flights to and from Iran.
Europe discussing plan for diesel stock releases amid pressure from U.S., Reuters reports
European Union nations have discussed a proposed release of additional diesel reserves amid U.S. pressure to ease fuel prices, a source with knowledge of the discussion told the Reuters news agency on Friday.
In a Friday call, various EU governments debated a French proposal for a joint release of 50 million barrels of diesel, the source told Reuters, and for International Energy Agency member countries to release 50 million barrels of crude oil.
The countries also discussed the idea that any agreement on diesel reserve releases should include a commitment from the U.S. to not unilaterally ban diesel exports, the source said. G7 leaders may discuss the proposal further on Friday on a call, Reuters reported.
Saudi coalition accuses Houthis of drone attack on holy city of Medina
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said Thursday that the Houthis struck an electricity distribution station in Medina, Saudi Arabia, a city that is home to the second holiest site in Islam. The alleged attack drew strong condemnation from the Muslim world.
Fighting has intensified significantly in Yemen in recent weeks, with government forces reporting multiple airstrikes on Houthi targets overnight and AFP journalists hearing explosions in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthi drone struck Medina's Taibah electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque, Islam's second holiest site. The Houthis denied any involvement.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station early Tuesday morning.
"The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the Terrorist Houthi Militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used," he said in a statement.
The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network.
CBS/AFP
Trump says Iran "ready to fold up" and "will be very quickly ended"
Speaking in Denton, Texas, Thursday night at the Peterbilt Motors facility, President Trump said Iran "is ready to fold up."
He said he believed the U.S. would win the war "right after the election," referring to the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
"Maybe before the election," he added.
"I'm ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended," the president said, promising that U.S. energy prices, which have soared due to the war, would be "rapidly, rapidly coming" down.
Mr. Trump said the U.S. was "trying to be nice" to Iran's current leader, but "we don't know who the hell to deal with, to be honest with you. Nobody wants to be president."
U.S. military deployment in the Middle East set to swell by some 9,000 forces
The USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Group are headed to the Middle East, a U.S. official confirmed to CBS News on Thursday.
That could mean a total of three U.S. carrier strike groups and two amphibious ready groups being deployed to the region at the same time, at least unless and until one of the groups is rotated out of the region.
A U.S. official told the Associated Press that some 7,000 sailors and 2,000 U.S. Marines were on their way as part of the deployment. That would bring the total number of U.S. forces in the region to approximately 20,000, along with hundreds of vessels and aircraft.
The forces could arrive by the end of October, the official told the AP.
The USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are already in the area, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
Trump suggests Iran may be linked to FlyDubai incident
President Trump suggested Thursday that Iran could be linked to the alleged attempted hijacking of an Israel-bound FlyDubai plane.
When asked by reporters if he had been briefed about any links between Iran and the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the flight's captain and attempted to crash the plane before being subdued by passengers, Mr. Trump said, "we're working on it right now."
"I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes," Mr. Trump said. "But we're working on it right now."
Mr. Trump did not provide further details.
When asked if the co-pilot could have been working for or with Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, Mr. Trump said he "could've been, yeah."
In response to a question about potential U.S. retaliation if Tehran was connected to the attack, Mr. Trump said, "they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry."

articles.title: How Vyacheslav Volodin secured a record third term as speaker of Russia’s State Duma — and why Putin keeps him there
articles.body:
How Vyacheslav Volodin secured a record third term as speaker of Russia’s State Duma — and why Putin keeps him there
Newly elected State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin opened the new parliament’s first session with some advice for lawmakers:
History shows that our country cannot be defeated from the outside. All our problems come from within: conflict, betrayal by the elites, weak leadership. So we need to learn from this. We must not lose our country.
Volodin became speaker of parliament’s lower house for the third time, breaking Boris Gryzlov’s record. Gryzlov served twice, during the fourth and fifth parliamentary terms.
In 2021, ahead of elections to the eighth State Duma, United Russia leader Dmitry Medvedev expressed interest in becoming speaker. But Vladimir Putin did not approve putting him at the top of the party’s candidate list.
The same thing happened in 2026. Kremlin-friendly media reported that Medvedev might head the top three or top five candidates on the party’s list. Meduza’s sources said Medvedev himself was lobbying for this arrangement, but Putin had not approved it.
Medvedev was again left off the party’s national candidate list, closing off his path to the speakership. The main beneficiaries of the former president’s exclusion were Volodin and the Kremlin’s domestic policy team, which feared that Medvedev’s involvement in the campaign could further depress United Russia’s already low approval ratings.
Volodin began his political career in the Saratov region. In 1990, the 26-year-old, who held a doctorate in agricultural sciences, won a seat on Saratov’s city council as an independent, defeating a candidate from the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
After the Soviet Union collapsed, Volodin effectively worked as a political consultant, helping Yury Kitov, a member of the Russian republic’s Supreme Soviet, become mayor of Saratov. He persuaded city council members to approve Kitov’s candidacy, even though the regional administration backed someone else.
Once Kitov took office, Volodin became his deputy and chief of staff at city hall. He soon became deputy governor of the Saratov region, then led by one of Russia’s most colorful governors, Dmitry Ayatskov.
By the late 1990s, Ayatskov had grown suspicious of his young, ambitious deputy, whose responsibilities included finances, social policy, and infrastructure. Their conflict prompted Volodin to leave for Moscow, where he began building Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov’s political movement, Fatherland.
In 1999, Fatherland formed a bloc with All Russia, a movement of powerful regional governors, and secured the support of former Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov. As a result, the Fatherland–All Russia bloc was seen as a likely winner of the State Duma elections.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin was promoting the Unity bloc and the Union of Right Forces, whose main opponent was Fatherland–All Russia. Putin, then prime minister, openly backed Unity.
The Communists won the largest share of the vote (24.3%), Unity came second (23.32%), and Fatherland finished only third (13.33%). But Volodin won a seat in parliament, where he was appointed deputy leader of the Luzhkov–Primakov bloc’s parliamentary faction and later became its leader.
In 2001, Fatherland became Unity’s ally, and two years later they merged into a single party. “Our three organizations supported the president. His last name is Putin,” Volodin told Kommersant at the time.
Volodin rose quickly through United Russia’s ranks. In 2005, he was appointed secretary of its General Council, a key governing body. “There were no other candidates,” a party source told Kommersant at the time. “He [Volodin] has an appetite for this work and the political experience the job requires.” Another source told the newspaper that Vladislav Surkov, then head of the presidential administration’s domestic policy team, was entirely happy with Volodin as a candidate. Volodin owed his appointment to Surkov.
Volodin quickly imposed his own bureaucratic order on the party. A Saratov political consultant who has known him for years told Meduza on condition of anonymity that even before his appointment to the General Council, Volodin wanted to make United Russia’s branch in his home region a model for the rest:
Everything that later became standard practice in United Russia [nationwide] was tried out in Saratov. For example, they started collecting campaign money from businesspeople — developers, retailers — through a centralized system. “Want your own lawmakers? You need to pay.” They set up centralized propaganda on local TV. I’d worked in other regions, and United Russia didn’t have anything like that there. We felt we were ahead of the curve.
A political consultant who worked with the party’s national leadership told Meduza how closely Volodin managed party affairs once he became General Council secretary:
If the party had a crisis, a scandal, or a conflict somewhere in the regions, he could fly out there the next day. By the time he arrived, he already knew everything about the region. He tried to put his own people in place wherever he could. He worked closely with the authorities in regions that had set up systems for rigging elections, [because] he wanted to spread those practices elsewhere, too.
Volodin was one of the main organizers of United Russia’s 2007 State Duma election campaign. Putin headed its candidate list that year — the only time he has done so in the party’s history.
During that campaign, the president got to know Volodin better and “took note of the party manager,” according to a source who worked with the presidential administration’s domestic policy team at the time and another who worked in the federal government. In 2010, Putin, by then prime minister, “brought” Volodin “back” into the executive branch, offering him the job of government chief of staff.
That made the politician from Saratov Putin’s chief political strategist. Ahead of the 2011 State Duma elections, United Russia’s ratings were low, and Volodin proposed that the prime minister and party leader mask the party’s role in the campaign so its stale image would not put off Russian voters. The idea was to create a pro-Putin movement that would ostensibly run the campaign, with United Russia nominating candidates for the movement. Putin liked the proposal.
The new movement was named the All-Russia People’s Front. Putin himself was its formal leader, but in practice Volodin, who had devised it, ran it.
Soon after the 2011 State Duma elections, Volodin, then a deputy prime minister, became head of the Kremlin’s domestic policy team, which ran Putin’s campaign to return to the presidency. Under the team’s direction, the State Duma passed repressive laws and later earned the nickname “the mad printer.”
After the annexation of Crimea, Volodin made perhaps his best-known declaration: “No Putin — no Russia.” Speaking at the 2014 Valdai forum, he used those words to describe the mood among Russians. A source in the speaker’s circle believes that as far back as the 2000s, Volodin “realized that [to advance his career] he needed to work for one person — the head of state”:
He doesn’t belong to any influential group, though he may, for example, have good relations with certain security and law enforcement officials. But they don’t have a shared history or any joint dealings. If you belong to a group and lose your post in the broader power structure, your patrons will find you a place within the clan. They won’t abandon you. Volodin doesn’t have that option, so he constantly makes a show of pledging allegiance to the president.
But even this extreme loyalty did not help Volodin keep his job as deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for domestic politics in 2016. Both the source in the speaker’s circle and a source close to the current domestic policy team say he wanted to stay in the Kremlin.
That was when Volodin became State Duma speaker. One account attributes his move to parliament to election turnout falling short of the president’s expectations: in 2016, it did not reach 50%. Another holds that the president was deliberately moving officials who had grown more powerful to different jobs, “taking them out of their comfort zone,” as one Meduza source close to the presidential administration put it.
In parliament, Volodin made a show of enforcing discipline while continuing to make pro-Putin statements. He repeatedly said lawmakers should support the president, and after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he became one of the most prominent officials voicing ultrapatriotic views. Russians who had emigrated became one of the speaker’s favorite targets: he repeatedly called them “traitors” and demanded that they be punished.
“Volodin often goes too far. He knows why he does it — to make his loyalty more visible. But he also knows where to draw the line and doesn’t turn into Medvedev,” said the source in the speaker’s circle. On his Telegram channel, the former president regularly insults the leaders of Ukraine and European countries and threatens to use nuclear weapons.
According to the same source, this loyalty is the main reason Volodin remains close to the president. The speaker shows it in different ways, the source said, for example by telling Putin about proposals that influential players bring to the Duma:
Often these are things that are nowhere near important enough to bring to the president — some perks buried in clauses of bills. But the speaker is showing that he’s keeping an eye on things. All he has to offer is this show of loyalty. You couldn’t say he’s interesting to talk to, for example.
The source believes Volodin retained the speakership because of his loyalty and because he keeps an equal distance from all influential groups: “That way, Putin preserved the balance.”
Once it became known that Medvedev had been left off the candidate lists, Volodin began attending meetings about committee assignments and “drawing up a legislative agenda” even before the elections, the same source said: “Who else on the lists could [be] both a public figure and a political operator?”
Another political consultant who works with the presidential administration said Volodin kept his post because of “his good relations with [Putin aide Nikolai] Patrushev and the fact that Putin has long preferred to keep people in their posts when he is happy with their work.”
A political consultant who worked with Volodin’s domestic policy team praised his “instinct for bureaucratic maneuvering” and called him a “bureaucratic animal”: “He can orchestrate intrigues and elaborate schemes, and the people involved often have no idea they’ve been drawn into anything.”
The same consultant said the speaker has no real friends. He sees the people around him as “temporary allies” or “tools for achieving his goals.”
The source gave the example of former State Duma Deputy Speaker Sergey Neverov, a longtime Volodin ally. In April 2023, Neverov proposed inviting Yevgeny Prigozhin, founder of the Wagner private military company, to the Duma. Prigozhin was sharply critical of the Defense Ministry’s leadership. In June that year, he and his private military company staged a mutiny and marched toward Moscow. Afterward, Volodin made a show of cutting ties with Neverov. A year later, Neverov lost his post as deputy speaker, and this year he failed to win a seat in the new Duma.
But the political consultant who worked with Volodin’s domestic policy team cautioned against confusing a “bureaucratic animal” with a “political animal”:
As a politician, he’s still stuck in the 1990s, in the backwaters of the Saratov region. Of course, compared with today’s party leaders — [Liberal Democratic Party leader Leonid] Slutsky and [New People leader Alexey] Nechayev — he’s a god and Michael Jackson rolled into one. But overall, he’s a pretty crude, provincial politician. Maybe that suits the higher-ups.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: South Korea warns of 'further measures' if Ukraine refuses public apology over POW transfer disclosure
articles.body:
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Friday that Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean prisoners of war being sent to South Korea.
Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.
North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families.
Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South.
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.
Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives.
Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential.
"If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," the South Korean president said on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar."
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X.
Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia.
In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic," Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North.
"The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied."
Diplomatic misunderstanding
Lee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday.
Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident," describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.
Seoul's spy agency said that Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland.
But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

articles.title: CCTV Captures Russian Drone Slamming Into Kyiv School With 104 Children Inside – Warhead Fails to Detonate
articles.body:
A terrifying CCTV video from Kyiv on Thursday captured the moment a Russian drone slammed into a school where more than 100 children had begun their day – another chilling reminder of how Russia’s expanding aerial war is reaching into the places Ukrainian children are supposed to be safest.
At around 9 a.m., a Russian drone struck School No. 12 in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district, smashing through the building, shattering windows and partially destroying a wall and staircase.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside were 104 children and 60 members of staff.
They survived because classes had already moved into the school’s underground shelter after an air raid alert sounded.
But there was another extraordinary stroke of fortune: the Russian drone’s warhead failed to detonate.
The explosive payload was found inside the damaged school after the strike. Had it functioned as designed, the consequences inside a building holding 164 children and staff could have been dramatically more devastating.
Two things stood between the children and a potential catastrophe: Ukraine’s decision to send them underground and the failure of the weapon that struck their school to explode.
No children or teachers were injured.
The 21-second CCTV recording captures the sudden violence of the impact, followed by debris and smoke engulfing part of the school.
“They spare no one,” headteacher Valentyna Chorna said as she surveyed the damage.
Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
“Children are our future, the future of our nation. In order to destroy a nation, of course, they need to destroy children.”
A Relentless Pattern
Thursday’s near-disaster comes amid an intensifying wave of Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with schools, homes and other civilian facilities repeatedly caught in the strikes.
The danger is growing as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones that are more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
That makes the strike on School No. 12 particularly chilling.
This was not simply debris falling from an interception high above the capital. A Russian attack drone crashed directly into the building carrying an explosive warhead.
The weapon failed to complete the destruction it was capable of causing.
The strike came amid a broader pattern of attacks affecting Ukrainian children and educational facilities.
Human Rights Watch reported in September that 314 educational facilities in Kyiv alone had been damaged since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, including at least 107 during 2026.
Across Ukraine, the scale is far greater. UNICEF told the UN Security Council earlier this year that more than 1,780 educational facilities had been verified as damaged or destroyed since 2022, disrupting education for children already entering another year of wartime schooling.
Recent Russian attacks have repeatedly reached places where children live, study and shelter.
On Sept. 29, Russian forces struck Sumy with four glide bombs, hitting a school while pupils were sheltering inside. Children were among those injured, while civilians were killed elsewhere in the city.
A day earlier in Kharkiv, a Russian glide bomb struck a residential area, injuring dozens of people, including children.
For Ukrainian families, everyday routines – walking to school, sitting in class or sleeping at home – continue to unfold under the threat of another missile or drone alert.
Schools under the laws of war
Under international humanitarian law, schools are civilian objects unless and for such time as they are being used for military purposes.
Parties to a conflict are required to distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives and to take feasible precautions to avoid harm to civilians.
Intentionally directing an attack against a school that remains a civilian object can constitute a war crime.
But the repeated destruction and damage inflicted on educational facilities across Ukraine has left children learning under conditions that would have been unimaginable before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has responded by expanding underground classrooms, school shelters and remote education.
At School No. 12 on Thursday, those precautions proved decisive.
More than 100 children were underground when the Russian drone tore into the floors above them.
Had they still been sitting in ordinary classrooms – or had the drone’s warhead detonated as designed — the outcome could have been catastrophic.
Zelensky visits Kyiv school after Russian Shahed strike
President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the school, where he met with the principal and teachers following the morning Russian Shahed strike.
“Most importantly, everyone is alive,” he wrote on X, thanking the school staff for their “clear and coordinated actions,” which he said saved lives.
“Striking schools and kindergartens is a deliberate Russian tactic aimed at making ordinary life a target,” Zelensky wrote.
“And we are working nonstop to strengthen our air defense and increase the production of Ukrainian interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds – in order to protect our cities and communities from such strikes.”
