articles.title: Ukraine sends mixed signals on F-16 repair delays
articles.body:
- Zelensky told the Financial Times that about half of Ukraine's F-16s have spent long periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance.
- Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later called reports of catastrophically low F-16 availability false, saying overhauled jets are returning at an increasing pace.
About half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets have spent long stretches in Europe for repairs and maintenance, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, and some have taken so long to come back that Ukraine lost time when it needed them most to defend its skies.
Zelensky made the comments in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2. He said Kyiv wants Western partners to help move more of the maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the jets closer to the front would get them back into service faster. He did not say how many aircraft are affected, where in Europe the work is done, or how long the jets have been away.
Zelensky said the F-16s have been effective against Russia’s newer jet-powered drones, which fly faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia has used for most of the war. In the same interview, he said Ukrainian forces are shooting down about 57% of jet-powered drones and between 85% and 90% of conventional ones.
Hours later, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry pushed back on reports describing a readiness crisis in the F-16 fleet. Spokesperson Heorhiy Tykhyi said on X that claims of catastrophically low aircraft availability and excessively long maintenance turnaround times were false. He said Ukraine’s industrial partners are returning overhauled aircraft at an increasing pace and that maintenance times are getting shorter, not longer.
Tykhyi acknowledged that the fleet is hard to keep flying. Ukraine flies the jets intensively under demanding conditions, he said, and some components for its early-model F-16s are no longer produced and are getting harder to find. He warned that such reports should not undermine international funding for F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for more jets from partner nations.
Ukraine’s F-16s are older jets from European air forces, mainly the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. The first ones arrived in the summer of 2024. They have been used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and to strike ground targets, and Ukraine has lost several of them in combat and accidents.
Because the jets are Western-built, much of their deeper maintenance has been done outside Ukraine, where parts, tools and trained technicians are available and the aircraft are out of reach of Russian strikes on airfields. Moving that work into Ukraine would bring the jets closer to the fight but would also put repair sites within range of Russian missiles and drones.

articles.title: US sends third carrier strike group to Middle East in biggest buildup since 2003
articles.body:
The USS Theodore Roosevelt left San Diego on Sunday accompanied by a Marine expeditionary unit of more than 2,000 troops, bringing the potential total US military presence in the region to more than 60,000.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left San Diego on Sunday and is heading for the Middle East, adding to the two US aircraft carriers already operating against Iran in the biggest buildup in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, according to US officials.
The Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class nuclear-powered supercarrier and flagship of Carrier Strike Group 9, departed without ceremony — no sailors manning the rails, according to ship-spotter photographs.
It is accompanied by the guided-missile cruiser USS Chosin and destroyer squadrons, with Carrier Air Wing 11 embarked, including F-35C and F/A-18 Super Hornet jets, electronic warfare and early-warning aircraft.
A day later, the amphibious ready group led by the USS Makin Island also sailed from San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit of more than 2,000 Marines aboard three ships including the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage.
Citing US officials, AP estimated the combined deployment at 9,000 to 10,000 additional troops, with arrivals expected by the end of November. The US already has more than 50,000 military personnel in the Middle East.
A US official told Al Jazeera that by the end of November, three carrier strike groups and two amphibious ready groups would be in place around Iran, adding that "leaders will have many options for dealing with Iran."
The USS George HW Bush and USS George Washington are currently in the Arabian Sea conducting operations against Iran, according to the US Naval Institute's report from Tuesday.
The Navy has maintained a two-carrier presence in the region since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on 28 February. The USS Boxer amphibious-ready group is also already in theatre.
Theodore Roosevelt is scheduled to relieve USS George Washington, according to USNI News. Whether George Washington departs before or after USS Theodore Roosevelt arrives will determine whether the US briefly operates three carrier strike groups in the region simultaneously.
If all three overlap, it would be only the second such deployment since April, which was itself the first time since 2003 the US had three carriers in the region at once.
The Wall Street Journal reported that if USS George Washington remains on station until Theodore Roosevelt arrives, all three carrier groups would be in theatre together. Whether that represents a sustained increase in posture or a temporary overlap during rotation remains unclear.
Trump has not ruled out a new round of strikes against Iran as the November midterm elections approach.

articles.title: Putin vows Russia will respond with 'all weapons at our disposal' if attacked by NATO
articles.body:
Putin vows Russia will respond with 'all weapons at our disposal' if attacked by NATO
Speaking at the annual Valdai Discussion Club forum on Oct. 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that Russia may respond with nuclear weapons in the event of a military conflict with NATO.
"We understand that we'll be facing an adversary twice our size," Putin said about a potential conflict with NATO. "The point is that we have competitive advantages in our means of self-defense. Yes, of course, France and Great Britain are nuclear powers; we understand this perfectly well and are fully aware of it. But no one else has the weapons that Russia has today."
Putin's comments echoed warnings Russia issued to NATO on Sept. 30, saying that it would be ready to use nuclear weapons if alliance members attempt to isolate the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
"Can we be sure this weapon will never be used? Of course not," Putin said about nuclear weapons in his speech. "We're all familiar with the saying: If a gun is hanging somewhere on the stage at the beginning of a performance, on the wall, it's bound to go off eventually."
Russia has repeatedly used nuclear rhetoric in its confrontation with Western countries over its full-scale war against Ukraine. The U.K. has previously condemned Moscow's nuclear signaling as destabilizing and warned that such rhetoric increases the risk of miscalculation.
Putin went on to say that Russia has "no intention of attacking anyone," despite Russian drones increasingly violating NATO airspace, the Kremlin being accused of multiple attempts of sabotage, and Moscow launching near non-stop attacks across Ukraine.
On Sept. 28, Putin signed a decree raising the total personnel of Russia's armed forces, days after it was reported that Moscow plans to raise military spending to record levels.
Putin also echoed threats from Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova that European factories manufacturing weapons for Ukraine could become military targets for Moscow.
For months, European leaders have raised concerns over what they describe as growing Russian hybrid operations against NATO members, particularly countries on the alliance's eastern flank and those supporting Ukraine.
At the Discussion Club, Putin reiterated his familiar gripes with the West and demanded Ukrainian land in exchange for ending the war. The Russian president also effectively rejected proposals for a mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure with Ukraine, and for the restoration of safe shipping in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Spain, Belgium, and Poland are sending Ukraine F-16 cannon rounds to fight Russia’s jet drones
articles.body:
Ukraine may soon receive a multimillion package of 20-mm rounds for its F-16 fighter jets, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists, Hromadske reported. He called the ammunition critical for shooting down Russia's jet-powered drones and said several partners have already begun transferring it. He expects the larger package after an upcoming high-level visit.
Russia now strikes Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities daily, increasingly with jet-powered drones that outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower Shaheds. Fighter jets are among the tools Ukraine uses against them, while its overall interception rate for jet drones still trails its rate against propeller drones.
"Critically important" ammunition
Sybiha said Ukraine has yet to build up its capability to repel jet drones.
"Given that we have not yet built up the capability to repel jet drones, and given the preparations for new strikes, it was critically important to help our military shoot down these drones. Apart from air defense systems, which are too expensive to use constantly against drones, the most effective tools right now are F-16 fighter jets," Sybiha said.
He thanked Spain, Belgium, and Poland, which have begun the process of transferring the ammunition, and said that thanks to them Ukraine will "very soon" have the rounds it needs.
Belgium will send three F-16 fighter jets, but maintenance delays may keep Ukraine from using them
A "very serious visit" ahead
Sybiha linked the larger package to a visit he did not name.
"We will soon have one very serious visit. We think that one of the decisions following this visit will be a multimillion package of this ammunition for Ukraine," he said.
Talks on buying the rounds from private manufacturers are also underway, he added.
Ukraine has already received urgent batches of F-16 ammunition from Belgium, Spain, and other partners, and Belgium plans to send three more F-16s by the end of 2026 under an accelerated procedure. The jets' air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds are imported and not always in stock.
Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
Another night of Russian strikes
Overnight on 2 October, Russia launched 108 drones at Ukraine, 47 of them jet-powered, and air defenses downed 88 of them. In Kyiv, a Russian strike on a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district killed one person and injured two. Russia also targeted the Southern Bridge again, after striking it three times the previous day, and the city restricted public transport across several bridges.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a Russian FPV drone hit a car in the Solonytsivka hromada on the afternoon of 1 October, injuring a man and a boy. A Russian strike damaged a civilian enterprise in Rivne Oblast and started a fire that forced an evacuation of nearby homes, regional head Oleksandr Koval said, and drones attacked Cherkasy Oblast.
In neighboring Romania, an object believed to be a drone crashed near the village of Plauru in Tulcea County during the attack, starting a fire that caused no casualties, Romania's Defense Ministry said.

articles.title: Putin Warns West Over Kaliningrad, Admits Ukrainian Strikes Cut Russia's GDP by 1%
articles.body:

Putin Warns West Over Kaliningrad, Admits Ukrainian Strikes Cut Russia's GDP by 1%
Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow will consider using all available weapons, including its nuclear arsenal, if Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory faces a direct attack or blockade.
Speaking at the Valdai Foreign Policy Forum, Putin addressed Western claims of potential Russian aggression by 2029 or 2030, claiming that Moscow has no intent to initiate hostilities against European nations, as reported by BBC on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He noted that Ukrainian strikes on domestic energy sites reduced Russia's gross domestic product by approximately 1%.
The statements follow claims from Moscow accusing NATO of planning a blockade of Kaliningrad, the Baltic exclave bordering Lithuania and Poland. Putin pointed to NATO naval drills in the Baltic Sea as a threat to the region's security.
NATO General Secretary Mark Rutte rejected these claims, emphasizing that alliance exercises are purely defensive and calling Moscow's nuclear messaging unhelpful.
Addressing the situation in Ukraine, Putin alleged that Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and economic targets were direct responses to strikes on Russian oil refineries and Black Sea vessels, according to BBC.
Ukraine maintains that targeting oil infrastructure aims to weaken funding for the military operation. Meanwhile, strikes continue across Ukrainian territory, including drone attacks on critical infrastructure and key transit points.
Putin reiterated his position that broader international instability is driven by Western policies, warning of rising global risks associated with advanced weaponry and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, BBC reported.
He called for updating global international rules, arguing that global tensions will shift as traditional international power dynamics continue to adjust.
Amid growing security concerns over potential aggression around Kaliningrad, Lithuania designed its future Gizai power substation, located 30 kilometers from the Russian exclave, to withstand physical sabotage and drone strikes, including attacks from multiple explosive-laden Shahed drones.
The 35-hectare facility, which formed part of the Harmony Link project connecting the Baltic power grid to Poland, featured reinforced concrete protective walls, vehicle-proof fencing, and underground tunnel sensors.
Litgrid CEO Andrius Semeskevicius emphasized that the grid was planned for hybrid and military threats following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Baltic states' disconnection from the Russian electricity system in 2025. Regional security concerns had escalated due to recent infrastructure sabotage in Germany and fears of potential false-flag operations near the Suwalki Gap.

articles.title: Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
Zelensky also said in the interview that Ukraine is unable to use all of its F-16 fighter jets during Russian attacks because around half of the aircraft are undergoing scheduled maintenance and repairs in Europe.
F-16s, which Ukraine first received in the summer of 2024, are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used to intercept Russian missiles and drones during aerial attacks on Ukraine. They could also be deployed to launch missiles and bombs against Russian positions along the front line.
The lengthy maintenance periods leave some aircraft unavailable when they are particularly needed for air defense. Kyiv wants to move some F-16 maintenance work to Ukraine to allow the jets to return to service faster.
Zelensky also said Ukraine faces a budget shortfall that is limiting the development and mass production of critical defensive weapons.

articles.title: Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
articles.body:
Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered his annual keynote address and answered audience questions at the Valdai Discussion Club’s international forum outside Moscow on Thursday.
During a more-than-three-hour session moderated by foreign affairs expert and RT contributor Fyodor Lukyanov, Putin spoke on a broad range of topics, including tensions with the West, the Ukraine conflict and artificial intelligence.
A world in turmoil and the emergence of a new global balance
The world has reached a pivotal moment shaped by profound transformations in global politics, the economy and demographics, as well as the rapid development of technology, including AI, Putin said.
“We are confident that, in the long term, as we move away from Western hegemony, the global situation will gradually change for the better – toward a more stable, democratic, and free multipolar international order,” he said.
The risk of new conflicts
Technological and social change is fueling a sense of uncertainty and greater international tensions, Putin said. Governments may seek to preserve stability at home by “exporting instability” abroad, while new opportunities “fuel ambitions” and encourage countries to take greater risks.
As a result, “the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, highly likely,” Putin said.
AI could herald an era of ‘digital totalitarianism’
The proliferation of AI could lead to “digital totalitarianism,” shaping individuals and stripping away their individuality through the use of algorithms configured by others, Putin warned.
“Such digital totalitarianism would be just as much of a dead end – as bleak and inhumane – as the totalitarian societies of the past that we know so well,” he said.
Countries and communities must join forces to find broadly acceptable solutions to the challenges posed by AI and other technologies capable of influencing human behavior, identity and thought, Putin said.
While AI can be a useful tool, any final political decision must remain in human hands, he stressed.
Relations with the West
Russia’s current tensions with the West date back to the fall of the Soviet Union, when certain Western leaders sought to further weaken Russia instead of welcoming it into the European security system, Putin argued.
“Despite the many years – and I want to emphasize this, many years – of attempts by the new Russia to become part of so-called Western civilization, in practice they did everything they could to truly isolate and further break apart the Russian Federation itself,” the president said.
“They still say this at various events and gatherings even today: ‘We need to finish breaking up the empire,’” Putin added.
He pointed to NATO’s eastward expansion, which he claimed violated assurances given to Moscow. Putin further argued that European politicians were using escalatory rhetoric toward Moscow to draw attention away from political and economic problems at home.
No saber-rattling around Kaliningrad
The president reiterated that Russia would respond to any potential attack on its Kaliningrad Region, an exclave on the Baltic Sea sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Any assault on Russian territory would “inevitably” be viewed as grounds for using all the weaponry at Moscow’s disposal, he said.
Putin was referring to recent statements by Western officials, including Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who have argued that NATO should be prepared for a potential conflict involving Kaliningrad.
Nuclear weapons as ‘Chekhov’s gun’
The president warned that a conventional war could escalate into a nuclear conflict.
“Today, when the world’s leading powers possess weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, bringing the Earth to a catastrophic state, can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Of course not,” Putin said.
Putin compared the risk posed by the continued existence of nuclear weapons to “Chekhov’s gun,” a dramatic principle attributed to Russian playwright Anton Chekhov that holds that a gun introduced early in a story should eventually be fired.
”We all know the famous saying: if a gun is hanging on the wall at the beginning of a play, by the end it is bound to go off,” the Russian leader said. “We must bear that in mind and prevent it from happening.”
“If we want to live – and everyone wants to live – then, as I once said in a public speech, let’s live in peace. Let’s work together to find ways to make that happen,” he said.
The Ukraine conflict and Russia’s goals
Putin said the Ukraine conflict, which is on track to enter its fifth year next February, is about Russia’s security rather than territorial ambitions. He reiterated Moscow’s demand that Ukraine abandon its plans to join NATO in favor of permanent neutrality.
Russia is ready to end the conflict, but only on terms acceptable to Moscow, he said.

articles.title: Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
articles.body:
Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Russian biker Oleg Lyovushkin, who is linked to a Russian military intelligence officer, may have organised an attempted sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany.
Source: a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the investigation, Lyovushkin presumably organised the attempt to plant explosives at the airport. German investigators believe that Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov was supposed to carry out the plan.
Journalists analysed intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, and also spoke with representatives of Western secret services. According to their data, Lyovushkin and Karshakov arrived in Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect that Lyovushkin conducted reconnaissance of the airport shortly before the attack, after which he instructed Karshakov to execute the plan.
Investigators also found similarities between the incident in Leipzig and other attempted Russian sabotage operations in Poland, Lithuania, and Germany.
Specifically, the explosive device seized in Leipzig was reportedly similar to devices used in other sabotage operations in Europe.
Lyovushkin, who holds a Russian passport and is an avid motorcyclist, is also linked to Denis Smolyaninov, a man Western secret services consider to be one of the coordinators of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
According to Lithuanian intelligence, Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian desk in Russian military intelligence and specialised in psychological operations, among other things. Documents also link him to secret sabotage campaigns in Europe.
It is noted that Lyovushkin and Smolyaninov met back in 2007. Reportedly, they have kin repeated contact over the many years.
German security agencies link the Leipzig attack to GRU Unit 29155, which, according to German intelligence assessments, plays a key role in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
German security agencies assess that the goal of such operations could be to create a sense of insecurity among European society due to its support for Ukraine and to influence the debate on further assistance to Kyiv.
Lyovushkin himself publicly leads an inconspicuous life. He takes part in motorcycle races, travels around Europe, fishes, and skis with his family.
At the same time, journalists claim that this lifestyle may conceal his involvement in Russian sabotage operations in Central Europe.
According to German intelligence, he travelled to Germany via Türkiye this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. Investigators stated that Lyovushkin rented a car at Berlin airport a week before the attack and over the next few days drove it to several locations where weapons were suspected of being stored.
They believe that the explosives used in the operation were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in the cavities of trucks, and were likely temporarily stored along the route.
The journalists say that Lyovushkin's links to the GRU were known at the time he entered the country. However, he was not placed under surveillance upon his arrival.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.
- On 6 September, it was reported that German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser was planning a set of measures to cover protection against drones, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

articles.title: Taiwan receives first new F-16s three years behind plan
articles.body:
- Taiwan's Air Force took delivery of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Oct. 2.
- The $8 billion order, approved in 2019, was expected to begin deliveries in 2023 but was delayed by production and software problems.
Taiwan’s Air Force has received the first two of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets bought from the United States, after the aircraft landed at Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung around noon on Oct. 2.
The arrival comes about a month later than expected and roughly three years behind the original schedule. The two jets had been due in Taiwan by late August or early September, but stayed in Hawaii for weeks without explanation, Focus Taiwan reported, after local media said they had turned back shortly after taking off for Guam.
The United States approved the $8 billion sale of 66 F-16 Block 70 jets in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term. Deliveries were supposed to start in 2023 and finish by the end of 2026, but production delays, supply chain problems and software integration issues pushed the schedule back. Lockheed Martin unveiled the first newly built F-16 Block 70 for Taiwan at its plant in Greenville, South Carolina, in March 2025.
The new jets will be based at Chihhang, where they will go through ground inspections while pilots and maintainers convert to the aircraft. Taiwan’s government budgeted NT$247.2 billion, about $8 billion, for the purchase between 2020 and 2026, and says the jets will strengthen air defense along the island’s east coast, the side facing the open Pacific, where Chinese aircraft and ships have operated during large-scale drills around Taiwan.
The Block 70 is the newest production version of the F-16, built at Lockheed Martin’s South Carolina line. It carries the AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, a newer mission computer and updated electronic warfare and communications systems, along with conformal fuel tanks that hug the fuselage to add range without taking up weapons stations. It also has strengthened landing gear to handle heavier takeoff weights and weapons loads.
Taiwan already flies more than 140 older F-16A/B fighters, which have been upgraded to a similar F-16V standard in a program completed in 2023. The 66 new jets will take Taiwan’s F-16 fleet to more than 200 aircraft, giving it the backbone of a force that scrambles almost daily to shadow Chinese military aircraft.
The delivery came about a week after Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. Taiwan is still waiting for U.S. approval of a separate arms package worth about $14 billion that Trump paused after Chinese objections, AFP reported.
Taiwanese officials have said more F-16 Block 70s will arrive before the end of the year, but they have not given a number. Remaining deliveries are expected to stretch into 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Russia plans to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa to isolate them in winter, FT says
articles.body:
Russia plans to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa to isolate them in winter, FT says
Russia is preparing to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa in an attempt to isolate them from the rest of Ukraine when winter arrives. Lviv also features in Russia's plans.
Source: Financial Times, citing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian and European officials familiar with intelligence data
Quote from the FT: "Specifically, the president said, Russia was gearing up to intensify attacks on Ukraine's largest cities with the aim of isolating them from the rest of the country as winter sets in. Kyiv, the eastern stronghold of Kharkiv and the southern port city of Odesa are the main targets, according to Zelenskyy and a Ukrainian intelligence assessment described to the FT by Ukrainian and European officials."
Details: The Ukrainian and European security officials said that Lviv, an important logistics hub near the Polish border, also features in Russia's plans.
The Ukrainian officials told the FT that Moscow intends to strike nuclear facilities in order to disconnect them from the power grid. They said Russia wants to increase pressure on Kyiv to force it to give in to Russian demands in early 2027.
Another element of Russia's strategy, according to the officials, is to create a new flow of refugees to the EU. They fear that a large influx of Ukrainians would place additional pressure on countries where anti-immigration sentiment is growing.
Zelenskyy told the FT that Ukrainian intelligence services received information about Russian ruler Vladimir Putin ordering the removal of restrictions that had governed previous aerial campaigns. According to Zelenskyy, the intelligence included intercepted communications between Kremlin officials.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "He said there are no rules now."
Details: The president said Putin issued the order in September, when Russia began intensifying its airstrikes on Kyiv, hitting schools, hospitals and data centres.
According to Zelenskyy, the aim of the attacks is not only to destroy infrastructure but also "to pressure people", frighten civilians, force them to leave cities and weaken Ukraine's ability to continue the war.
Background: According to an approved Russian plan reportedly intercepted by Ukraine, Russia intends to use winter strikes to cut Ukrainian nuclear power plants off from the power grid by hitting targets within a kilometre of the plants, while also launching large-scale attacks on water supply systems.

articles.title: World ‘amazed’ by Iranian nation’s ‘courage, resilience
articles.body:
“The whole world is closely following what is happening and is amazed at the courage and heroism of the Iranian nation and its resilience,” Putin said on Thursday at the plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow.
He also pointed to a deep “bench” of high-level figures in Iran’s administration, armed forces and the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), “people ready for self-sacrifice in the name of their people.”
The remarks come months after the United States and the Israeli regime launched an unprovoked war of aggression against the Islamic Republic, assassinating senior political and military leaders. At the same time, Tehran was engaged in indirect talks with Washington.
Putin called the killing of Ali Larijani, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, a tremendous mistake.
“Mr. Larijani — I knew him personally well — was a very positively minded person, ready to seek mutually acceptable compromises, above all in the interests of the Iranian people,” the Russian president said, according to TASS and RIA Novosti.
“Besides any legal assessments, this is of course a mistake, because such a person would be needed today to find compromises and solutions that could bring peace to the Persian Gulf,” he stated, accoridng to Press TV.
Putin said Larijani had visited Russia for talks on Iran’s enriched uranium and was a figure with whom constructive dialogue was possible.
He recalled that Tehran had at one stage agreed to a Russian proposal to relocate the material, an arrangement Washington, and even the Israeli regime, initially accepted.
Moscow, he said, had already carried out such a transfer in 2015 and remained ready to repeat it. The Americans later hardened their position and demanded that the uranium go only to the United States, after which Iran toughened its own stance.
Larijani, Putin said, then proposed a joint Russian-Iranian enterprise on Iranian territory to dilute the material.
The Russian leader added that Moscow’s offer remains on the table.
Putin also expressed hope that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and that illegal sanctions against Iran would be lifted, “an objective that Tehran is rightfully pursuing.”
Once that happened, he said, there would be no reason for restrictions on passage through Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb. “We support that.”
Iran and Russia have deepened strategic ties in recent years in the face of sweeping US sanctions and Western isolation. A 20-year comprehensive strategic partnership agreement was signed last year, and Moscow continues work on new units at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.
Russian officials have repeatedly condemned the US-Israeli war of aggression and offered to help mediate a settlement that respects Iran’s sovereignty.

articles.title: Ukrainian firm fields 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO’s biggest naval drone drill
articles.body:
UFORCE, a Ukrainian defense company, says it fielded 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO's largest unmanned-systems exercise in Portugal, Militarnyi reported. The firm's crews acted as both mock enemy and allied forces alongside Ukraine's Navy during the 31 August–25 September drills. The turnout more than doubled the company's presence at last year's exercise, when it brought five vessels.
Ukraine began the all-out war without large warships, yet uncrewed boats drove Russia's Black Sea Fleet out of its main base on the Black Sea—a result that now pulls far larger navies to the same ranges to test the weapon for themselves.
Ukraine brings its sea-drone playbook to Portugal's NATO exercise
UFORCE joined REPMUS 26, the Portuguese Navy's annual exercise, co-organized with NATO, where member states try out robots and drones built for combat at sea. This year the company widened its presence sharply, UFORCE said on LinkedIn. Across the scenarios, its crews ran strikes, reconnaissance, and defense.
At the center sat the MV7, an uncrewed boat UFORCE showed in every setup it offers. Across its configurations, the MV7 carried interceptors, FPV drones, other kinetic weapons, and electronic-warfare gear. Crews launched flying drones straight off the decks while the boats sat on the water, all run by a single control program.
The company brought three systems to REPMUS for the first time: the Nemesis SeaStrike drone, which launches from the MV7, the MV11 boat, and a supply vessel called L11. UFORCE teams worked beside Ukraine's Navy throughout. Portuguese President António José Seguro inspected the MV7 on the pier, the company said.
Not Ukraine's first visit

Ukrainian forces have marked the first successful operational deployment of the domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on October 1.
Footage shared on official social channels captured the launch from an undisclosed firing position.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next is production. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy stated in a message accompanying the video.
The deployment marks a significant transition for Ukraine’s defense industry as it expands domestic production of long-range strike systems.
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point updated its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor with a combined infrared and radar seeker, replacing the missile's previous infrared-only design.
The dual-mode seeker allowed the system to track targets using both heat signatures and radar reflections during its final flight phase, helping maintain lock-on even through bad weather or decoys.
Developed as part of a joint initiative with nine other European nations, the 7.25-meter-long interceptor was designed to reach speeds up to 7,200 kilometers per hour to counter short-range ballistic threats during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Fire Point made significant progress on its domestic missile program during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, aiming to complete its 850-kilometer FP-9 ballistic missile by late 2026.
Company CEO Iryna Terekh revealed in a September interview that the shorter-range FP-7 had already entered codification after roughly two years of rapid development, costing approximately $200 million for research and initial production setup.
The company worked to finish testing the long-range FP-9—designed to potentially reach distant targets, including Moscow—while overcoming tight international export controls by engineering critical components internally.

articles.title: 'He has good ideas': Putin lauds PM Modi's peace push to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday lauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to seek an end to the Ukraine conflict, saying that he has “good ideas” for achieving a peaceful resolution.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.
Asked about the issue at the Valdai Club forum, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been actively working to find mutually acceptable solutions to the Ukraine conflict.
"He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict. I think it's my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas," Putin said.
Putin thanked PM Modi for his efforts and continued support for resolving the Ukraine conflict through dialogue.
"We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible," he added.
Prime Minister Modi and Putin last met in September on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they discussed strengthening trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, along with cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.
PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
"India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. In line with this, both the leaders spoke to me to share their perspectives on the developments related to the conflict. I reiterated India's principled and consistent stand and encouraged dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict," the Prime Minister said during an interview with Japanese news outlet 'The Yomiuri Shimbun' while on a visit to the country in August.
Responding to a question on India’s role in peace efforts between the two countries, Prime Minister Modi said, "I have already indicated India's willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict. I believe, by virtue of our good relations with both sides, including key stakeholders, we can strengthen efforts dedicated to the restoration of an early and lasting peace in Ukraine."
This comes as Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons” at its disposal.
He also accused Western countries, particularly in Europe, of escalating tensions by discussing preparations for a possible war with Moscow, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea and seizing Russian vessels.
European leaders and intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could be capable of launching an attack on another country within the next few years, particularly if it emerges victorious from the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian troops shoot down own Mi-8, killing three crew
articles.body:
- Russian forces shot down their own Mi-8 helicopter over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
- A ground-based air defense crew mistook the helicopter for an enemy drone, the latest in a series of Russian friendly fire helicopter losses.
Russian forces shot down one of their own Mi-8 military helicopters over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
The helicopter was hit by a Russian Su-35 fighter during operations to move aircraft out of the way of a Ukrainian drone strike, sources said. The Su-35 crew apparently mistook the helicopter for a Ukrainian drone.
The Mi-8 came down in a field in the Anninsky district, about 80 km (50 miles) from the city of Voronezh and roughly 200 km (125 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The crew of three, a pilot, a navigator and a gunner, were killed, Russian Telegram channel Mash reported on the evening of the crash.
The Mi-8 is the Soviet-designed twin-engine transport helicopter that forms the backbone of Russia’s military rotary-wing fleet. Armed versions carry rockets and machine guns and are used for troop transport, resupply, medical evacuation and, increasingly, for hunting Ukrainian long-range drones at low altitude.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in wide service and is regularly sent up to intercept Ukrainian drones over Russian territory. A slow, low-flying helicopter can be hard to tell apart from a large drone on radar or at night, especially when Russian pilots and air defense crews are working in the same airspace during a raid.
Russian officials have not publicly acknowledged that the helicopter was downed by friendly fire. Several Russian military bloggers have hinted at the cause without stating it directly.
“The cause is a classic one, which humanity is unlikely ever to defeat, despite AI, robots, neural networks, ‘friend or foe’ and other wonders of science and technology,” wrote Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel and is known for his ties to Russian military aviation.
The shootdown is the latest in a series of friendly fire losses involving Russian helicopters, many of them during Ukrainian drone raids.
On July 2, a Ka-52 attack helicopter crashed in the same Voronezh region. Russian military blogger Vladimir Romanov said it was hit by a Verba shoulder-fired missile fired by a mobile fire group from Russia’s BARS reserve units, according to The Insider. One crew member was killed.
On March 3, Russian forces likely shot down one of their own helicopters near Millerovo in the Rostov region during a Ukrainian drone attack, The Defence Blog reported, after pro-government Russian sources said air defenses had mistaken it for a drone.
A Russian fighter jet has been linked to at least one earlier case. When a Ka-52M was shot down during a counter-drone operation in late 2025, the Telegram channel Pozivnoi Katsman suggested the strike may have come from a Russian fighter.
In June 2024, air defenses near Anapa shot down a Russian Ka-29 helicopter, killing all four people on board. By late 2025, The Insider counted at least 17 Russian aircraft lost to friendly fire since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine secures 20mm ammunition for F-16 jets to counter jet-powered drones – Sybiha

Several partners, including Spain, Belgium and Poland, will soon deliver 20mm rounds for F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, which are effective against Russian jet-powered drones, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said.

I thank all our ambassadors. The president was calling leaders from the front line. The defense minister was calling his counterparts. I was calling foreign ministers. This is critical. articles.title: 9,000 troops head to Mideast as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Third aircraft carrier, thousands of troops head to Mideast as Trump weighs new Iran strikes
The U.S. military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump's war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation — despite his initial promises to Americans of a campaign that would last a matter of weeks — remains a viable option. Further complicating matters, Trump told reporters Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
In an exchange with reporters at the White House, Trump raised the connection when asked by a reporter if there were any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
"I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is 'yes,' but we’re working on it right now," Trump said, without offering details.
Trump added that if the link to Iran is established, the United States would retaliate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a Fox News interview earlier Thursday that investigators believe the flydubai suspect underwent "Islamist, radical indoctrination" but did not provide further details.
"Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry," Trump said. "You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard."
Thousands of US sailors and Marines head to the Middle East 
Meanwhile, the group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group. The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Trump explains why he rejected Iran's latest truce proposal 
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is "possible" that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the 3 November elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
"I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?" Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted on Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because "things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today."
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to "open up" the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was "not good enough."
The war shows signs of getting more complicated 
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, "It’s possible." But then he added, "It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon."
The president said "100% of the people" oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities "including worldwide."
"So, when you say it that way, it would help," Trump added. "If you don’t say that, it could hurt."
Yet, there's also growing concern that Tehran might be turning to asymmetrical tactics following the flydubai attack and another suspicious incident in the U.K.
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies' oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
British authorities announced on Thursday the arrest of a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.

Drone firm linked to Trump sons eyes Ukrainian tech
A US drone company linked to President Donald Trump’s sons wants to bring Ukrainian military technology to America, Reuters has reported, as Kiev pursues billions in arms exports despite multiple corruption scandals in its procurement programs.
Powerus is negotiating with Ukrainian defense firms and wants to manufacture their technology in the US, potentially including long-range attack drones. Its Guardian interceptors, introduced in March, were also jointly developed with Ukrainian partners, according to company president Brett Velicovich.
The company completed a merger with golf course operator Aureus Greenway Holdings on Thursday. Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump hold an indirect investment in Aureus through American Ventures, which regulatory filings projected would own 9.9% of the combined business.
Velicovich, a former US Army Special Operations intelligence analyst, told Reuters he wants Powerus to become a “one-stop solution” for the Pentagon, offering foreign technology with an “American face.”
Company executives and representatives of the brothers say they are passive investors with no operational role. However, Powerus adviser Keith Kellogg, Trump’s former Ukraine envoy, said “it never hurts to have their name on something.”

Kiev has meanwhile been seeking billions in weapons-export revenue while continuing to rely heavily on Western military and financial assistance. Vladimir Zelensky has announced overseas export hubs and previously touted a proposed US drone agreement worth $10-30 billion.
Kiev’s weapons export ambitions come as multiple corruption scandals have rocked its military procurement system, including programs intended to supply drones to its own forces.
On September 23, Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) announced new charges in a case involving border guard officials and a private supplier. Investigators say a manufacturer won a drone tender by offering a lower price, only for a rival working with officials to demand $1 million to allow the contract and equipment deliveries to proceed.
In a separate investigation, NABU said in August that suspected losses from drone purchases reached approximately $5.7 million. Investigators alleged prices were inflated by 60-90%, competing bids were staged, and illicit proceeds were transferred to company accounts, including abroad.
