articles.title: How a failed attack in Leipzig revealed a wider Russian campaign
articles.body:
BERLIN — If the explosive had actually detonated, investigators might not have gotten their clearest look yet at what European officials believe is a wider Russian campaign of attacks.
On Aug. 4, a drone struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig Airport and fell onto the tarmac. Strapped beneath it was a tin can packed with explosives. The device remained intact.
That gave investigators something unusually valuable: the bomb itself. The can was sealed with a metal plate stamped with seven circular indentations, according to an investigative file from German federal police reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
Advertisement
It wasn’t the first time such an improvised explosive had been discovered on European soil. Almost two years earlier, on Aug. 20, 2024, police investigators arrived at a cemetery in Kaunas, Lithuania, with a bomb disposal team. They had received a highly sensitive tip from Poland concerning explosives and a Ukrainian man alleged to have deposited them there for Russian intelligence, according to investigation files from the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau.
At a weathered grave, beneath artificial flowers and concrete slabs, officers recovered a plastic bag containing two tin cans. According to their labels, they contained corn. Forensic analysis, however, found they contained 968 grams of explosives, around 700 grams of TNT equivalent per can — roughly the lethal force of four hand grenades.
In January and June 2025, investigators unearthed more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four were fitted with metal plates stamped with circular indentations. Investigators say they were intended to act as projectiles in an explosion. Forensic examinations found that the plates were highly likely to have been manufactured by the same machine, according to a report by the Forensic Science Service of the Police Department of Lithuania.
The device attached to the drone in Leipzig bore striking similarities to those recovered from the Lithuanian caches, including the explosive-filled tin can and the stamped metal plate.
The resemblance alone does not establish that the devices belonged to the same operation. But two Western security officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss security matters, say it fits with other evidence — including travel records, suspected logistics routes and intelligence reporting — linking the cases to a broader Russian intelligence mission.
The resemblance is one element of a pattern that German and European officials believe points to an escalating campaign of sabotage and violence across Europe, planned and coordinated by Russian intelligence officers.
Advertisement
According to three senior German and European security officials, the main driver of the campaign is Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. At its core, they say, is Unit 29155 — a military intelligence outfit linked to destabilization operations in European countries.
German authorities say they expect further “hybrid” operations as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.
“The population is supposed to fear a direct military confrontation and therefore question the purpose of supporting Ukraine,” said Gerhard Schindler, former president of Germany’s BND Federal Intelligence Service. “That is why he will increase both the military pressure on Ukraine and the hybrid pressure on the West.”
In response to an inquiry, the Russian Embassy in Berlin denied any Russian involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe. “We firmly reject the baseless allegations concerning Russia’s purported involvement in the alleged ‘drone incident’ at Leipzig Airport, as well as in other ‘sabotage activities,’” a spokesperson said.
Russian connection
One of the clearest trails leads to Oleg Levushkin, a dual Latvian-Russian national whom German authorities suspect of helping prepare the Leipzig attack. According to a senior German security official and investigative files reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Levushkin is not a low-level recruit but a GRU-linked logistics operative with longstanding ties to senior figures in Russian military intelligence.
On social media, Levushkin offers glimpses of a seemingly ordinary life: motorcycle trips to Crimea and the Hungarian-Serbian border, a visit to Volgograd’s Motherland Calls statue, and time spent fishing, skiing and travelling across Europe with his family. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network reviewed his profiles on the social media sites VKontakte and Odnoklassniki.
Advertisement
According to one German intelligence official and documents related to the case, investigators believe Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin Brandenburg Airport in late July to prepare the Leipzig operation. He rented a car there on July 27, according to location data mentioned in German investigation files. Investigators believe the explosives entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia in the cavities of long-haul trucks, according to the senior official from Germany.
On July 31, the rental car was recorded near Leipzig Airport, where investigators believe he was carrying out reconnaissance ahead of the attempted attack, according to documents from the investigation. Levushkin did not reply to a request for comment.
Levushkin’s alleged links reach into the upper ranks of Russian military intelligence. According to reporting by German media as well as the London-based non-profit Dossier Center, he has maintained a close relationship for roughly two decades with GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov.
A December 2025 report by the State Security Department of Lithuania says Smolyaninov is “the head of the GRU’s Ukraine department, specializes in psychological operations and is linked to covert sabotage campaigns organized in Europe using the social network Telegram.”
According to the 2025 intelligence report, Smolyaninov also coordinated the activities of the Russian-linked private military company Longifolia, registered in Panama. European investigators suspect several shareholders in the company of involvement in an operation where incendiary devices were sent to Poland and Britain, according to Lithuanian investigation files. One of the parcels caught fire on July 20, 2024 while being transferred at Leipzig Airport. Another ignited two days later in Birmingham, England.
Lithuanian intelligence explicitly attributes the parcel operation to the GRU, and in particular to Unit 29155. A November 2025 dossier by Lithuania’s State Security Department reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network describes the unit as being “tasked with carrying out killings, operations to destroy infrastructure, disrupting the activities of institutions that run counter to Russia's interests, and terrorist attacks in Western countries.”
Advertisement
Its agents, the November 2025 dossier says, are “trained in handling explosives and firearms [and] can identify human sources and build agent networks.”
Unit 29155 has previously been linked by Western governments and investigators to a series of operations across Europe, including explosions at ammunition depots in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic and the 2018 poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal in Britain, according to the dossier. The Lithuanian dossier also links the unit to more recent arson attacks, including at an Ikea store in Vilnius and a post office in Bucharest.
The Russian government’s press service did not respond to a request for comment about GRU Unit 29155 and Smolyaninov.
German officials have blamed the GRU for a failed incendiary attack on a defense company in Munich in September, while Estonia’s intelligence service said this week in a public statement that an August arson attack on defense company Milrem Robotics had been commissioned by Russian intelligence.
European security authorities interviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network expect such operations to increase in the coming months, with defense companies, critical infrastructure and people involved in supporting Ukraine among the potential targets.
The Kremlin views its relationship with Europe as a “systemic conflict,” said Omar Haijawi-Pirchner, the former head of Austria’s domestic intelligence service. Like others interviewed for this article, he said he expects an increase in drone incursions and hybrid attacks.
Advertisement
“We believe that Russia is currently under remarkably high pressure — probably higher than at any previous point during the war and at any time during Vladimir Putin’s tenure,” said a senior NATO official who was granted anonymity to discuss security matters.
“From the Kremlin’s point of view, the best option available to them seems to be to intensify the hybrid campaign they are waging against the West,” the official added.
Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent for WELT. Alexander Dinger is head of investigations at WELT. Richard Holmes is forensic investigations editor at the Telegraph.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: US invokes Iran war to unlock military aid to Egypt
articles.body:
US invokes Iran war to unlock military aid to Egypt
Washington has waived human rights conditions on $320 million in military aid to Egypt, citing the North African country’s assistance during the US-Israeli war against Iran. The move comes despite continuing concerns over Cairo’s treatment of government critics.
The State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying top diplomat Marco Rubio approved the waiver “in the interest of US national security.” It cited Egypt’s importance to Washington and security cooperation between the countries, AP reported.
A September 21 letter to congressional committees, cited by Reuters and AP, said Rubio “has made a determination to waive the certification requirement with respect to $320 million in FY 2025 Foreign Military Financing for Egypt.” An accompanying September 4 memo described the decision as essential to US security priorities, “particularly in light of Egypt’s helpful role following Operation Epic Fury.”
The memo did not explain that role. Operation Epic Fury is Washington’s name for the campaign launched alongside Israel against Iran on February 28. The war has killed thousands across the region, disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and driven up energy prices. Egypt has been working with other countries to mediate between Washington and Tehran. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty discussed proposals to de-escalate the conflict with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in New York on September 24, urging renewed US-Iran negotiations and safeguards for international shipping, according to Egypt’s Foreign Ministry.
Egypt has received around $1.3 billion annually in US military aid since the late 1980s, following its 1979 peace treaty with Israel, which formally ended decades of conflict between the two countries. Part of the funding requires certification of progress on human rights and democracy, subject to national security waivers. The military financing enables Egypt to buy US-made weapons.
The announcement comes after Egyptian security forces arrested six journalists from Matsadaash, an independent fact-checking and investigative outlet, late last month. The Interior Ministry accused the platform of spreading misinformation and having links to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement banned in Egypt as a terrorist organization since 2013. Matsadaash denied any political affiliation.
US-based democracy watchdog Freedom House rates Egypt “Not Free,” with 18 out of 100 points for political rights and civil liberties in its 2026 report. It claims government critics risk prosecution and imprisonment, and that press freedom and public assembly are tightly restricted. Human Rights Watch’s February report also accused Egyptian security forces of torture, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions. Egyptian authorities say they are improving rights, with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi emphasizing stability and meeting basic needs.
Aid restrictions have previously strained relations between Washington and Cairo. In 2013, the US suspended $260 million in cash assistance and deliveries of tanks, fighter jets, helicopters, and missiles after Egypt’s army removed its first democratically elected president, Mohamed Mursi, amid mass protests. Cairo condemned the decision and said it would not bow to American pressure.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden also withheld portions of Egypt’s military aid over human rights concerns before approving its full allocation in September 2024. It waived conditions on $225 million and released another $95 million after certifying progress on political prisoner releases, citing Cairo’s Gaza ceasefire mediation.

articles.title: Russian military strikes strategic bridge in Kiev – media
articles.body:
Russian military strikes strategic bridge in Kiev – media
The Russian military has targeted a strategic bridge in Kiev in a series of drone strikes, Ukrainian media outlets have reported.
The Pivdennyi Bridge (Southern Bridge), one of Kiev’s main road crossings over the Dnieper River, carries up to 90% of transit road traffic between Ukraine’s left-bank and right-bank regions, Strana.ua reported, citing a local official. It also serves as a key transport corridor for military equipment and other goods being sent to the front, the outlet added.
Russia reportedly hit the bridge in at least three drone attacks on Thursday, with the strikes targeting areas around its supports and roadway. Videos posted on social media showed major explosions at the site, with plumes of thick black smoke rising into the sky.
Initial inspections following the first two strikes found no critical structural damage, and surface traffic was subsequently restored. A later strike, however, damaged a bridge support, guardrail, roadway and the protective concrete structure surrounding the metro line, according to Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Traffic across the bridge was again suspended.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not confirmed the strikes on the bridge. Moscow has previously said its forces target critical infrastructure and logistics used by the Ukrainian military.
Ukrainian media and officials have been sounding the alarm over Russia’s new jet-powered Geran drones, which fly much faster than earlier propeller-driven models and are more difficult to intercept.
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range strikes against each other in recent months, with Moscow describing its operations as a response to a “pressure campaign” announced by Kiev over the summer. The Russian Defense Ministry has said its forces struck port infrastructure, ships carrying military equipment and weapons factories, including facilities producing components for drones and missiles.

articles.title: US boosting military presence in Middle East – AP
articles.body:
US increasing Middle East military buildup – AP
Washington is sending more warships and troops to the Middle East as US President Donald Trump is considering the resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran after the midterms, AP has reported.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that he has “to make a decision: either Iran signs a very fair deal, or it won’t exist any longer.” In a Time magazine interview published the same day, he said that new attacks on the Islamic Republic were “possible” after the US election on November 3, but declined to reveal any further details.
In its article on Thursday, AP said that a third aircraft carrier and some 9,000 additional service members, including 7,000 sailors and 2,000 marines, are currently on their way to the area of the conflict with Iran.
It would increase the US military presence in the Middle East to more than 20,000, which is “an unusually high number,” it stressed.
The forces on the move include the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, with the cruiser USS Chosin and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships, an unnamed American official told the agency.
With the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington already being deployed, three US aircraft carriers could be in the Middle East simultaneously as early as the end of October, according to the source.
Washington last had as many carriers in the region in April at the height of the American-Israeli missile exchanges with Iran. Before that, it happened back in 2003.
Axios reported on Friday, citing a US official, that it wasn’t yet clear if the USS Theodore Roosevelt would join the two carriers or replace one of them.
Washington also sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar in recent weeks, according to Axios. It was done to make it easier to get permission from Riyadh to use Saudi airspace for possible strikes on Iran, the outlet explained.
When asked by Time if the conflict with Tehran would harm the Republican Party’s chances in the midterms, Trump first acknowledged that “it’s possible,” but then said that “it should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
A poll by AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, which was published on Thursday, suggested that some 70% of Americans disapprove of the war with Iran.
After the initial US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic in late February, Trump claimed that the conflict will be over in a few weeks, but it’s still ongoing, with the diplomatic process remaining in a stalemate.
Trump told Time that he rejected Iran’s latest peace proposal, made during the UN General Assembly last week, because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
In September, Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases were only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

articles.title: Digested week: My heart sank at seeing Labour’s ‘Hope Again’ conference slogan. But then came Andy Burnham | John Crace
articles.body:
Monday
Words I thought I’d never write. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to the Tory party. Look, I know we ended up with Theresa May and Boris Johnson in the Conservative party leadership contests of 2016 and 2019 – and they were shockers, both of them – but at least the Tory MPs twice ensured we dodged the bullet of Michael Gove. Last week, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians and former senior civil servants and military officers. The setup was that the Russians had engineered an attack on a British warship in the North Sea and over the course of four episodes set in the Cobra emergency situation room, the assembled cast had to figure how to respond. We were left hanging at the final credits, but a nuclear apocalypse felt like the most likely outcome. And for that we have The Govester to thank. He was playing the prime minister and – to be blunt – he had an absolute shocker. For the first two episodes he seemed to be in a coma. All he could manage was to repeat back what the last person had said to him and then shout “asap”. But that was far more preferable to the Gove that turned up for the last two episodes. Despite frequently being warned about the dangers of escalation and the inadequacy of the UK war machine, Mikey kept on taking the option that would get the most people killed. Why bomb one Russian city when you can bomb two? The game ended with what were almost certainly nuclear warheads minutes away from destroying a major city in the UK. Still, Gove wasn’t the only deadbeat. Nicola Sturgeon, acting the deputy prime minister, was as hopeless as you would expect of someone who failed to notice her kitchen filling up with new appliances. It was terrifying TV. Not so much in the premise. What was really scary was the knowledge that our politicians were even more clueless than the rest of us.
Tuesday
Pep Guardiola timed his departure well. Perhaps he had an inkling of what was coming down the road. The top bods at Manchester City have predictably responded to being found guilty of 114 charges of financial misconduct by insisting they will appeal and drag out proceedings. No doubt hoping that either the charges will go away or they can reduce the potential penalties. I wouldn’t bet against it. My main reaction when the news broke that City had been found guilty was surprise. Not that I thought they were innocent – there wasn’t a football fan who didn’t think they were bang to rights – but that the Premier League finally got round to doing something about it. The earliest charges date back 17 years and it just felt as if nothing was ever going to happen. What happens next is anyone’s guess. Obviously any fine would be more or less meaningless as the City owners have bottomless pockets. Removing titles is equally pointless. Who would turn up for an open-topped bus ride for a cup won years ago? The issue of compensation is more nuanced. Because where does it all end? Can I file a claim for mental distress, not to mention the travel and ticket costs, for having paid to see countless matches which had been financially rigged against Spurs that are now null and void? There again, I have had two of my best nights ever at the Etihad. When Spurs secured a Champions League place for the first time and when we won a Champions League quarter-final thanks to City having an injury time goal disallowed by VAR. There has also been talk of a 50-point deduction. Probably not enough to ensure they finish behind Spurs. We’re only five games into the season and already 13 points adrift.
Wednesday
By a very rough calculation, I reckon I’ve spent the best part of six months of my life at party conferences. And yes, I am a lucky man to be doing a job I love, but it is sometimes hard not to feel a wee bit jaded during the conference season. Living out of a suitcase and listening to a series of speeches from politicians who can often barely hold their own attention let alone an audience’s, can make the days feel very long. And I was prepared for more of the same when I arrived in Liverpool for this week’s Labour conference. My heart sank when I saw banners, mugs and T-shirts with the slogan “Hope Again” everywhere. There’s nothing more guaranteed to see me sliding into despair then people loudly instructing me to look on the bright side. To make it worse, I had to endure the chancellor, John Healey, lie through his teeth and say “I am an optimist”. You’re fooling no one, John. He had clearly been told to be upbeat and dropped the H-word about 20 times. But on every occasion he gasped “Hope” it looked like a dagger had been plunged into his heart. Come the end, the whole audience was signing up to Dignitas. But then, Andy Burnham. By far and away the most powerful, emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech of the century. I can’t tell you how rare it is for a politician to hold an audience in his hands for an hour and say exactly what he thinks, feels and believes. Only Nigel Farage comes close, though what he offers is only anger, grievance and division. Burnham was offering something else. I may not have agreed with the details of all of it and most of it may never happen, but this was a world of social care, closer ties to the EU and electoral reform to which most in the socially progressive world could sign up. It was as though the sun had come out.
Thursday
When I turned 50, friends used to assure me that 50 was the new 40. That felt almost true. I can remember my Dad’s 50th birthday and he looked ancient to me. For my 60th birthday, those same friends were confident that 60 was the new 50. There was the slight drawback that I had already had a knee replacement, but I still went to the gym four times a week and my career was in good shape. Next week I will be 70. No one has even tentatively suggested that 70 might be the new 60. Seventy is unequivocally old. Some might even say that 70 is the new 80. I am now undeniably at the business end of life. My children are both in their 30s and have gone on to live their best lives. Much of my work as a parent is done. I had a heart attack two and a half years ago and am doing my best to avoid another one. My wife is being treated for cancer. Yes, I still enjoy my work and go to the gym four times a week but, as the great Leonard Cohen so exquisitely put it, “I ache in the places where I used to play”. It’s been weird watching the series 70 Up. I’ve always felt a kinship with the men and women in the documentary because I’ve followed them since I was 14 when they were the same age and felt grateful that my own life had not been part of the social experiment. But now we hear that 70 is to be the end point of the series. As though the lives have come to a meaningful end. I’m not quite so ready to go quietly into the night. I plan to keep going for a while yet. And for those of you who would like to join me trying to make sense of the world, there are still tickets available for my shows at the Komedia in Brighton on 18 October and at the MAC in Birmingham on 31 October.
Friday
My happy place. The Celebrity Traitors is back and all is more or less well with the world. The first episode may not have quite lived up to the hype but as a scene setter it was more than good enough. The side missions increasingly feel pointless – we all know everyone is in it for their ego and career rather than the charity cash – and in any case the celebs always need time to bed in and show their true colours. Though not Ross Kemp, who was showing worrying levels of paranoia from the off. Who will be the Alan Carr, a true star of the series? Who will be the Stephen Fry, all affected diffidence? And who will be the David Olusoga, the one who tried to work things through with careful intelligence yet always comes to the wrong conclusion? The first to show his face was actor Michael Sheen who declared that he didn’t know what he was letting himself in for and then said “I’m a huge fan of the game”. Hmm. Maybe he’s been watching with his eyes closed. The rest of the celebs trooped in one by one and we were up and running. Things soon hotted up when Claudia nominated Maya – never heard of her – and Richard E Grant as traitors. Richard was so thrilled – he had been desperate to be a traitor – that he promptly blew the show wide open by telling all the other celebs that he was a traitor. A move that may prove to be utterly inspired or catastrophically dim. Given a night to sleep on it, Richard was inclined to believe it might have been the latter and spent the rest of the day trying to persuade everyone it was a bluff. Sit back and enjoy the next five weeks.

articles.title: Putin Ordered Russian Military to Abandon Any Restraints on Airstrikes, Zelenskyy Tells FT
articles.body:

Putin Ordered Russian Military to Abandon Any Restraints on Airstrikes, Zelenskyy Tells FT
Russian leader Vladimir Putin ordered his military leadership in September to abandon previous restraints on air attacks against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times, citing intelligence obtained from intercepted Kremlin communications on October 1.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian intelligence learned that Putin issued the directive as Russia began sharply intensifying strikes against civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals and data centers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian President said the order came as Moscow stepped up attacks on Kyiv and other major cities, marking a broader effort to increase pressure on Ukraine through strikes far beyond the battlefield.
Zelenskyy pointed to the October 1 Russian drone strike on a school in Kyiv as an example of how widespread such attacks have become.
Children were inside the school’s shelter when the drone struck the building and sparked a fire. No casualties were initially reported at the site.
The latest Russian air campaign has also hit energy, communications and commercial infrastructure across Ukraine.
According to the Financial Times, the escalation has unfolded alongside Ukraine’s expanding long-range campaign against Russian oil refineries, ports, storage facilities and other infrastructure deep inside Russia.
Those Ukrainian strikes have disrupted parts of Russia’s fuel industry and brought the consequences of the war increasingly into Russian cities and regions previously considered far removed from the front.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence believes Moscow’s response has been to remove earlier limitations on how Russian forces conduct their air campaign.
Russia has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians, even as strikes have damaged or destroyed residential buildings, schools, hospitals and other civilian facilities across Ukraine throughout the full-scale war.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia has significantly intensified its aerial strikes against Ukraine during September, launching 3,177 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles compared to 2,850 recorded in August.

articles.title: Iran weighing options against US, Israel as nuclear talks stall, Israeli defense official says
articles.body:
Iran is weighing how to respond to growing US pressure as nuclear negotiations with Washington remain stalled, creating an increasingly complex regional situation, a senior Israeli defense official said on Friday.
"The Iranians are looking for tools within this campaign. They are asking themselves how they can get out of this situation. It is reasonable to assume that they are also discussing the possibility of influencing the elections in order to understand the other side," the official said.
The senior defense official said there had recently been a large number of unresolved incidents, some of which could potentially develop into attacks on the Israeli home front from a variety of directions, and not necessarily from Iran.
"There were many warnings and many nights when the system was occupied with clarifying the situation and raising and lowering the alert level. There were many nights of heightened readiness. Hezbollah? It definitely factors into Iran's calculations if Iran enters into a confrontation with Israel," the official said.
According to the defense official, the Iranians are constantly assessing the situation in the US and the extent of Washington's readiness to enter into a confrontation with them, and this affects Tehran's own assessment of the situation.
Economic pressure mounts on Iran
The official also stressed that conditions in Iran are deteriorating and that the effect of US sanctions can be clearly seen.
The number of tankers leaving the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz has been rising, and according to IDF data, an average of 30 to 40 tankers are now passing through each day. That figure reflects levels seen before the war. In other words, Iranian influence in the strait is declining.
The official also noted that the Iranian rial had reached a new low in recent days, with nearly 2.5 million rials now equivalent to one US dollar. At the same time, he clarified that Iran had not yet reached hyperinflation.
The official illustrated the economic situation by citing a critical article in an Iranian newspaper identified with the regime that compared the price of eggs in Iran with the average salary, adding that the cost of living in Iran was now "unbearable."
Compounding the economic pressure is what the official described as a US naval blockade of Iran that began this week. In addition to the sanctions, he said, the measure contains elements that are humiliating for Tehran because it prevents even family visits to neighboring countries.
As a result, the Iranians quickly approached neighboring countries and asked them to restore civilian flights. So far, according to the official, only Iraq has agreed, while there are currently no flights with Azerbaijan.
Israel prepares for risk of escalation
Israeli defense officials assess that Tehran is considering how to respond to the situation, what tools remain available to it, and what form its response should take. As evidence, they point to Iranian efforts to target vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that have so far failed.
The defense establishment believes Iran's range of options has narrowed significantly because of the naval blockade. This comes alongside Iranian attempts to carry out attacks abroad that have also failed, according to the assessment.
Israeli defense officials further assess that unless Iran attempts to break the blockade through a deliberate military move or reaches understandings with the US, it will be forced to contend with worsening domestic problems caused by the sanctions.
The IDF is therefore preparing for the possibility that an Iranian initiative could spiral out of control, such as a cruise missile striking a US vessel and causing fatalities, creating a situation in which it would be unclear how Washington would respond.
Israeli defense officials also assess that if the Iranians conclude that they are about to come under attack, or that the regime is losing ground in its confrontation with the US, they could potentially launch attacks against US assets in Jordan or Israel.
A senior official said the Iranians understand very well what the price of such a move would be, and that this is why they have not attacked Israel.

A Russian attack on Kyiv early Friday damaged the upper floors of a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district, killing one person and injuring two others, authorities said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike caused a fire on the upper floors of the high-rise, prompting emergency crews to respond to the scene.

articles.title: Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
articles.body:
Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
October 2, 2026
Two new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets landed in Taiwan on Friday, the first of a batch of 66 US-made planes ordered back in 2019 as the island nation looks to bolster its defenses in the face of threats posed by neighboring China.
The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at Chihhang Air Base near Taitung on Taiwan's mountainous east coast at midday local time (0400 GMT).
The arrival of the fighter jets was delayed by several months due to reported software issues, and Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more were on the way.
"Of course we won't only have delivered these two by year-end," he told reporters in the capital, Taipei, without providing further details.
"At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed tests," he said.
Taiwan fears drop in US support
The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan regarding the United States' commitment to arming Taiwan – and a week after US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
The US insists that there has been no change in policy towards China and Taiwan but Trump has stalled signing off on a new $14 billion package for Taipei. In May, he called it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with Beijing, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.
"We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan," said a US State Department spokesperson when asked about the new F-16Vs.
The jets, made by US defense contractor Lockheed Martin as part of an $8 billion sale agreed seven years ago, are equipped with advanced avionics, and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters — but Washington has been unwilling to provide its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35.
The Taiwanese air force, which scrambles on an almost daily basis in response to aggressive Chinese maneuvers, is expected to have over 200 F-16Vs once deliveries are completed.
"China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," said Defense Minister Koo, referring to Beijing's claims that the democratically governed island belongs to China.
The Chinese foreign ministry has not commented on the arrival of the F-16s but US officials told the Reuters news agency that a Chinese invasion before 2028 is considered increasingly unlikely in Washington.
Taiwan: locals welcome arrival of F-16Vs
That assessment didn't stop dozens of locals – some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras – gathering near the air base's perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.
"The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities," Eric Chan, a 57-year-old former air force servicemen, told the AFP news agency, referring to the Chinese Communist Party and stating that the F-16Vs will "play a very important defensive role."
"In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement," added Kimi Chi, a 37-year-old salesman from the central city of Taichung who had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft.
"But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots."

articles.title: US to deploy 10,000 troops, third aircraft carrier strike group to Middle East — newspaper
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 2. /TASS/. The Pentagon will deploy a third aircraft carrier strike group and additional Marine Corps ships to the Middle East, increasing the US military presence in the region by another 9,000 to 10,000 servicemen, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials.
According to the newspaper, the ships, fighter jets, Marines, and sailors are expected to arrive in the region by the end of November. The article noted that US President Donald Trump is considering resuming strikes against Iran after the midterm elections and recently told aides that he expects to resume the bombings in November.
The Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier departed San Diego on September 27 as part of a scheduled deployment. The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, consisting of three ships carrying Marines from the 13th Expeditionary Unit, also set sail on September 28.
Currently, the George H.W. Bush and George Washington aircraft carriers are already in the Middle East. If the George Washington remains in the region after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives, it will be the first time since April that the US has three aircraft carrier strike groups concentrated there at once.

articles.title: Speed up EU health security prep, says NATO chief medic
articles.body:
Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
SNEAK PEEK
— Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure.
— Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension.
Advertisement
— Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein,with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight.
Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter. This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe.
GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein.
Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference.
Advertisement
Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.”
Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.”
Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.”
Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care.
Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here.
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health.
Advertisement
On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting.
We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said.
Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.”
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
**A message from EFPIA: Fierce competition means the global life science landscape is shifting, demanding a bold response. The Biotech Act is an important signal of the kind of ecosystem Europe wants to create, but it cannot deliver change alone. Europe cannot expect to attract greater investment in medicine innovation while access remains slow and unpredictable. Read more.**
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure.
Recap: France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”
Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response.
Advertisement
Austria is on board: “As Europe… if we do not now see the need to act more [uniformly] and more together, I don't know when we should see it,” said Stefan Eichwalder, director of the health systems division at the Austrian health and social affairs ministry.
It doesn’t mean not doing anything: “It would be dangerous not to act now, but then I think we need to find ways of working together,” he said. Eichwalder added that it was important that national deals — with industry or the U.S. — do “not weaken the position of the EU, and in the end, the position of any member state within the EU.”
The bottom line: Countries should work together “no matter how difficult it is,” he said. “I don't see a solution for Europe to go 27 different different routes.”
Think this through: Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform, said countries should be asking themselves this question: If we were to accept paying higher prices, what can we get in return? “From a first reading of this agreement, France is committing to pay higher prices in return for what exactly? And what are companies committing to delivering in exchange for these higher prices?”
The bigger picture: “Many narratives are going around. Narratives that are used by different sectors to serve specific interests,” Natsis said. “And in this case, this narrative is used to ask and demand higher prices. But again, the question is: if we were to pay these higher prices in Europe… what happens to the other countries? Because if France signs an agreement, if Germany signs an agreement, what about the rest of us?”
Pushing back: Richard Bergström, vice president of European affairs at health data firm IQVIA and former chief of pharma lobby EFPIA, pushed back. “If you read the French deal… there’s a lot of wins for the governments as well,” he told panelists from the audience. “There are requirements on clinical trials, requirements on manufacturing in Europe, and most importantly, there is a gain at the end of life cycle.” It’s a “quite balanced deal,” he added.
Advertisement
OVER IN BRITAIN: The U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal — which is hailed by the Trump administration and industry as a blueprint for other European countries — is running up against some challenges, our colleague Caroline Hug writes in. Four pilots rolled out to try to meet U.S. demands to double medicines spending as a percentage of GDP by 2028 are currently falling short. Britain’s new Science Minister Chris McDonald has signaled the government is willing to try new ideas.
Pilots ongoing: The government — with industry and the U.S. administration — launched the pilots running through September 2027, and the results will inform the next drug-pricing scheme.
The line: “What’s really important here is that we start with what is the objective we want to achieve, rather than the means by which we want to achieve it,” McDonald told Morning Trade U.K. during a fringe event Tuesday at the Labour Party Conference. “I don’t mind trying things, and then if they don’t work, then learning from that and moving on and trying some other things.”
New blood: McDonald replaces former Science Minister Patrick Vallance, who played a key role in the U.K.-U.S. pharma negotiations. One pharma industry figure told MTUK that McDonald “brings rare commercial instinct to the policy debate.”
Deal mode: “It was quite hard to reach an agreement across the entirety of the industry [on pilots],” said Shaun Grady, AstraZeneca U.K. chairman, pointing to varying demands of some pharma companies versus big pharmas like GSK and AstraZeneca which “invest very significantly in the U.K.” He added that conversations are “now moving much more into a bilateral phase where each company will engage with the government.”
BIOTECH ACT
APPROVED: Parliament’s environment committee has confirmed its position on the Biotech Act, with 53 in favor of adopting the opinion led by Nicolás Gonzalez Casares and 11 against. It supported keeping a 12-month extension of patents under certain conditions. Parliament’s legal committee also voted to keep the one-year extension in its opinion.
Advertisement
Coming to the table: The co-leads on the Biotech Act — Vytenis Andriukaitis (S&D) in the health committee and Wouter Beke (EPP) in the industry committee — will meet in Strasbourg next week to try and find a compromise on the patent extensions they can bring back to shadow rapporteurs.
Making progress: Andriukaitis told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of Gastein that political groups will likely have “more compromised solutions” on supplementary protection certificates, cross-border clinical trials and financing for the law by the end of October.” Read more about what he said here.
Feedback: Shadow rapporteurs on the Biotech Act on Thursday submitted their feedback to the co-rapporteurs following a roundtable between MEPs, Commission officials and industry on Tuesday.
Remember: Some MEPs weren’t happy at being offered a roundtable in lieu of an independent assessment on the supplementary protection certificate extension (SPCs) while some NGOs were also upset they didn’t get a seat at the table. Catch up on the controversy here.
UCPM
COMMITTEES BOOST PREPAREDNESS, CIVIL PROTECTION FUND: Lawmakers in the health and environment committee adopted their position on the EU’s next civil protection mechanism (UCPM), which now includes health emergency preparedness and response.
Details: The compromise text boosts the budget of the mechanism from €10 billion to €12.42 billion, earmarking 40% of the funding for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility. The position was approved with 61 votes in favor, nine against and nine abstentions. It will now need to be put to a vote in Parliament.
Advertisement
Sneaky global health reference: The adopted text includes several references to strengthening global health infrastructure. For example, it says that “strengthening cooperation … as well as the global health infrastructure and the World Health Organisation is essential to enhance the global ability to act.”
WHAT WE’RE READING
There have been four more deaths from the West Nile virus in the Netherlands, the NL Times reports.
**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act can be an important step towards Europe’s life sciences future. Done well, it can make clinical research faster, attract more investment to Europe, help biotech companies scale, and ensure Europe is the place where the next generation of medicines is developed. However, it cannot deliver the change that Europe urgently requires in isolation. Access shapes where capital flows right from the start. When market access is slow or fragmented, investors notice and capital follows opportunity elsewhere. Reversing Europe’s decline in research and development investment would require sustained structural reform, stronger action at the Member-State level, and a rethink of how healthcare systems invest in innovation. Europe has both scientific excellence and talent. Now it must create the right conditions for companies to choose Europe as a place to research, develop and deliver new medicines to patients. If we get it right, the reward is higher growth, greater resilience, and better health. The choice is ours. Read more.**

articles.title: Russia Wants to Force Kyiv Residents Out of Capital, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russia is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and schools in Kyiv to force residents to leave the capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Speaking to Spain’s El País near a Kyiv school hit by a Russian drone, Zelensky said Moscow’s strategy is aimed not only at damaging the city but at driving out its population.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He also said Russia is timing its escalation around the US political calendar, with the US midterm elections serving as a key target for the Kremlin’s strategy.
According to Zelensky, strikes on civilian sites and schools are designed to create the impression of Russian strength while putting enough pressure on Kyiv residents to leave the city.
The president said Moscow was using tactics similar to those seen at the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, when Russia sought to seize or paralyze Kyiv and undermine Ukraine’s government.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko on Friday warned that the capital was facing an increasingly severe situation as Russian attacks continued to damage critical infrastructure, logistics, housing and social facilities.
“We cannot pretend that we can live as we did in peacetime,” Klitschko said after a meeting of Kyiv’s Defense Council, attended by military officials, the Security Service of Ukraine, emergency services and law enforcement.
“The enemy is destroying Kyiv,” he said, adding that Russia had also resumed attacks on the city’s energy infrastructure.

Klitschko called on the city’s services to coordinate their response, make measured decisions and provide residents with honest information about the situation.
“We are ensuring the city’s vital functions with all our strength under constant devastating attacks,” he said. “This is no longer about the usual comfort, but about safety and survival.”
Klitschko said Kyiv would “withstand the attacks” but warned that doing so would require a united response from residents and authorities.
Zelensky also acknowledged that defending against the attacks has become more difficult because of limited resources and gaps in the international sanctions regime. He said those gaps allow Russia to continue expanding its military capabilities, with support from China and India.
The comments came as Kyiv faced major transport disruptions on Oct. 2 following Russian attacks. Traffic across several bridges was partially or completely restricted, while at least four hits were reported on the Southern Bridge within 24 hours.

Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike oil facilities in Russia's Volgograd, Samara regions
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces strike oil facilities in Russia's Volgograd, Samara regions, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck oil infrastructure in Russia's Volgograd and Samara oblasts overnight, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 2.
The General Staff reported fires and explosions at the targeted facilities, including 'Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka' in Volgograd Oblast and the 'Samara' line-production control station near the settlement of Prosvet in Samara Oblast.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 2 that "successful operations" were carried out in the Black Sea and in Russia's Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd, Samara, and Krasnodar regions. Airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a missile and space center, and an ammunition depot belonging to the Russian forces were targeted over the last day.
"We are giving justified responses to Russia's escalation with our own long-range sanctions. Important results are achieved practically every day," Zelensky wrote on X.
Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko and the Exilenova Plus monitoring channel had previously identified the targets as the Volgograd Oil Refinery and the Samara oil distribution station, a major oil-transport facility previously targeted by Ukrainian forces.
The Volgograd refinery, owned by Russian energy giant Lukoil, is one of the country's largest oil-processing facilities, with an annual capacity of roughly 15 million metric tons of crude oil.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted the refinery during the full-scale war, including strikes earlier this year that damaged primary and secondary refining units and temporarily halted production.
The Samara oil distribution station near the settlement of Prosvet plays an important role in Russia's oil transportation network. The facility blends different grades of crude to produce Urals, Russia's main oil export blend.
Ukrainian drones previously struck the Samara station in April, causing a large fire and damaging five crude oil tanks, each with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters, a source in the Security Service of Ukraine told the Kyiv Independent at the time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 1 that Ukrainian forces had successfully struck an oil facility in Samara Oblast as part of a series of long-range attacks on Russian military and energy targets.
Ukraine has intensified strikes against Russian oil refineries, depots, and transportation infrastructure in recent months in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.

articles.title: Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
articles.body:
Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine could produce around 400 units of one model of high-speed interceptor drone for countering Russian jet-powered drones as early as October, but there are questions over their effectiveness.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the Financial Times, as cited by the president's press service
Details: Zelenskyy said F-16 fighter jets currently destroy 50-60% of jet-powered drones. This is one method, and Ukraine is working extensively to obtain weapons for the F-16s. The second method is high-speed interceptors. Ukraine is currently testing five interceptor models.
However, their effectiveness is problematic: it is 70% one day and 30% the next. Therefore, the answer to the question "When can we scale up the production?" is that Ukraine does not have billions to produce a million ineffective interceptors.
The main issue is the engines. Zelenskyy said Ukraine imports a lot and produces some itself, but these volumes are insufficient.
Quote: "So out of these five samples, some were used five times, some ten, and some only once. But you had one, and destroyed one Russian drone. This is the problem. I don't know the exact date, but in October, we will have 400 of these interceptors. And it is normal when you use 400 interceptors over several days of attacks, and you say, 'Look, guys, sorry, but it destroys only 10%. It doesn't work.' Or, for example, if it is 30% or more, 'Great, guys, you have to work a little bit on it, and when the percentage is 60-70% – huge success'."

articles.title: U.S. in mega deal to build more long-range anti-air missiles
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy has awarded Raytheon a five-year contract worth up to $24.4 billion to accelerate production of the Standard Missile-6, its principal long-range anti-air and anti-surface weapon.
Announced on 1 October by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, the multi-year procurement agreement includes two additional option years. The U.S. Navy says the long-term commitment is intended to give the RTX business the stability and predictability needed to expand production capacity, while delivering cost savings through a negotiated deal rather than year-by-year buys.
“Maritime strength demands weapons at speed and scale,” Cao said in the release. “This investment expands production and delivers the firepower our warfighters need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The SM-6 has become one of the most versatile weapons in the surface fleet’s inventory. Fired from the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, it can engage aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles in their terminal phase, and can also be used against surface ships. Its active radar seeker allows it to engage targets beyond the horizon of the launching ship when cued by other sensors, a key element of the U.S. Navy’s Cooperative Engagement Capability. U.S. warships have fired SM-6s in combat during operations in the Red Sea and Middle East since late 2023, including against Houthi anti-ship missiles, drawing down stocks of a weapon that costs several million dollars per round.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations, linked the contract directly to the size of the fleet’s magazines. “Combat credibility depends on having enough weapons, produced at the speed and scale the Fleet requires,” he said. “This SM-6 award gives industry the demand signal and stability to expand production, strengthen the munitions industrial base, and build the magazine depth our Fleet needs. That is the Foundry delivering for the Fleet – and ensuring our Sailors have the combat power to fight and win.”
The award is being managed by the U.S. Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) Munitions, an organisation responsible for the development, procurement and delivery of naval munitions and strike capabilities. It follows a recent Tomahawk contract, which the service describes as part of the same effort to speed up weapons production across the portfolio.
“This award demonstrates what is possible when the Department leverages innovative acquisition approaches to deliver capability at the speed of relevance,” said Van Hendrey, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions. “Through PAE Munitions, we are bringing together the authorities, resources, and partnerships needed to accelerate production, reduce costs, and strengthen the industrial base that supports our warfighters.”
Raytheon produces the SM-6 at its facilities in Tucson, Arizona, with final assembly at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. The missile has also been cleared for export to a number of U.S. allies, with Japan and Australia among the nations to have pursued it for their own air defence destroyers.
According to the U.S. Navy, the agreement will support a larger workforce, higher manufacturing throughput and stronger supply chains for the missile, as part of a wider push to rebuild the defence industrial base and keep Navy and Marine Corps forces supplied with advanced weapons.

articles.title: Ukraine's General Staff reports 207 combat clashes on front over past 24 hours

Ukraine's General Staff reports 207 combat clashes on front over past 24 hours
A total of 207 combat clashes were reported on the front line on 1 October. Russian forces attacked 30 times on the Pokrovsk front and 27 times on the Kostiantynivka front.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on X (Twitter), information as of 08:00 on 2 October
Details: A total of 207 combat clashes were reported over the past 24 hours.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, no Russian assault operations were reported. The Russians carried out five airstrikes, dropping 10 glide bombs, and conducted 151 strikes on Ukrainian troops' positions and settlements, including four from multiple-launch rocket systems.

On the Lyman front, Russian forces' attempts to break through Ukrainian defences were repelled. The occupiers launched three attacks in the areas of Nadiia, Novoselivka and Dibrova.

articles.title: US Announces $24.4 Billion Contract to Speed Up Missile Production
articles.body:
The Pentagon on Thursday announced the award of a $24.4 billion contract for Raytheon to accelerate production of SM-6 missiles as Washington works to replace the large amount of munitions expended during the Iran war.
The missiles are “critical anti-air and anti-surface warfare munition. This five-year agreement, with two additional option years, will drive faster production,” the Pentagon said in a statement.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The deal “provides the defense industry with the long-term predictability needed to expand workforce capacity and secure critical supply chains,” the Pentagon added.
President Donald Trump has so far brushed aside questions about the major toll taken on US munition supplies by the war against Iran, which the United States and Israel launched on February 28.
But the Defense Department’s inspector general said last month that “the munitions expenditure on Operation Epic Fury has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” using the official name for the operation against Iran.
And a September 15 report by the Congressional Budget Office cited the hit to missile defense supplies that “will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years.”
Raytheon confirmed in a statement Wednesday that their SM-6 “has been successfully fired from various US Navy ship-based platforms and launchers on land,” calling it a “combat-proven weapon.”
‘Never Hurts to Have Their Name on Things’ – Drone Startup Linked to Trump’s Sons
The weapons-maker also acknowledged increased efforts to meet demand.
“By continuously investing in our operations and facilities, we are removing constraints and boosting capacity to ensure we deliver this critical capability our sailors depend on,” Raytheon President Phil Jasper said in the statement.
Tehran continues to exert control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz more than seven months after the initial US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic, while Washington is blockading Iran’s ports.
Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran by late November, the Wall Street Journal reported, which would set the stage for further Iranian strikes and more expenditures of American munitions.

Putin warns Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in arsenal if any of its territory is attacked
Moscow has told Nato it won’t hesitate to use nuclear arms to defend Kaliningrad against attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal.
In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.
His remarks followed Moscow’s warning to Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia.
Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”.

articles.title: US looks to expand use of canoe-sized drones to deter migrant crossings
articles.body:
US looks to expand use of canoe-sized drones to deter migrant crossings
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 - The Pentagon may expand its use of autonomous surveillance boats on the Rio Grande and in the Gulf of Mexico after the canoe-sized vessels helped authorities detect and deter illegal border crossings and narcotics trafficking during a pilot program that began in January, a US official said.
The unmanned surface vessels, built by San Diego-based startup Seasats, patrol the river for long periods without crews and are part of a growing push by the military and law enforcement agencies to use relatively inexpensive, autonomous systems for surveillance and security missions.
The border mission also highlights how a new generation of venture-backed defense startups is positioned to win business once dominated by traditional contractors, as the Pentagon looks for faster, cheaper ways to deploy emerging technologies that can operate around-the-clock.
Defense officials are studying whether the boats, which draw power from solar panels, could be deployed more widely as part of broader efforts to monitor remote stretches of the Rio Grande. Aside from Seasats, companies named Saronic, Saildrone and Splash provide similar marine drones.
Defense officials want to increase the robotic fleet from its current test group of 10 vessels by as many as 50 to relieve the strain on Coast Guard cutters and crewed aircraft patrolling the border with Mexico as part of President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration.
Maritime drones are "cost-effective solutions to interdict and put people in these areas that narco traffickers are now moving towards," said M. Roosevelt Ditlevson, assistant secretary of defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs.
Small drones and other unmanned platforms have proliferated across the US military in recent years after their repeated successes in the war in Ukraine.
DRONES CAN OPERATE FOR MONTHS
Seasats' 11-foot, 340-pound Lightfish is a low-profile autonomous vessel that costs roughly $240,000 and can be launched from a boat ramp or the back of a pickup truck. The drone can operate for months at a time in rough seas.
The vessels carry sensors — including electro-optical, infrared and sonar sensors — that feed real-time tracking data directly into military software networks, including Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System and Anduril Industries' Fortress platform, alerting Customs and Border Protection and Coast Guard units.
The Pentagon said that in an average month, the Lightfish drones have assisted in 452 detections, 350 apprehensions and 100 turnbacks, which refer to when a group of people abort a border crossing attempt after realizing they have been discovered.
They "see that the vessel is waiting there for them, and they know that they've basically been found out," Ditlevson said.
The drone maker gained international attention in July when Reuters reported that a commercial Lightfish vessel operating inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone navigated close enough to a Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy guided-missile destroyer to capture detailed close-up video, demonstrating how low-cost autonomous craft can monitor multibillion-dollar military assets.
With continued success, Ditlevson said Lightfish orders could rise by 50 boats and potentially also operate in the Gulf of Mexico, forming a radar fence between Texas and Key West. But Ditlevson said use will expand in increments, exploring different technologies.
"We're agnostic to the vendor. We want the best technology," he told Reuters in an interview.
Seasats Chief Executive Mike Flanigan said uncrewed systems provide persistent coverage that traditional, fuel-heavy assets cannot match.
"A plane or a ship might go really far really fast, but if you say, 'I want to keep that Boeing 737 over a patch of ocean for a day,' it just can't do it," Flanigan said. "The boat doesn't cover nearly as much territory as fast, but it can stay there for months at a time, which is the key differentiator for these security and monitoring applications."
As tighter border security and targeted military operations have reduced drug smuggling routes, cartels have increasingly pushed into coastal waterways and near-coastal regions. The expanded drone use in the Gulf of Mexico is a precursor to testing the vessels in the harsher seas of the Pacific Ocean near San Diego. REUTERS

Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 drones - how many were destroyed
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 2, Russia launched 108 drones at Ukraine. Air defense shot down or suppressed 88 of them; hits were recorded at 11 locations.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 drones during the night of October 2. A total of 88 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What the enemy attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 2 (from 18:00 on October 1), the enemy attacked with 108 Shahed-type attack UAVs (47 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Bryansk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation, the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiyske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 88 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 11 locations, as well as the falls of downed objects (debris) at 5 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs in the airspace.

articles.title: South Korea unveils new laser combat vehicle
articles.body:
- South Korea publicly showed its Cheongwang Block 2 8x8 laser vehicle and a 100-kW towed laser prototype during Armed Forces Day events on Oct. 1.
- In a live demonstration, the Cheongwang Block 1 shot down two target drones, while two others crashed or were brought down before engagement.
South Korea put its Cheongwang laser weapons on public display for its 78th Armed Forces Day on Oct. 1, showing two new prototypes for the first time, but a live demonstration of the system already in service ran into trouble before the laser burned two target drones out of the sky.
The new hardware included the Cheongwang Block 2, a prototype laser combat vehicle built on an 8×8 wheeled armored chassis, and a prototype 100-kW towed high-energy laser designed to shoot down incoming rockets, artillery shells and mortar rounds. South Korea has not said how far along either program is or when they could enter service.
The demonstration at Gyeryongdae, the military headquarters complex in South Chungcheong province, used the 20-kW Cheongwang Block 1, a fixed-site laser that has been in service since late 2024. Four target drones were prepared. The first crashed on takeoff after a gust of wind damaged the fiber-optic cable used to control it. The second could not complete its flight in poor weather and flew outside the designated safety zone, so the military cut its power and brought it down.
The remaining two drones flew into the laser’s engagement area, and Cheongwang shot both down, setting them on fire as they fell trailing black smoke. Because the other two never reached the laser, the demonstration does not show how well the system would perform against a larger group of drones or in tougher conditions.
Cheongwang works by holding a high-powered fiber laser on a small drone until the heat damages its airframe or key parts and it can no longer fly. The main attraction for militaries is cost. Hanwha Systems, which helped build the system, has put the cost of a single laser shot at about 2,000 won, roughly $1.40, compared with interceptor missiles that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars or more. That figure covers only the electricity for a shot, not the cost of buying and maintaining the system, and a laser still needs enough power and cooling to keep firing.
The Block 1 was developed under South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development, making South Korea one of a small number of countries able to build its own laser weapon. South Korean officials say replacing an imported part, the laser oscillator that generates the beam, with a domestic one raised the system’s local content from 76% to 90% and increased its output from 20 kW to 30 kW. They also said the upgrade cut the time needed to bring down a small rotary-wing drone from two to four seconds to one to two, and for a fixed-wing drone from over 10 seconds to a few seconds. It is not clear whether the laser used in the Oct. 1 demonstration had the new oscillator.
The setbacks were not the first for South Korea’s unmanned systems at public events this year. On Sept. 16, several civilian drones, including a jet-powered one, crashed during an unmanned technology demonstration hosted by the Ministry of National Defense. In August, two medium-sized loitering munitions crashed into the sea during live-fire tests by the Republic of Korea Navy and the Agency for Defense Development aboard the amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado.
President Lee Jae-myung said at the Armed Forces Day ceremony that the government would speed up development of high-energy laser interceptors and artificial intelligence-based command and control systems.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Giant Samara Oil Hub—Fire Erupts at Europe’s Largest Tank Farm
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil-industry facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 2, as explosions were followed by a fire at what open-source analysts believe was the massive Samara oil pumping and dispatch complex.
Russian outlet ASTRA, after analyzing eyewitness imagery, reported that the blaze likely broke out at the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station, or LPDS Samara.

Residents across the region reported drones overhead during the night, while a missile alert was declared in the city of Samara at 5:51 am. A particularly powerful explosion was reported at around 6:30 am.

Reports also tracked a drone flying toward Chapayevsk, roughly 55 kilometers west of the Samara oil facility.
Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+ separately reported a fire at LPDS Samara and published coordinates pointing to the site.

LPDS Samara is part of Russia’s Transneft pipeline network and functions as a major storage, pumping, and crude-blending hub.
The complex covers more than 216 hectares and includes 71 oil storage tanks with a combined capacity exceeding 1.6 million cubic meters. Russian reporting has described the site as the largest oil tank farm in Europe.

Four major trunk pipelines converge at the hub, carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan before it moves farther through Russia’s pipeline system.
