articles.title: Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
articles.body:
Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
In August 2021, after the withdrawal of U.S. troops, the Taliban, an armed religious and political movement, seized power in Afghanistan. Active fighting has since ended, but life has hardly improved for many Afghans. The Taliban established a Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice and severely curtailed women’s rights. The authorities also tried to block internet access nationwide and ban officials from using smartphones. At the same time, the Taliban declared war on drugs, specifically opium, and it appears to be waging that war quite successfully.
In August 2026, Middle East scholar Ruslan Suleymanov traveled to Afghanistan to see how the country had changed over the past five years. He visited three cities and had dozens of conversations. Meduza has translated his report.
‘Russia? Welcome!’
“Get out of the car!” a Taliban fighter dressed entirely in camouflage tells me firmly, but without aggression, at one of the many checkpoints on the Herat–Kandahar highway. He asks me to follow him.
A local Taliban commander sits on the grass near the highway, surrounded by his aides. He takes his time examining my documents. When he realizes I have a Russian passport, his face lights up with joy, almost elation.
“Oh, Russia! Welcome!” the commander says in Pashto. Only a moment later do I notice that his left leg is missing. A prosthetic leg lies beside him.
He invites me to join him for tea from a thermos and even to stay the night. Hospitality is central to the culture of the Pashtuns, who make up Afghanistan’s ethnic majority and the backbone of the Taliban.
The roughly 500-kilometer (310-mile) journey from Herat in the north, considered Afghanistan’s cultural capital, to Kandahar in the south, where the Taliban movement originated in the mid-1990s, is much the same throughout: poor pavement — in places, very poor — document checks almost every hour, and enthusiasm at the mere mention of Russia.
That enthusiasm is understandable. Russia remains the only country in the world to officially recognize the Afghan government the Taliban formed in September 2021, shortly after seizing power.
For more than 40 years before the Taliban took power, Afghanistan’s roads were the scene of fighting, ambushes, and kidnappings. Today, long-distance travel around the country is relatively safe. Foreigners, however, are still better off traveling with someone local.
In 2026, Afghanistan ranks 11th in the world for terrorism risk, according to Australia’s Institute for Economics and Peace, which compiles the Global Terrorism Index. This is the first time it has fallen outside the top 10 since the ranking began.
In the first years after the Taliban took power, the main source of terrorism in Afghanistan was the Taliban’s bitter enemy, the Islamic State group — specifically its Afghan affiliate, Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISIS-K).
The group became known in Russia in March 2024 following the terrorist attack at Crocus City Hall in Krasnogorsk, outside Moscow, which killed 145 people. U.N. experts estimate that ISIS-K still has around 2,000 fighters. Afghans dissatisfied with the current authorities and people from Central Asia, mainly Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, periodically join its ranks. Over the past five years, ISIS-K has recruited at least 600 volunteers from those countries.
In any case, improved security is one of the few achievements the Taliban can claim over the past five years. That is partly because, before August 2021, the Taliban itself carried out most of Afghanistan’s major terrorist attacks.
How popular is Taliban rule?
In nearly 300 years of statehood, Afghanistan has yet to develop a shared national identity. “We remain a deeply divided community, but we are not yet a nation. Everyone understands the word ‘Afghan’ differently,” Amin, a 31-year-old employee of the nationwide radio station Salam Watandar, tells Meduza.
The main divide is ethnic. Broadly speaking, the country can be divided into Pashtuns in the south and Tajiks, Uzbeks, Hazaras, and others in the north. The government formed by the Taliban is almost 100% Pashtun. The Taliban’s reasoning is simple: the country is led by those who contributed most to the fight against foreign forces from 2001 to 2021. That means exclusively Taliban members and allied groups that fought most actively against the U.S. and its allies.
“Claims that our government supposedly isn’t inclusive are part of an agenda imposed by the West. Afghans are happy with their government,” an ethnic Pashtun employee of the Ministry of Information and Culture told Meduza, asking not to be named. But in private conversations with Meduza, members of six minority groups — Baloch, Qizilbash, Sikhs, Tajiks, Uzbeks, and Hazaras — said they lacked equal rights and equal opportunities to pursue their ambitions in Afghanistan.
Ethnicity, however, is far from the country’s only dividing line. At least 74% of Afghans live in rural areas or are nomads; only 26% live in cities. In rural areas and mountain valleys isolated from the outside world, ways of life have remained unchanged for centuries. The village elder or mullah commands the greatest respect and generally has ties to the Taliban.
That is why, under the previous government, most Afghans heeded Taliban calls to boycott elections. The militants called the elections illegitimate and threatened to cut off the fingers of anyone who went to a polling station. Turnout in Afghanistan’s last presidential election, in September 2019, was less than 20%.
The Taliban’s propaganda about defending Islamic values or fighting foreign invaders, meanwhile, met with understanding, if not approval, among local people.
“The front line used to run through here. Shells were exploding. Today I can grow potatoes and fruit,” Najib, 57, who lives on the outskirts of Lashkar Gah, the capital of Helmand province in southern Afghanistan, tells Meduza.
Najib’s father was killed in the mid-1980s during the Soviet invasion. In the late 1990s, he lost his older brother, who fought for the Taliban against the Northern Alliance — a coalition of northern warlords led by Ahmad Shah Massoud. In 2006, during the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan, his eldest son was killed after accidentally stepping on a mine on the road into Lashkar Gah.
“The war is over. For the first time in more than 40 years, we’re living in peace. That’s all I’ve asked the Almighty for in recent years,” he says. Like Najib, many Afghans are willing to forgive the Taliban for everything else because it has brought long-awaited peace.
‘We have to find a way to survive’
Before the Taliban took power, Helmand was known as Afghanistan’s leading producer of opium poppies. The province accounted for more than half of the country’s opium production.
In April 2022, Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered a crackdown on the drug trade. His decree said offenders would be punished under Sharia, or Islamic law. It did not specify how.
Over four years, the Taliban has achieved impressive results: the area planted with poppies in Afghanistan has fallen by roughly 95%, according to the U.N. In our conversation, Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani went further, insisting that the figure was 98%.
As a result, around five million Afghans across the country have lost a steady source of income. So far, the Taliban has been unable to offer them another way to earn a living legally. Unemployment stands at no less than 75%. More than 90% of the population now lives below the poverty line, and more than 70% of Afghans depend on humanitarian aid.
“We all used to grow poppies. The Taliban themselves controlled the sales and made huge amounts of money from them. We just got what was left over. But we could survive on that,” Ahmad, 62, who also lives in Helmand, near the city of Gereshk, tells Meduza.
He says that now, like many former poppy growers, he has to grow fruit and vegetables and take them into town to sell. “I used to earn up to 20,000 afghanis a month [about $300 at the current exchange rate]. Now I barely make 10,000 [about $150],” Ahmad says.
For many Afghans, that is a substantial amount of money. The U.N. estimates that the country’s average salary is now around $100. Meanwhile, prices keep rising, and inflation had already exceeded 7.5% at the beginning of the year.
Gasoline in Afghanistan now costs around 84 afghanis ($1.20) per liter, liquefied gas costs 66 afghanis ($1) per liter, and beef costs 500 afghanis ($7.60) per kilogram (2.2 pounds). Monthly electricity bills come to nearly 1,000 afghanis ($15.30).
The huge influx of Afghan refugees and migrants from neighboring countries, primarily Iran and Pakistan, has made the situation worse. Over the past three years, more than five million people have been forced to return to Afghanistan at those countries’ insistence, increasing its population by 10%.
Two of Ahmad’s sons, ages 23 and 26, spent several years working in construction in neighboring Pakistan. But Islamabad’s tighter immigration policy forced them to return home in late 2024. They now help their father harvest his crops and sell them at the market in Gereshk.
“Life isn’t getting any easier. We have to find a way to survive. What matters most is that there’s no war,” Ahmad says, alluding to the periodic armed clashes between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which have become more frequent over the past couple of years.
How has the Taliban changed
When the first Afghan state emerged in the 18th century, Kandahar was its first capital. It was also here, in 1994, that graduates of religious schools known as madrasas, mostly from neighboring Pakistan, founded the armed Taliban movement. By 1996, it controlled most of Afghanistan, including Kabul.
Kandahar, now often called the country’s political capital, is home to the headquarters of Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada, who also holds the title amir al-mu’minin, or “commander of the faithful.” He is consolidating his power, which rests on his high standing in the Taliban’s religious hierarchy.
Akhundzada relies on his own military guard and the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, effectively the morality police. The ministry was reestablished in September 2021 in place of the Ministry of Women’s Affairs. It enforces his draconian laws and restrictions, including those imposed on women.
Over the past five years, girls in Afghanistan have been barred from attending school beyond the sixth grade and from pursuing higher education. Women are also banned from beauty salons, fitness centers, parks, and other recreational spaces. The Taliban’s supreme leader has prohibited women from working in government institutions, nongovernmental organizations, and U.N. agencies.
Some Taliban members, mostly in Kabul, do not share the rigid conservatism of their leader, who once turned his own son into a suicide bomber. During the movement’s 20 years underground, some militant leaders lived in countries such as Pakistan and Qatar. They saw that life in a Muslim country could be very different — certainly different from Afghanistan under Taliban rule in 1996–2001.
Some militant leaders are known to have sent their daughters to schools and universities in those countries. These experiences changed Taliban leaders, who became less radical than their predecessors. This is especially true of the movement’s younger generation, those born in the 1980s and 1990s.
In February 2023, for example, Taliban Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani sharply criticized the supreme leader over the ban on education for girls, accusing him of “usurping power.” He later had to leave the country for several months, reportedly because he faced the threat of arrest.
Another member of the Kabul-based Taliban leadership, Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Abbas Stanikzai, also repeatedly called for girls to be allowed to return to school and young women to university. As a result, he was dismissed in May 2024 and later left Afghanistan altogether.
Kandahar itself is more conservative than Kabul. Most women here wear dull purple burqas that cover their faces completely. Boutiques and malls are rare, and most commerce takes place informally at simple stalls or carts on the streets.
Over the past five years, many of the movement’s members most loyal to the supreme leader have moved to this birthplace of the Taliban. Among them is Zabihullah Mujahid, spokesperson for the “Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan” and the Taliban’s public face.
Three years ago, we met in Kabul at the Ministry of Information and Culture, where he is deputy minister. This year, we met at a hotel in Kandahar.
“Education authorities are continuing their efforts. They are trying to create the conditions needed to resolve this issue, which is strictly an internal matter,” Mujahid says when I ask when girls in Afghanistan will be able to return to school beyond the sixth grade.
He says attempts to pressure the Taliban or force it to change any of its restrictions will never succeed. “We urge all countries not to concern themselves with Afghanistan. These are matters for our nation, and they do not concern other states,” Mujahid says, making his reluctance to discuss the subject clear.
He has more to say when asked about the “Islamic Emirate’s” relations with Moscow. “Russia has a very important role in Afghanistan. Russia also plays a very important role in our region, especially economically. You could say that Russia is needed,” Mujahid says. “Moreover, Russia’s recognition of the ‘Islamic Emirate’ government is a very important step that sets an example for everyone else. It shows Western countries in particular that there is no need to be afraid of taking such a step.”
The distance from Kandahar to Kabul is also roughly 500 kilometers (310 miles), but the journey takes a couple of hours less. The pavement is much better here, probably because Taliban officials themselves regularly use this highway.
There was once heavy fighting here, too, and kidnappings were frequent. In July 2007, for example, the Taliban abducted 23 Christian missionaries from South Korea on this road. Two were executed; the others were released more than a month later in exchange for Seoul’s commitment to withdraw its roughly 200 troops from Afghanistan by the end of the year.
Now, the only reminders of the war are the burned-out wrecks of cars and military vehicles occasionally visible beside the highway.
There are checkpoints roughly every 100 kilometers (60 miles), as well as at the entrance to Kabul. At the final checkpoint before entering the Afghan capital, security officers thoroughly inspect the car and record detailed information about every foreigner in a logbook.
As one might expect of a capital, Kabul is different from the rest of Afghanistan. Modern malls, fitness clubs, and fashionable coffee shops from before the Taliban’s return to power are still open. Before the Taliban’s return, those coffee shops were gathering places for Kabul’s cosmopolitan young people, hipsters, and LGBTQ people.
Strangely enough, the Taliban itself no longer shuns the trappings of Western civilization. This sets its members apart from their older comrades who controlled Afghanistan in 1996–2001. Back then, the militants banned music, confiscated photographic equipment and video recorders, forced people to follow a strict dress code, and held public executions in stadiums.
Today’s Taliban members happily take selfies, set up Facebook and Instagram accounts, watch the national cricket team’s matches, and order cappuccinos or lattes at coffee shops.
When Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered Afghanistan’s internet blocked in the fall of 2025 to “prevent immorality,” Taliban leaders in Kabul opposed the move, and service was restored after just three days. In June this year, the supreme leader ordered a ban on smartphones for government employees because, in his view, modern technology threatens Islamic norms and leads to “the destruction of the next generation.” From what I have seen, most officials, and not just in Kabul, still have smartphones.
Unlike in Kandahar, cafes and ordinary eateries in the capital also often show broadcasts from London-based Afghanistan International, the leading anti-Taliban TV channel run by Afghan exiles.
The militants in the Afghan capital also turn a blind eye to many of the restrictions on women imposed by the leadership in Kandahar. Roughly half the women in Kabul, for example, leave their faces uncovered and disregard the requirement to be accompanied in public by a male relative, known as a mahram.
Since August 2024, women in Afghanistan have officially been forbidden even to speak loudly in the street: the supreme leader ruled that “a woman’s voice is a source of impurity.” But this unrealistic rule is barely enforced either.
Perhaps the only thing women really cannot do in the streets is protest against Taliban rule. Immediately after seizing power in August 2021, the militants were shocked by the many protests by young women. Demonstrations took place in all of Afghanistan’s major cities, including Kabul, Herat, Mazar-i-Sharif, and Jalalabad. Typically, each drew between 100 and 300 young women.
This was largely a result of higher levels of education in the country. According to the U.N., primary school attendance among girls in Afghanistan rose from 0% to more than 80% between 2001 and 2021.
Now, at least 80% of the country’s 2.5 million women and girls of school age receive no education. In May and June this year, Afghanistan held entrance exams for public universities. A total of 120,000 applicants took them, without a single woman among them.
Nevertheless, an entire generation has grown up in the country with ideas about freedom, rights, and personal space that are completely different from those of the conservative Taliban. The Taliban, in turn, sees all of this as an intrusion by Western culture.
Can outside pressure influence the authorities?
“My life ended three and a half years ago. I’ll never forget that day. We were on our way to university classes, as usual, but people in uniform with assault rifles stopped us,” Shukriya, 24, tells Meduza, recalling the introduction of Afghanistan’s ban on university education for women in December 2022.
At the time, she was in her third year at Abu Ali ibn Sina (Avicenna) Medical University in Kabul. By now, she could have been working and supporting her loved ones. During decades of unrelenting war, it became commonplace for girls and women to support an entire family financially. But the Taliban’s return to power has made life much harder for women.
“For the first year, I was deeply depressed and thought about killing myself. I couldn’t imagine how to go on living. Even now, I don’t know what will happen to me tomorrow or how to build a life for myself,” Shukriya says. Women now account for up to 80% of all suicides in Afghanistan. Every day, at least one or two Afghan women take their own lives.
She says what kept her from suicide was knowing that she needed to care for her sick father and help raise her two younger brothers. At first, she wanted to work in a beauty salon, but the Taliban banned those, too, in July 2023. These were places where many young Afghan women found work, met, and spent time together.
Only men’s salons now operate openly in Afghanistan. Even the men’s faces on posters advertising these businesses have been painted over. Women’s salons continue to operate only in private homes, and their customers visit in secret, afraid of the “morality police.”
Shukriya now makes dresses to order and sells them through social media. “The money I make barely covers food for the family. But I’m getting more and more orders, and I hope to save as much as I can so I can leave and bring my loved ones with me,” she says.
Education for women and girls is one of the clearest examples of the conflict between urban and rural Afghanistan. Even before the Taliban returned to power, women in rural areas wore burqas, and girls were often kept out of school beyond the sixth grade. While primary school attendance improved dramatically in 2001–2021, average secondary school attendance among girls across Afghanistan never exceeded 40%.
Another source of tension is the Taliban’s particular understanding of Islam. Officially, the Taliban professes Sunni Islam, but its interpretation also incorporates the rules of the Pashtun ethical code, Pashtunwali. Under that code, a woman’s place is “either in the home or in the grave.”
Despite their extraordinary hospitality, Pashtuns fiercely guard their culture against foreign influence. Graffiti on a fence outside the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice in Kabul reads: “The hijab is a shield against the intrusion of foreign culture.”
The Taliban’s draconian laws have baffled even the Muslim world. In January 2023, for example, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the ban on university education for women “has nothing to do with Islam.”
During the Taliban’s first period in power, in 1996–2001, three Muslim countries recognized its government: the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. Today, even those countries do not. Nor does Qatar, which has hosted the movement’s political office since 2013.
At the U.N., Afghanistan is still represented by a diplomat from a state that no longer exists: the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. Taliban spokesperson Mujahid told me this was because “the countries that waged wars in Afghanistan, the countries that occupied Afghanistan, have political influence over the U.N.”
Further isolation appears likely to make life even harder for Afghanistan’s population. Five years of ultimatums and attempts to pressure the Taliban have failed and instead led to a sharp reduction in international humanitarian aid, from $4 billion to $1 billion.
“We want the international community to cooperate with the authorities in Afghanistan, who have ensured security and eradicated corruption, drug trafficking, and other forms of crime,” Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani tells Meduza.
For ordinary Afghans, particularly women and Kabul residents, all the Taliban’s achievements pale beside the restrictions imposed over the past five years. But they, too, see little point in trying to pressure the Taliban from abroad.
“The West was traumatized by its experience in Afghanistan and would rather forget about the country. All it does is try to lecture the Taliban. But they’ll never change. We need some other way to talk to them,” Shukriya says firmly.
“All I want is for people not to forget us or put all the responsibility on the Taliban. The world is responsible for us, too. Otherwise, our lives will become even more hellish,” she says.

articles.title: US sends third aircraft carrier to Middle East amid stalemate in Iran war
articles.body:
The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as President Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The deployment, which includes a specialist amphibious attack group, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as midterm elections in the US loom large.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation remains a viable option – despite his initial promises that the war would last a matter of weeks.
The group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines. It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, with its two amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to a US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
It is possible the Washington could move to seas off Japan, once the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group arrives.
In a Time magazine interview published on Thursday, Trump raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough”.
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican party chances in November, Trump at first responded: “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide”.
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

articles.title: DARPA wants AI built into running its biotech research
articles.body:
- DARPA awarded Systems Planning and Analysis a $10.9 million task order to support management of its new and ongoing biotechnology programs through October 2031.
- The order calls for AI-enabled support, drew three offers, and obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at award.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s research arm that funds high-risk military technology, has hired Systems Planning and Analysis to help manage its biotechnology programs, and it wants artificial intelligence built into how that work is done.
The Alexandria, Virginia-based company received a $10.9 million task order for operational and program support services, the U.S. Department of War said. The order covers technical, administrative, programmatic and financial management of new and ongoing biotechnology programs, carried out in what the notice calls an “AI-augmented, -integrated, and -enabled manner.”
The notice does not explain what that means in practice. It does not say which tasks AI tools would handle, which tools would be used, or whether DARPA requires specific software.
Work will take place in Arlington, Virginia, where DARPA has its headquarters, and is expected to run through October 2031. DARPA obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award. The order was competed, and three companies submitted offers.
The deal is a cost-plus-fixed-fee and award-fee order. SPA will be reimbursed for its costs and paid a fixed fee, plus an additional fee that depends on how DARPA rates its performance.
DARPA has no labs of its own. Its program managers fund outside teams at universities, laboratories and companies, and lean on support contractors for engineering, science, financial management, administrative and acquisition work. That support role is what SPA will fill for the biotechnology portfolio.
The notice does not name the DARPA office involved. The agency’s biotechnology research is run by its Biological Technologies Office, whose most recent office-wide solicitation, issued in October 2025, sought proposals in AI and machine learning for biology, combat casualty care, human performance under extreme stress, and bio-inspired materials and sensors. That solicitation stopped accepting proposals on Sept. 30.
SPA has done this kind of work for DARPA before. In 2023, it was one of six companies, along with Booz Allen Hamilton, ManTech, Amentum, ECS and Strategic Analysis, selected for DARPA’s Technical and Analytical Support Services II contract, a five-year vehicle with a combined $1.25 billion ceiling covering advisory work for all of the agency’s technical and support offices. DARPA received 12 offers for that contract.
Earlier this year, SPA won a five-year, $151.4 million contract to provide scientific, engineering and technical assistance to DARPA’s Information Innovation Office, which runs the agency’s AI and cyber programs. The company said at the time that it had supported DARPA for more than 17 years.
Founded in 1972, SPA employs nearly 3,000 people and is owned by private equity firm Arlington Capital Partners. Much of its work is analysis and engineering for the U.S. Navy, including the Strategic Systems Programs office that manages the service’s submarine-launched ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Poland is preparing a law on the state’s full readiness in the event of war - media
articles.body:
Poland is preparing a law on the state’s full readiness in the event of war - media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland’s Ministry of National Defence has drafted a bill to coordinate defence management and speed up the deployment of troops to a state of war. The document is undergoing consultations.
Poland is preparing a bill on the state’s full readiness in the event of war. The bill aims to streamline the national defense management system and accelerate the process of redeploying troops to critical locations. Rzeczpospolita reports on October 2, UNN writes.
Details
The Polish Ministry of Defense has reportedly drafted a bill on national defense readiness. According to the publication, until recently the title itself included the phrase "on the state’s defensive readiness for war." The bill is currently at the stage of interministerial consultations.
The country’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that work on such a bill is ongoing. According to the information, the aim is "to strengthen the defense capabilities of the Republic of Poland, improve cooperation between the armed forces and services responsible for internal security, and adapt existing legislation to modern threats, including hybrid, cyber, and disinformation threats."
"This is the preparation of the state for the pre-war period, which Prime Minister Tusk spoke about some time ago," said a source connected with the presidential center. It is reportedly intended to fill the gap between the functioning of the state in peacetime and the formal introduction of martial law.
Its aim is also to "organize organizational and legal arrangements and increase the readiness of public administration bodies to perform tasks during a state of permanent and full defensive readiness of the state, in particular by clarifying the duties and competencies of the authorities." The Polish Ministry of Defense notes that currently, decisions concerning the preparation of the state for defense and the functioning of the defense management system are scattered across several resolutions of the country’s Council of Ministers issued after the adoption of the Homeland Defense Act in the spring of 2022.
"This regulatory model makes it difficult to ensure regulatory consistency and a unified approach to the performance of defense tasks by public administration bodies and other entities participating in the state’s defense system. Another significant problem is the scope of issues currently regulated at the level of subordinate legislation. Some existing provisions directly concern the tasks, competencies, and responsibilities of public administration bodies and other entities performing defense tasks, which justifies regulating them by law," the Polish Ministry of Defense stated.
The purpose of the law is to increase the readiness of state institutions for the threat of war
The bill aims to streamline the state defense management system and improve the readiness of public administration to perform tasks in a state of permanent and full defensive readiness, that is, even before the official declaration of martial law. Among other things, this will allow the earlier deployment of troops, including allied forces, link Poland’s Defense Response Plan with the NATO Response System, and prepare infrastructure.
The law will also expand the number of organizations participating in the permanent service system and the national defense management system, regulate the rules governing the work of civilian officials in command positions with limited leave to return home, amend the planning of non-war operational activities, and amend documentation concerning defense programs. Amendments will also be made to the rules for training, defense courses, and defense exercises.
According to the Polish Ministry of Defense, "due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm." The publication’s conclusions indicate that the National Security Bureau (BBN) is also awaiting the submission of such a bill.

articles.title: Russian strikes undermine production of military products in Ukraine — State Duma deputy
articles.body:
SIMFEROPOL, October 2. / TASS/. Russian strikes on Ukrainian enterprises have shut down the steel industry used to make military products, which will hurt Kiev’s military output, State Duma deputy from the Republic of Crimea, Reserve Major General Leonid Ivlev said in an interview with TASS.
Reuters quoted the Federation of Metallurgists of Ukraine as saying that production in the country, which was one of the world's ten largest steel producers by the beginning of 2022, was stopped after the last enterprises were put out of operation.
"Ukraine's steel industry suffered as a result of targeted missile attacks by Russian troops on key metallurgical enterprises in the country, which effectively led to the cessation of production of various grades of steel, the most important raw materials for the military-industrial complex of the Kiev regime," Ivlev said.
He said that Russia had many times warned that in response to the Ukrainian strikes on its cities and energy companies retaliatory strikes would be launched against Ukraine's infrastructure facilities - ports, air bases, locomotives, warehouses and logistics chains. At the same time, not a single peaceful object was damaged.
Yulia Mendel, Vladimir Zelensky's former spokeswoman, said that in September Ukraine did not produce steel at all for a week, for the first time in 100 years. According to her, the export shutdown already causes losses of $200 million per month.
Steel industry in Ukraine
On September 22, Interpipe Steel pipe rolling plant shut down, and on September 18, Zaporozhstal and Kametstal became idle. Another large metallurgical enterprise, Dneprovsky Metallurgical Plant, stopped operations earlier due to financial problems (in January 2022, the plant stopped working, and in 2026, the process of declaring it insolvent began). Besides, explosions hit it in early September.
Metallurgy annually provides $6.2 billion in foreign exchange earnings for Ukraine (about 13%, second only to agricultural products), ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog paid about 8.5 billion hryvnias ($189 million) annually to the budget, Interpipe Steel - 5.56 billion hryvnias ($123 million), Zaporozhstal - 4 billion hryvnias ($90 million), Kametstal - 2.5 billion hryvnias ($56 million).

articles.title: Elon Musk to co-lead Pentagon's 120-day future-warfare study, Project Meridian
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump's government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war.
Musk served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he spearheaded sweeping job cuts across the US federal government, before departing in May 2025.
In a speech on Wednesday at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said "Project Meridian" will be "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
"We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists," Hegseth said.
Musk will be a co-leader of Project Meridian alongside Palmer Luckey, the 34-year-old co-founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries, and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year-old Republican former House speaker.
Musk's companies are already major Pentagon contractors, including SpaceX building satellite networks for Trump's planned "Golden Dome" missile defence shield.
His artificial intelligence firm xAI this year signed a deal allowing the military to use its Grok chatbot on classified systems.
Project Meridian's findings
In 2024, Musk threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, but the men later had a high-profile blow-up over the president's spending legislation.
The two have since reconciled, and Musk has again become a frequent presence at the White House, though less visibly than during his previous stint, when he often visited the Oval Office, most memorably with his young son on his shoulders.
On Tuesday he was seated next to Trump at a lunch with artificial intelligence executives, where he joined other tech leaders in signing a voluntary AI safety accord that the president described as "morally binding."
Last week, Musk attended the state dinner Trump hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in May he flew to Beijing on Air Force One as part of the business delegation accompanying Trump on his state visit to China.
He also resumed giving to Republican causes, including multimillion-dollar donations to individual candidates and conservative political groups.
Musk, who spent more than $250 million backing Trump and other Republicans in the 2024 election, has given at least $90 million toward November's midterm elections, according to tallies of Federal Election Commission filings.
Hegseth said the project's purpose is to "creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master."
Project members will include hand-picked private sector leaders and subject matter experts from across the innovation, academic and policy ecosystems.
Hegseth said he has directed Project Meridian's findings to be completed and submitted within 120 days.

articles.title: UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear legacy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear fallout legacy
The United States needs to take additional steps to remedy the nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands by providing healthcare and releasing secret archives, according to a UN report presented to its human rights body on Thursday.
The US, which administered the Pacific islands after World War Two, conducted 67 nuclear weapons tests in the Marshall Islands from 1946 to 1958, including "Castle Bravo" at Bikini Atoll in 1954
The human cost of these tests has been "severe and lasting", the UN human rights office report said, adding that there has not yet been a just settlement of the claims
"The damage needs to be repaired," Awa Dabo, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva
The UN cited examples of the ongoing impact, such as elevated levels of cancer, displacement from contaminated areas and lasting social stigmas affecting exposed persons who are referred to as "poison people"
The report called for the US to provide remedy in the form of healthcare and to declassify all information pertaining to the nuclear legacy
The US State Department said it had already reached a full and final settlement of all claims with the Marshall Islands in 1986 and said it continues to provide medical and cancer assistance and environmental monitoring programmes for those affected
"The United States has recognised the effects of its nuclear testing program and has accepted and acted on its responsibility to the citizens of the Republic of the Marshall Islands," the State Department said.
Marshallese residents, including Alson Kelen who was displaced from Bikini and lost both parents to cancer, addressed the council and called for a meaningful resolution to the legacy
The Marshall Islands' representative, Senator David Anitok, told the UN body: "The continued denial of an effective remedy has forced us to come before this Council to ask for help"
Washington disengaged from the UN Human Rights Council last year, alleging an anti-Israel bias, and its seat was left empty on Thursday

articles.title: NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
articles.body:
NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
Russia plans to disable Ukraine's energy system in three stages. This is according to a plan published by journalists based on information intercepted by Ukraine.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The plan lays out three stages of attacks.
The first is to disable substations near Ukraine's western borders that import electricity from Europe. The second is to disable hydroelectric power plants. The third is to disconnect Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants: Khmelnytskyi, Rivne and Pivdennoukrainsk.
Russia plans to use up to 1,000 missiles, drones and aerial bombs. The targets include substations, thermal power plants, hydroelectric power plants, boiler houses and other energy infrastructure.
The ultimate goal is to cut major Ukrainian cities off from electricity, heating and water supplies, potentially causing a humanitarian crisis.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa have been identified as the main targets. Russian forces plan to cut electricity supplies to these cities by 90%, reduce heating supplies by up to 90%, and seriously disrupt their sewage systems.
However, The New York Times notes that it is unclear whether Russia will follow the strategy outlined in the plan and whether it would succeed if it did.
Background: Ukrainian officials have said they are concerned that Ukraine does not have a sufficiently developed plan in case of large-scale Russian strikes on water supply systems.

articles.title: Half of Ukraine's F-16s undergoing repairs in Europe, with returns delayed – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Half of Ukraine's F-16s undergoing repairs in Europe, with returns delayed – Zelenskyy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that around half of Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets spend extended periods in Europe undergoing repairs and maintenance. He said the return of some aircraft is delayed for so long that Ukraine loses valuable time when the fighter jets are most needed to protect its airspace.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The president spoke about the difficulties Ukraine faces in countering Russian drone attacks. He said F-16 fighter jets had proved effective against new Russian jet-powered drones, but too many of the aircraft – around half – spend extended periods in Europe undergoing repairs and maintenance.
Zelenskyy also said Kyiv was seeking help from its Western partners to move more maintenance work to Ukraine, arguing that keeping the aircraft closer to the theatre of operations would allow them to be returned to service more quickly.
He stressed that efforts to keep pace with Russian drone capabilities were facing obstacles, including a shortage of engines for interceptor drones.
"Engines [are] the key, we really import a lot of engines. There are some engines of our production, but not enough," Zelenskyy said.
Background:
- In late September, Zelenskyy announced an agreement with Belgium under which Ukraine is to receive three F-16 fighter jets by the end of the year.
- He also recently told the Norwegian prime minister about Ukraine's need for air defence systems and support for its F-16 fleet.

articles.title: US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China
articles.body:
US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China
Amid threats from China, Taipai is growing concerned about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming the island.
The United States has delivered two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China.
The aircraft, built by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin, are part of an $8bn deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. They landed on Friday following months of delay due to repeated requests from Beijing to the US to stop arming Taiwan.

- list 1 of 4From ‘cheats’ to ‘great friendship’: How Trump’s rhetoric on China changed
- list 2 of 4US, China list goods recommended for tariff cuts following Trump-Xi summit
- list 3 of 4China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit
- list 4 of 4Arming an adversary: Why Trump’s offer to sell China weapons belies US policy
The jets, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (04:00 GMT) local time. They arrived a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Taiwan is eyeing a rising military threat from Beijing, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory.
“Of course we won’t only have delivered these two [F-16Vs] by the end of the year,” Minister of National Defence Wellington Koo said.
The arrival of the planes comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei.
The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.
Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding out on a new $14bn package for Taiwan, though he did approve one worth $11bn in December 2025.
Washington has said there has been no change in policy.
“We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about the delivery.
The F-16Vs, which received an upgrade in 2023, have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its J-20 stealth fighters.
However, Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan with its most advanced fighters, such as the F-22 or F-35.

articles.title: U.S. anti-ship missiles head to Japan’s westernmost island
articles.body:
- The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Japan's Yonaguni Island during the Keen Sword exercise, Kyodo News reported.
- Keen Sword is set to begin Oct. 19 and run 11 days, NHK reported, marking NMESIS's first deployment on Yonaguni.
The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island and about 107 km (66 miles) from Taiwan, during a major U.S.-Japanese exercise this month, Japan’s Kyodo News reported on Oct. 2, citing the Yonaguni town government.
The launcher will take part in Keen Sword, a large joint exercise held every two years. Japan’s public broadcaster NHK reported that this year’s live field training will start on Oct. 19 and run for 11 days, with both countries bringing their newest ground-based anti-ship missiles, and that it will be the first time NMESIS is deployed on Yonaguni, SBS reported.
Neither government has said how many launchers will go to the island, how long they will stay, or whether any missiles will be fired.
NMESIS, short for Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, is a U.S. Marine Corps weapon built on an unmanned Joint Light Tactical Vehicle that carries two Naval Strike Missiles. The missiles can hit ships at ranges of more than 185 km (115 miles), and the remotely driven launcher is designed to move between islands and hide, so it can threaten enemy warships from shore while staying hard to find.
The system belongs to the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment, a unit based on Okinawa that the U.S. Marine Corps reorganized to defend and hold key islands in a conflict. The regiment formally received NMESIS, along with the MADIS counter-drone system, in June 2026. Its Hawaii-based sister unit, the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, was the first to field NMESIS in late 2024 and took it to the Philippines for the Balikatan exercise.
NMESIS first arrived in Japan in July 2025. During the Resolute Dragon exercise that September, Marines moved a launcher to Ishigaki, about 240 km (150 miles) from Taiwan, and displayed it alongside Japan’s Type 12 anti-ship missile at the Japanese base there, though no missiles were fired. Yonaguni is closer to Taiwan still.
Japan has stationed troops on Yonaguni since 2016, when a Ground Self-Defense Force coastal surveillance unit and radar began operating there. Tokyo announced in February 2026 that it plans to place surface-to-air missiles on the island by 2031. The 12th Marine Littoral Regiment has also used the island before, deploying its AN/TPS-80 G/ATOR radar to the Japanese base there during Resolute Dragon in 2024.

articles.title: Inside Washington's tougher position on Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Inside Washington's tougher position during the latest talks with Iran
Just a few weeks ago, the administration of US President Donald Trump was prepared to reach a deal with Iran that would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz. But, today, it is rejecting in the current negotiations with Iran what it had been prepared to accept less than three months ago.
On 26 September, Trump publicly rejected a ceasefire proposal from Iran that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for lifting the US naval blockade, ending sanctions on oil exports and resuming nuclear negotiations. He said Iran was losing badly and wanted to reach a deal.
So what changed for the Trump administration?
The United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports on 13 April, before Trump announced on 19 August the start of what he described as the "most crushing economic operation ever"; part of a broad campaign of economic warfare and isolation against Iran, which included sanctions on banks, companies and importers, a ban on Iranian aviation, coordination with foreign countries and threats of sanctions against countries cooperating with Tehran.
Trump and his team believe the United States can achieve more by waiting and tightening the military naval blockade and economic sanctions.
His administration and Treasury Department officials estimate that the amount of Iranian oil available at sea will run out by the end of next week, which will increase Tehran's hardship and may push it to make further concessions.
The US president said earlier this week that he does not know "whether the Iranians will surrender now, but they will surrender".
On Sunday, 27 September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in comments to Fox News that the blockade on Iran was succeeding and that the remaining Iranian oil at sea amounted to no more than an additional 15 million barrels and expected the final shipments to reach China within the next two weeks, adding that "after that, it will have nothing left to bargain with".
Iran already acknowledges that the new sanctions are highly effective, although it has stressed that surrender is impossible.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in comments to Fox News on Sunday, on the sidelines of his attendance at United Nations meetings, "One of the problems we face is that our money is being held in China."
"We cannot even recover our money from countries to which we exported goods," he added.
No shipment of Iranian crude oil has passed outside the US-imposed blockade area since 14 July, according to data from tracking companies.
The figures cited by the US Treasury secretary also match shipping-tracking data.
Data from Kpler, according to what was published by The Wall Street Journal, showed that the amount of Iranian crude oil aboard tankers at sea outside the blockade area stood at 29 million barrels on 1 September, compared with 90 million barrels in mid-July.
It is expected the supply to run out by mid-October and the flow of payments to stop by mid-March next year.
President Trump argues that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to pre-war levels and has again called for Tehran's surrender.
However, Kpler data published by Reuters indicate that total volumes leaving through the strait amounted to about 9.7 million barrels out of a total of about 16.3 million barrels of oil exported by major Middle Eastern oil producers during September, compared with 19.5 million barrels in February.
The remaining volume is being transported through alternative routes.
Paulo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University, told The New Arab that the reason for the notable change and tougher US position is that Washington has found a pressure point that is actually affecting Iran.
"As the blockade continues and its actual effects on the Iranian economy begin to emerge, Washington is no longer prepared to accept what it had previously agreed to," he said.
He further explained that the US realised that the economic blockade and sanctions were actually working, and that they were the strongest pressure tool, with Iran suffering the most, in turn led them to see any negotiations to lift the blockade in return for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of initial talks as "unacceptable at the present time".
Schirach added that months ago, Washington could have accepted a deal that would have reopened the strait to end the war and the impasse that had led to Iran controlling it.
He also noted that the factor of time is now in the US' favour, saying that "the current stalemate serves the pressure on Iran", and that the US blockade is working effectively despite Iranian claims that the domestic situation remains stable.
"The blockade prevents the movement of goods through Iranian ports and prevents Tehran from selling oil as usual, despite the existence of land routes and railways with China," he said.
He pointed to another variable, namely that Washington believes it has, to some extent, secured "the use of the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool".
"The United States has succeeded in escorting oil tankers through the strait so that traffic has become more than 75% of what it was before the war," he added.
Schirach also noted that "global markets have begun to adapt and no longer see the situation as an existential threat, unlike what Tehran had sought by using the strait as a tool to impose its conditions".
He estimated that the chances of reaching an agreement at the current time appear extremely slim, given the wide gap between the two sides' positions.
He pointed out that Washington's current goal is the complete halt of Iran's nuclear programme, while Tehran refuses to completely give up enriched uranium.
Iranian demands go far beyond what Washington can accept, such as the release of frozen assets and the closure of military bases, which he described as "ridiculous".
Although the Iranians have extensive experience in dealing with sanctions and pressure, they have not faced a crisis like the current one or such a large and highly complex and interconnected set of sanctions, according to the US researcher.
He argued that the continuation of the blockade for several more months could put the regime before a genuine survival crisis, and they may rely on land routes through the Caucasus, but this will not compensate for the losses.
Schirach also noted that the United States has "a lack of patience in dealing with long-term conflicts, especially as the current situation affects public opinion and citizens, which could save Tehran before its economy completely collapses".
President Trump shared on his platform on Monday an analysis written by Alexander Stahl, an investor and energy analyst, arguing that Iran had lost the Strait of Hormuz as a pressure tool and that oil levels had returned to pre-war levels.
However, Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International Studies who specialises in Iranian political economy and the effects of sanctions, wrote on X, pointing to several factors that go beyond the issue of control over the strait alone.
"Yes, Iran may no longer be able to disrupt the flow of energy as effectively as it did during the first phase of the war, but it still retains a significant ability to destroy assets (in the Middle East), including production, refining and distribution infrastructure," he said.
He added that saying Iran had lost control overlooks the fact that it can still escalate and target these facilities if it believes it needs to send a message that it can inflict damage that forces Trump to accept the diplomatic options on the table.
He cited the 2019 attacks on Aramco facilities in Abqaiq and Khurais.
He noted that Trump's unpredictable and volatile approach and his strong insistence on victory in the war could push Iran towards escalation.
He also said that the strait is not the main source of Iranian leverage in this war, but rather Iranian attacks on infrastructure, countries and US bases.
He added that this is being downplayed because acknowledging it would mean recognising the United States' inability to neutralise Iran's capabilities.
He warned that Iran could resort to a "scorched earth" policy if the current situation continues for a long period.
He said, "The US Navy can certainly escort ships at great cost and ensure the continued flow of oil, but the deeper problem remains unresolved, which is the failure of US security guarantees across the Gulf region, and this gives Iran leverage in negotiations."

articles.title: In 2027 budget, Kremlin readies for long war
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to Vlast! This is a special edition newsletter looking at the record defense spending in Russia’s recently-released 2027 budget.
There is no paywall this time! If you want to support our work, please consider upgrading to paid.
⏳ This newsletter contains 727 words and will take approximately 3 minutes to read. It was translated and edited by Howard Amos.
The Russian government submitted to parliament on Wednesday a 3-year draft budget that included a post-Soviet record for defense spending in 2027. The huge resources being committed suggest that the Kremlin does not expect the war with Ukraine to end any time soon—and may even be preparing to expand the conflict.
“This is an ultra-militarized budget,” an official who worked on the document told Vlast.
Spending on what the government terms “national defense” next year will be significantly higher than expected, according to the draft, amounting to about 17.1 trillion rubles ($196 billion), or 6.9 percent of projected GDP. When spending on “national security” (the police, National Guard, and intelligence agencies) is added, a staggering 44 percent of Russian spending in 2027 (8.8 percent of GDP) will be related to the military and security services. That is an absolute record.
Before the full-scale invasion, Russia’s defense bill was far lower. Between 2011 and 2022, 29 percent of all spending went toward the military and security services (5.3 percent of GDP).
It’s important to remember that real spending in 2027 is likely to be even higher. Over the course of the war in Ukraine, Finance Ministry planners have repeatedly lowballed defense spending. Notably, the budget deficit was almost five times higher than the official target in 2025, and grew 52 percent between January and August this year.
According to the official who took part in drafting the budget, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and warehouses earlier this year influenced the decision to make such big increases. “This was all happening in the spring and summer, precisely when the budget was being prepared,” he said.
The defense spending plans come despite the Finance Ministry expecting a decline in oil and gas revenues this year and next. According to official estimates, oil and gas revenue will be at historic lows: just 16.2 percent of total revenue in 2026 and 16.6 percent in 2027.
Where will the Kremlin get the money for defense?
First, tax increases are planned for next year (although they will not be as big as recent ones). The Kremlin wants to increase taxes on income earned from securities and bank deposits, as well as tax companies that earn extra income from the sale of gold, some base metals, and fertilizers amid higher global commodity prices. Russian mining and fertilizer companies will pay a 30 percent windfall tax, while gold producers will pay 20 percent.
Second, social spending and investment will fall. This clearly shows that the Kremlin does not have enough money to finance both the war and social and economic development projects—and that it is prioritizing the war. In previous years, the authorities had avoided across-the-board cuts to non-military spending.
Finally, almost the entire budget deficit in 2027 (as well as the unplanned increases to the deficit this year) will be financed via government debt. For the first time in modern Russian history, public debt will exceed 20 percent of GDP (it was about 15 percent before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022).
The unveiling of Russia’s budget—which now needs to be rubber-stamped by parliament and then signed into law by President Vladimir Putin—has coincided with increasingly aggressive rhetoric from the Kremlin.
“After everything they [Ukraine] have done, we will think twice about what we need to do in response,” Putin said last month in response to a question about resuming negotiations. And, speaking on Thursday, Putin rejected a proposal from Kyiv and Washington for a halt to mutual energy infrastructure strikes, calling it “absurd.” In recent weeks, Russia has attacked energy facilities, data centers, and other infrastructure across Ukraine. Strikes on Kyiv have been an almost daily occurrence, with regular civilian casualties.
This newsletter was compiled with input from a journalist who wished to remain unidentified for security reasons.

articles.title: Australian Corvo Strike Interceptor Drone Receives Combat Payload Simulator Module
articles.body:
The Australian company NIOA has developed a training version of the combat payload for the Corvo Strike interceptor drone from SYPAQ Systems.
This was reported by NIOA.
The new system will be unveiled for the first time at the Land Forces 2026 international defense exhibition, which will take place October 6-8 in Perth.
The development is intended to conduct full-scale flight tests of the interceptor and collect telemetry data prior to proceeding to qualification tests of the combat version of the equipment.
The training module functionally replicates the future combat system and includes an electronic unit with telemetry transmission, a non-contact fuze, an inert electronic prevention, guidance, and activation device, as well as an inert mass-and-size simulator of kinetic munitions.
This allows for flight testing of a virtually complete interceptor configuration without the use of an explosive warhead.
The Corvo Strike itself is being developed by the Australian company SYPAQ Systems as part of the Mission Syracuse program run by the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator (ASCA). The program’s goal is to accelerate the development of Australian weapons capable of engaging small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with subsequent integration into the LAND 156 comprehensive UAV countermeasures system.
In April 2026, the Australian government awarded SYPAQ Systems 10.4 million Australian dollars for the system’s further development.
When announcing the contract, Australian Minister for Defense Industry Pat Conroy stated that the system is intended to be capable of intercepting attack UAVs, particularly Shahed-class drones.
In addition to the kinetic Corvo Strike, Mission Syracuse incorporates Fractl laser systems from AIM Defence, which were ordered in March 2024. In April 2026, the Australian government announced that it plans to allocate up to AUD 7 billion over the next decade to develop counter-UAV capabilities.
According to the company, the training module for the Corvo Strike NIOA will be unveiled for the first time at the Land Forces 2026 exhibition in Perth, where it will be displayed alongside the combat version at the company’s booth #4G16. The exhibition will take place from October 6 to 8, 2026, at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre.
SYPAQ continues to develop the Corvo family to meet the needs of the Australian Defense Force. In May 2026, the company delivered Corvo X drones to the Australian Army — vertical takeoff and landing aircraft designed to operate in challenging weather conditions.
In addition, in September, two Australian companies joined forces to develop and manufacture Arrow interceptor drones for delivery to Ukraine.

articles.title: The humans behind AI warfare
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The human and political choices behind AI warfare
Gaza is an AI-enabled genocide. But more importantly, humans are ultimately making the decision about who lives and dies.
The AI apocalypse in warfare may be coming, but I want people to think more about the humans who are behind warfare now and in the future.
I've written about the Palestine Laboratory for well over a decade, investigating how Israel trials, tests and markets its surveillance technology, its weapons and its military systems on Palestinians in Palestine, Gaza, the West Bank and beyond, and then sells them around the world to dictatorships and democracies, from Rwanda to India to Saudi Arabia.
And one of the things that often comes up is what we see in Gaza. Gaza is an AI-enabled genocide, but more importantly, humans are ultimately making the decision about who lives and dies. It is not being made by machines alone, at least not yet.
One of the most disturbing aspects of Israel's genocide in Gaza is, yes, the use of AI-enabled tools, quadcopters, Silicon Valley cloud companies such as Google, Microsoft and Amazon, and AI firms such as Palantir and Anthropic. They use huge amounts of data that ultimately goes to the Israeli military, which is still making the decision, sometimes with only 10 or 20 seconds to spare.
Who dies? Who lives? How many civilians are deemed acceptable to kill? That's why we have 70,000, 80,000, 90,000, 100,000 Palestinians dead, the vast majority of whom are civilians. It's why we see mass carnage in southern Lebanon.
It's why we see carnage in Iran.
It's why we see increasing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, partly enabled by AI software. One of the issues I see discussed so often these days in relation to US wars in the Middle East, and Israel's wars as well, is the idea that we should worry when machines take over. And yes, we should worry about that.
But how about worrying about the humans who are behind these systems now?
All the data being processed by these companies originally comes from people, from human beings. Yes, it's gathered through social media data, mobile phone information and a range of other sources.
But ultimately, humans are making the decisions. One of the things I worry about is that people ignore the ideology behind these companies.
So many of these firms, not least companies like Palantir, Anthropic and others, view their role as supporting and advancing Western supremacy. And it's that ideology that we should be opposing, not just the idea of weapons taking over the world and killing huge numbers of civilians.
